news.title: Must-read book that tells the stories behind inspiring gardens
news.text:
So to flick through the pages of Stephanie Mahon and her husband John Campbell’s new book, The Creative Gardener: Inspiring People, Remarkable Gardens (Quarto/Frances Lincoln, c €49, hardcover), is a treat for many reasons, not least because it highlights the hard graft, ingenuity, love and fierce effort that those featured amongst its pages have personally poured into the plots they tend. 

None are household names in the way that a rock star, famous actor, technocrat or billionaire might be, although a few will be familiar to some readers, such as the food writer Nigel Slater; the floral artist Bex Partridge; the Wicklow gardener, educator and social campaigner Jimi Blake of Hunting Brook Gardens; and the Cork-born, London-based garden designer and ceramic artist Declan Buckley.

Of the 30 individuals featured, many came to gardening by a circuitous route, such as the garden designer Sarah Price and the flower-farmer-florist Rachel Siegfried who both originally trained in fine art; Charlie Harpur, head gardener at Knepp who studied architecture; the landscape designer Thomas Blunt whose CV includes a stint as a dog-sledding guide in Canada and an unfinished degree in biochemistry; the Afghan war veteran turned professional horticulturist and head gardener Joshua Sparkes, and the former rock critic turned garden writer Alice Vincent. Others featured, such as the singer Kyla La Grange, discovered a love of gardening in adulthood, sometimes giving up well-paid, well-established careers to pursue professional horticulture in one shape or another.

What they share in common is that the gardens they tend are their spiritual touchstones, the places where they go to nurture their creativity and find a soothing, salving retreat from the relentlessness of modern life. By vividly sketching their stories, including the various tribulations along the way, Mahon gives a great sense of the intensity and intimacy of that relationship and how it feeds their life force. The elegant, atmospheric photography by John Campbell beautifully reinforces this, providing a rich sense of place and of people.

In a world where social media relentlessly markets "perfection" as the bar we all should aim for, The Creative Gardenerserves as a valuable reminder of the endless joy that gardening gives when we give up that fruitless pursuit. 

Real gardens, as Mahon says in her thoughtful introduction, aren’t perfect, just as life is never perfect, nor is perfection possible or indeed even desirable: "Every gardener works within limits, whether it’s the size of their plot or budget, their soil or aspect, or having to also manage full-time jobs, young children, illness or grief.” 

It’s also important proof of how the best gardens gradually evolve in parallel with those who tend them. 

One of the oldest gardeners featured in the book is the topiary artist Charlotte Molesworth (whom I coincidentally referenced in this column just a few weeks ago). 

She and her husband Donald have spent 40 years creating their wonderfully idiosyncratic garden at Balmoral Cottage, a place filled with giant topiary specimens reminiscent of the movie Edward Scissorhands that the couple grew from tiny cuttings and baby plants.

When they bought the property as a young, almost penniless married couple, it was “small and almost derelict, with a leaking roof, wonky foundations, bad wiring, one meagre lightbulb, and a Rayburn for warmth.” 

Unable to get a conventional mortgage, Donald instead agreed a payment plan with the sellers, who also happened to be his employers. 

Surviving on a tiny household budget, they succeeded in creating a uniquely magical space by dint of decades of hard work, patience, artistry, and a deep-rooted love of gardening, honing their considerable skills along the way.

Jonny Bruce, the British nurseryman, garden writer and botanical artist who tends the world-famous garden of Prospect Cottage, the starkly beautiful creation of the filmmaker and author, the late Derek Jarman, also features in the book. 

He too studied fine art as a young man but was considering dropping out of college when he headed to Italy one summer and found work in the gardens of Villa La Pietra. 

Being surrounded by the beauty of Florence’s historical gardens turned out to be a lightbulb moment that led him to Dungeness and a garden he describes as having "grown out of the landscape". 

Bruce eventually took on the role of its steward, balancing the responsibility to preserve Jarman’s unique vision with the need of any living garden to continue to evolve and change.

That’s equally true of John Little’s endlessly experimental garden, Hilldrop, where biodiversity and habitat creation are every bit as important as beauty. Campbell’s photograph of Little’s old blue Citroën van half-buried in the ground and surrounded by a drift of hops, sweet pea, and teasels tells us a thousand words about his maverick approach to the art of garden making.

In short, if you’re looking for a "how to" gardening book, this is not it. Instead, The Creative Gardeneris unabashedly a "why to" gardening book, and beautiful for it. To quote Mahon: "The key lessons I have learned from my time with these generous and talented people are these: be curious, be patient, be bold…and just care.”
news.summary: The 30 people featured in 'The Creative Gardener' treat their plots as their spiritual touchstones, writes Fionnuala Fallon
news.author: Charlotte Molesworth,Irishexaminer.com

news.title: Mother alleges addict son threatened ‘to burn the house down and kill me’
news.text:
A mother who said her adult son threatened “to burn the house down and kill me” after bursting into the family home demanding money from her obtained a barring order against him.

Aged in his 40s, her son is on crack cocaine, and the incident happened shortly after his recent release from prison, his mother told the emergency domestic violence court at Dolphin House in Dublin.

During the incident, he wrestled her phone from her when she was trying to call the gardaí and took money from her purse in front of her, she said.

“I’m afraid to sleep in my own home because he has smashed windows and doors.” 

A young relative lives with her, and her daughter regularly visits with her children, the woman added.

Judge Gerard Furlong granted the woman’s ex parte (one side only represented) application for an interim barring order (IBO). The case will return to court later this month when the son can either oppose or consent to a full barring order for a maximum of three years.

The woman was among several parents who came to court on Friday seeking emergency orders, under the Domestic Violence Act, against adult sons with addiction problems.

A father secured a two-year barring order against his son, aged in his late 20s. 

He previously got an IBO but, when the case returned to court on Friday, there was no appearance by the son.

“He is unlikely to be here because he runs away from everything,” said his father.

The judge proceeded to hear the barring order application because he was satisfied the son was served with the necessary legal documents.

In his sworn information to the court, he said his son has been an addict, using drink and drugs, since his early teens. 

He started on marijuana and moved to cocaine and is living a “chaotic” lifestyle affecting everyone in the family home, said his dad. His son is out four or five times weekly and returns at all hours, often causing disruption, “sometimes violent and always on the edge of it”. He damages the house and the family’s cars and has “threatened my life”, he added.

His son’s personality has altered; he is “clearly mentally ill”, constantly in trouble and does not seem to care for anyone or anything, said his father. “He is descending deeper into addiction, if that is possible.”

The family are traumatised by this “relentless behaviour” and he previously secured a barring order in 2023 against his son. 

He was seeking a two-year, rather than the maximum three-year order, he said. “There is always the hope of redemption. We’ll see. I’m here today for my family, but for him as much; he will never change as long as we maintain him in our home.” 

The judge said he sees many parents in similar circumstances and always tells them “not to give up hope” and they have the option to discharge the order if circumstances change.

The man thanked the judge, adding he was very thankful to the court for its support over the years.

A mother obtained a protection order against her son, aged in his 20s, whom she said had recently gone into psychosis due to cocaine use and was a danger to himself and others. He had a previous incident of psychosis earlier this year, she said. 

Gardaí had advised her to seek an IBO “but I want to give him a chance to get into rehab first”, she said. 

In another case, the judge continued an IBO granted earlier this month to a woman against her adult son after he heard the son was in custody over an alleged breach of it. 

The woman said, just days after she secured the IBO, her son kicked in her hall door and came upstairs when she was asleep. He had been put out of the house over drinking “and different things going on a long time” and recently “battered” and “choked” her other adult son, she said.

After he came into the house, she rang gardaí who removed him, she said. She is not afraid of her son but does not want to see him, she added.

In another application, a man who left the family home with his children earlier this week got a protection order against his wife. His wife previously agreed to his request to leave their jointly rented home after she was found by her mother and sister with cocaine. 

She later returned, promising to stop drinking and to end contact with a man with whom she had been having an affair and repair her relationship with their older children, he said. One evening this week, he said she had driven home drunk and, when their teenage daughter confronted her, said she was leaving with the youngest child and struck the teenager. That was when he left with all the children, and they stayed in his mother-in-law’s house, he said. 

The man said he did not want to return with the children unless his wife was barred from the family home.

Furlong said there was insufficient evidence for an emergency IBO, but he would grant a safety order. The barring order application would be heard at a later date when the wife is entitled to be present, he said. If she demonstrated any behaviour before that which put him or the children in fear, he should call gardaí, the judge added.
news.summary: Woman among several parents seeking barring orders against adult children with substance abuse problems
news.author: Mary Carolan

news.title: US ambassador to Israel condemns settler attack on journalist
news.text:
Ms Levine was seriously injured in the attack on Friday in the West Bank village of Abu Falah.

Israeli police are also investigating an attack by Israeli settlers on European diplomats on Saturday in another West Bank village.

Settler violence against Palestinians has soared this year and spiked further in recent weeks as Israel plans to hold elections on October 27.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was ambiguous in addressing Ms Levine’s assault, condemning “violence against anyone” but referring to the attack as “alleged” and saying its circumstances remain unclear.

Mr Huckabee said Ms Levine’s assault was “vicious” and “dishonourable”, and noted that she was clearly identified as a journalist when she was attacked.

Ms Levine, an award-winning photojournalist who has covered conflict zones around the world for more than four decades, remains in hospital in Tel Aviv as she recovers from hand surgery, broken ribs and other injuries she sustained in the attack.

She said she was forced to the ground and beaten for more than 10 minutes by the settlers, who also stole her camera, passport and phone.

The Washington Post reiterated its call for a full and transparent investigation, though Israel rarely investigates settler violence fully.

Yesh Din, an Israeli rights group, says around 94% of investigations into settler violence since 2005 have ended without an indictment, with just 3% leading to full or partial convictions.
news.summary: US ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee sharply condemned settler violence during an olive harvest in the West Bank that injured several Palestinians ...
news.author: Associated Press Reporter,Irishexaminer.com

news.title: US snapshot of Donald Trump’s hunger for adulation that has dragged us to this fraught moment
news.text:
Sometimes a candid photograph captures a moment in a presidency, and the essence of the officeholder, so tellingly that you get a penetrating portrait of an era.

It happened when LBJ (Lyndon B Johnson) yanked up his beagle by the ears for photographers and demonstrated his domineering leadership style.

It happened when a photographer captured George W Bush being told, while reading to children in a Florida classroom, that a second plane had hit the World Trade Center. His look of shock raised questions about whether, after his decades of winging it, a parlous rendezvous with destiny might be too much for him to handle.

It happened in 2009 when every living president gathered in the Oval office and Jimmy Carter so obviously kept his distance from Barack Obama, Bill Clinton and both Bushes that his sense of superiority was made clear.

It happened when Obama was photographed bending over in the Oval to let a black child touch his hair, to see if it was the same texture as his own, capturing the historic nature of his election.

It happened again when Doug Mills, the New York Times’ dazzling White House photographer, took a picture Tuesday of president Donald Trump on Marine One with his blond aides/acolytes Katie Zacharia, his wobbly new press secretary, and Natalie Harp, his special assistant for floofing.

Mills took the shot from far away with a long lens, but it bristles with intimacy.

The president is leaning in to talk to the two Ivanka knock-offs, who look like sorority-sister clones, four eyes glued on the man they adore, two fervent smiles glazed with pink lip gloss.

[ Katie Zacharia was fired after failing in the one arena Trump cares about: televisionOpens in new window ]

It is a snapshot of Trump’s hunger for adulation that has dragged us to this fraught moment in the United States.

He desperately craves being the centre of attention and seeing blind devotion mirrored back at him as that devotion wanes with an increasingly disgusted, exhausted public.

Trump was on a trip, part of a self-affirming odyssey to red states, which seemed to be designed not only to boost his unappetising slate of candidates but also to let him bask in applause from the last fanatical members of his dwindling fan base.

In Mills’ photo, marines are at attention beside the curved open doors of the helicopter, giving the impression that we are peering inside a bubble – at the very moment that Trump’s White House bubble is getting smaller and more ingrown and fractious than ever. Here he is in a cozy huddle with his most essential type of staff member: obedient helpmeets who help construct and perpetuate his absurd alternative reality and paranoid worldview.

Zacharia, the inept propagandist, and Harp, the so-called “human printer”, who trails – and sometimes sprints – behind the president with a portable printer, giving hard copies of soft coverage to Trump, offering him validation for his delusions and lies.

Zacharia reposted Mills’ photo with the caption, “Best President in US History!!!” But it really should have been the classic Henry Kissinger line: “Power is the ultimate aphrodisiac.”

[ Trump puts new Russia sanctions passed by Congress on hold amid deepening row with UkraineOpens in new window ]

Wags on X had their own captions, imagining Harp thinking homicidal thoughts about Zacharia.

But actually, the two women – scorned by colleagues eager to anonymously trash-talk them – were cloistered on the edge of the playground, clinging to each other and to their orange prophet, who told them to hang in there.

But it didn’t last, and by Friday, he was easing Zacharia out. “Honestly, if I were you, I’d reconsider,” Trump told her, as he later recounted to reporters. Soon after, she got the boot.

They were trying to fight back against their in-house critics. Harp showed Trump the Politico Playbook story Thursday reporting that the president is shopping around for a new chief of staff. It also named the advisers who have cashed in. The right to cash in, in Trump’s eyes, is for him and his family only.

“Trump has bristled at recent reports showing several long-time advisers are profiting from foreign consulting business,” Playbook said, noting that Susie Wiles’ daughter Katie is working for a firm representing Republika Srpska, a pro-Russian Bosnian Serb territory.

The Daily Beast headline about the Wiles report blared: “Natalie Harp Knifes Ice Maiden and Sparks Trump ‘Freakout.’”

Tellingly and perhaps prophetically, Susie Wiles is in Mills’ picture but mostly cut out of the frame. You can see her legs in red pants and the Louis Vuitton bag on her lap.

We can’t see the expression on Wiles’ face, but we know that she is no fan of the two gushing young women in the picture.

Alarmed by Harp’s fixation on the president and her emotionally raw letters to him in 2023, Wiles attempted – in vain – to curb her access. Trump’s decision to appoint Zacharia to a critical job where she was doomed to flounder and likely end up in an “SNL” cold open blindsided Wiles, according to news reports.

Even Trump seemed taken aback by the press gaggle after Zacharia’s debut news conference debacle and when the Times’ Shawn McCreesh, before the president and his aides took off for Alaska, asked Zacharia where she had passed the bar.

“When I moved to China,” she said, as Trump – who described her as an attorney when he announced her appointment – snapped his head around. The story unspooled that she hadn’t passed the bar anywhere.

But by the time they got to Alaska eight hours later, she was beaming at her boss and doing damage control.

(She told a far-right Pizzagate conspiracist in an interview that she wanted to be played on “SNL” by “a Scarlett Johansson-type character.”)

Zacharia tried to fight back on “Hannity,” no doubt assuming she would be in friendly territory.

But she wasn’t. Sean Hannity asked her why she had put up 15 media posts identifying herself as an attorney. She lamely protested that they were “retweets of a title that had been given”. (Mistakes were made.)

Hannity pressed on: “Why didn’t you just say ‘I never practised law’?” and asked about her first news conference, “Why only three questions in 14 minutes?”

Zacharia looked unnerved, as though she had been sandbagged by her foes in the White House.

As his hold on the country seems to be slipping through his pudgy fingers, Trump needs the unqualified love from his blond Praetorian Guard.

Not only do Democrats seem headed for success in the midterms, fuelled by a swell of Americans who see Trump as a crook, enriching himself while costs rise for everyone else, but the president’s inner circle is going up in flames. Aides are turning on one another and sinking in a cauldron of corruption and boneheaded policies.

[ Trump’s new press secretary faces mounting questions over her legal credentialsOpens in new window ]

The past week has been a cascade of embarrassing stories: Kimberly Guilfoyle getting iced as ambassador to Greece after a donor revealed that just before her Senate confirmation hearing, she tried to shake him down to pay her $100,000 American Express bill; Trump loyalist Ric Grenell, who was the head of the ill-fated Kennedy Center, accused by Trump loyalist Alina Habba Mildon and her new billionaire husband of misallocating a $5.6 million donation marked for the centre; and our ally Volodymyr Zelenskiy saying he felt betrayed by Trump’s sordid deal with Vladimir Putin over diesel oil and the restricted access to Elon Musk’s Starshield amid Russian bombardment. Trump even had to cancel the nitwit plan of his frat boy Pentagon chief to livestream an execution.

Instead of running the country and dealing with the world he has set on fire, the president is focused on settling petty squabbles and a web of corruption in his incompetent – and dangerous – court.

Doug Mills has proved once again that a picture is worth 1,000 words, or in my case, 1,273.

This article originally appeared in The New York Times
news.summary: In Doug Mills’ photo, here Trump is in a cozy huddle with his most essential type of staff member
news.author: Maureen Dowd

Over 1,200 arrested as fires, looting and violent protests leave streets devastated across France

Shops were looted, cars set alight and a historic town hall largely destroyed as demonstrations over the rising cost of living descended into violence.

8.29am, 18 Oct 2026

Share options

FRANCE HAS WOKEN up to devastated streets this morning after clashes between police and protesters, mass looting and fires erupted nationwide as marches against rising costs of living degenerated into “extreme” violence.

The widespread unrest followed weeks of student protests and comes just six months ahead of elections to replace President Emmanuel Macron.

Whole streets in Paris “have been devastated”, the city’s mayor Emmanuel Gregoire said as groups of masked young men torched parked cars and ransacked shops.

French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu, who had condemned the “extreme intensity” of the violence, said 1,200 people had been arrested and 150 police officers hurt.

It was “a miracle the toll isn’t higher”, Lecornu said.

The violence began on the sidelines of marches in the capital and other cities over the cost of living that the interior ministry said were attended by 550,000 people.

A car burning at Republique square in Paris.AP Photo / Thibault Camus

AP Photo / Thibault Camus / Thibault Camus

The CGT union, which took part, said 800,000 people participated.

Police used tear gas and water cannon against protesters who threw projectiles and aimed fireworks.

A 17-year-old boy had his right hand blown off by a crowd-control grenade in the southern city of Saint-Étienne.

During and after those demonstrations, gangs of youths roamed city streets, sporadically confronting police, while setting fires and attacking shuttered stores to break in and empty their shelves.

Scores of shops – supermarkets, pharmacies, luxury boutiques, clothing retailers, opticians, cosmetic vendors and consumer electronics stores – were looted in Paris, Marseille, Nice, Nantes, Bordeaux, Limoges, Lille, Toulouse and Strasbourg.

Protesters ransacking a tourism office in Lyon.Laurent Cipriani

Laurent Cipriani

AFP reporters in Paris saw groups of half a dozen young men attacking the shops in an organised way. Wearing masks and gloves, they first disconnected security cameras before smashing windows to get in.

The looting added to a day of destruction and vandalism, with town halls in several cities targeted.

The town hall in the city of Limoges – more than 140 years old – was largely destroyed by a blaze set by masked protesters who broke in, according to the region’s top official. Two others were broken into and vandalised in Marseille and Lille.

This is the moment a town hall collapsed as protests sweep across France.

The 140-year-old town hall in the French city of Limoges caught fire during protests in the city

Read the latest on the Sky News website and app: https://t.co/oaLTf7aDbP https://t.co/3OC3eU3Hf7— Sky News (@SkyNews) October 17, 2026

A police compound in Bordeaux was also vandalised, while in Lyon protesters set ablaze a tourist office.

Advertisement

The violence has drawn global headlines – in the United States, Vice President JD Vance blamed immigration for the unrest.

“Western liberals imported the Third World into France and other countries in the name of diversity and compassion. They ignored fundamental questions of assimilation and compatibility,” he said on X.

President Macron said that “those who carried out vandalism, attacked administrative offices or businesses, or carried out looting – even in our town halls, will be prosecuted and punished”.

Opposition politicians vying to replace Macron in presidential elections in April and May have seized on the chaos.

Far-right candidate Marine Le Pen condemned “the rioters” and claimed that the party of her far-left rival for the presidency, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, had “legitimised the violence”.

She vowed to protect the French “from the violence of the extreme left”.

Melenchon, who had prominently supported the demonstrations and the student protests preceding them, urged demonstrators to stay away from any looting, describing it as “contrary to our methods”.

‘Revolution’

France’s Yellow Vest movement, which staged street protests eight years ago against Macron’s government over planned fuel tax hikes, had called for Saturday’s “yellow and youth” demonstrations.

The principal grievance was the cost of living, pushed up in part by the war in the Middle East that has helped send inflation soaring in Europe as elsewhere.

Police officers pictured in Paris.EMMA DA SILVA

EMMA DA SILVA

“We’re sick of slaving away for poverty wages while our rents keep going up,” teacher Regine Monfroid told AFP in the eastern city of Strasbourg.

But there were other issues.

In Paris, tens of thousands marched across the east and north of the city in one major march, some shouting “Everyone hates the police” and “Macron, resign”.

High school student Kamil Alahyan (18) said he was protesting “for so many reasons – the elections coming up in 2027, politicians who lie, the ultrarich who’ve been taking more and more wealth over the past 10 years”.

Several protesters sought to draw parallels with the French Revolution of 1789.

“It’s the Revolution — we’re taking the Bastille!” some shouted in Marseille as they forced their way into the mayor’s offices.

In the western city of La Rochelle, marchers streamed behind a placard reading: “Revolution or death.”

And in the southern city of Montpellier, a giant blue sign reading “The people will win” was unfurled above a central square.

“The government is trembling and it’s right to tremble because when the French people are angry, they never let up,” Ryad Rani, the head of the LSU high school student representative body, told journalists in Paris.

news.title: Craig Casey says Munster victory over Racing was 'for Axel'
news.text:
Munster 33 

Racing 92 25

Craig Casey said beating Racing 92 was important to honour late head coach Anthony Foley as Munster got their Champions Cup pool campaign up and running on the 10th anniversary of his death with a 33-25 victory in Cork on Saturday night.

Munster needed scrum-half Casey’s 77th minute try in a player of the match performance to make sure of the win in their Pool 3 opener, played in front of 24,906 supporters on Leeside, having led 14-6 at half-time and 28-18 at the hour mark.

Brian Gleeson, playing in Foley’s position at No.8 but wearing the number 24 with the traditional starting jersey retired for the night as a mark of respect for man who died aged 42, had replied to an early Racing penalty with a sixth-minute try before wing Shay McCarthy scored a wonderful solo effort on 12 mintues, both scores converted by rookie fly-half Charlie O’Shea.

The second half saw Munster captain Tadhg Beirne scoring in the 42nd minute, Racing wing Wilfried Hulleu replying four minutes later and then the French Top 14 giants closing the gap further through a maul try for hooker Diego Escobar. Munster’s replacement lock Fineen Wycherley struck back on 60 minutes, replacement fly-half JJ Hanrahan converting, only for Racing centre Joey Manu’s try converted by Antoine Gibert to close the gap to 28-25 soon after.

A yellow card for an aerial tackle on Munster full-back Ben O’Connor by replacement back Arthur Roche handed the initiative back to Clayton McMillan’s side with nine minutes remaining and they saw out the game superbly by retaining possession before Casey made certain after peeling away from a strong lineout drive with two minutes to go.

"I think the confidence in the group is spot on, you can see where we're growing,” Casey told Premier Sport afterwards. “We've improved a lot, there's a good buzz in the group.

"This week, it was important to get the win for Axel, for our crowd, for Axel's family and all the Munster faithful.

"It was a different week, a different feel all week. You're trying to pull back on the emotion and concentrate on the performance, it felt different all week, it felt like a one-off game. It didn't feel like we were going into the first round, it felt a lot more special than that, a lot more meaningful.

"Thankfully we did pitch up, because that man deserved it. He deserved the performance today, hopefully he'd be proud of us."

The Munster squad and management had gathered in a circle around the centre spot at full-time to belt out Stand Up and Fight in Foley’s honour, a repeat of the team’s actions the day after the former captain’s funeral, when Glasgow Warriors were beaten on an emotionally charged day at Thomond Park.

"I was on the East Terrace the week after he died, I couldn't have been prouder of Munster that day,” Casey recalled.

"You want to be part of that, how well we rallied around everyone that week and I was only in sixth year, but it drove me to want to be a part of the club.

"It's a special week, he's a special man. His legacy will be with every Munster team from here until the very end of time.

"We talk about him constantly, we wrap up every game with 'Axel'. His family is very special to us, thankfully we honoured him with a win today."

MUNSTER: B O’Connor; S McCarthy, A Nankivell, D Kelly, S O’Brien; C O’Shea (JJ Hanrahan, 57), C Casey (B O’Donovan, 78); J Loughman (J Wycherley, 57), M van der Merwe (M Clein, 78), J Aungier (K Brookes, 57); T Ahern (F Wycherley, 59), T Beirne - captain; S Edogbo (J O’Donoghue, 53), J Hodnett, B Gleeson (G Coombes, 53).

RACING 92: G Prisciantelli; W Hulleu, V Habosi (S James, 49), J Manu, S Tupou (A Roche, 57); A Gibert, A Latrasse (M Machenaud, 49); E Jabea Njocke (L Leota, 44), D Escobar (Y Basse, 77), G Kharaishvili (D Bamba, 44); T Lainault, J Joseph (N Hughes, 61), L Tagitagivalu, N Martins, M Baudonne – captain.

Yellow card: A Roche 71 mins.

Replacement not used: S Camara.

news.summary: 10 years on from his death, Munster paid tribute to former captain and head coach Anthony Foley. 'It felt like a one-off game,' said Craig Caesy. 'It didn't feel like we were going into the first round, it felt a lot more special than that, a lot more meaningful'

news.title: Israeli settlers attack Palestinians and European diplomats in West Bank
news.text:
Israeli settler militants have attacked European diplomats, a French mayor and the archbishop of Cambrai in Taybeh, in the occupied West Bank, injuring three people and damaging a car, in the latest violent attempt to prevent Palestinians from harvesting olives on their own land.

Bernard Baudoux, mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries, was wearing his red, white and blue sash of office and attempting to enter a vehicle with diplomatic plates when he was assaulted and knocked to the ground on Saturday.

The masked militant shouted “Vive la France” as he launched the attack, a witness said. Badoux’s wife, and Vincent Dollmann, archbishop of Cambrai, were also threatened by the group of seven men, some armed with clubs.

The group had joined the olive harvest on lands belonging to the Christian town of Taybeh, along with the French consul general in Jerusalem, his wife and other diplomats, and the Belgian and Polish consuls.

Settlers first attacked a group working on the lower slopes of hills near Taybeh. As well as stealing olives, they kicked, abused and assaulted a Palestinian woman in her 70s and beat a man so badly he needed six stitches for a head injury.

Then they approached the diplomats and Badoux, who was in Taybeh for the launch of a twinning agreement with his town in northern France. During the attack, the militants smashed the window of an armoured car belonging to the Belgian mission.

Maxime Prévot, Belgium’s deputy prime minister and minister of foreign affairs, condemned the violence against Palestinians, foreign diplomats and journalists, and said his country would continue to push for European Union sanctions on settlers.

“Harvesting olives, reporting the news or carrying out diplomatic duties should never put anyone at risk of attack,” he said. “This violence cannot be separated from Israel’s illegal settlement policy ... the occupation of the Palestinian territory must end.”

Palestinian residents of Taybeh have lived with years of escalating attacks from Israeli militants, but settlers had never targeted foreign diplomats there, said Fr Bashar Fawadleh, the town’s parish priest.

“What happened today is not an isolated incident. It represents a deeply disturbing escalation in settler violence,” Fawadleh said.

Since the start of the annual olive harvest in late September, Israeli militants have used violence to stop Palestinians bringing in a crop that is economically and culturally vital to their communities.

Since September 27th, settlers have launched more than 170 attacks, Israeli rights group Yesh Din said. They killed at least four people, injured more than 100 and damaged thousands of trees, according to Palestinian authorities.

Even the presence of Israeli activists, diplomats, senior clergy and journalists no longer serves as a deterrence to extreme violence.

[ Why Israel fears settlement sanctions are just the beginningOpens in new window ]

“If such violence can take place before international witnesses, one must ask what protection remains for local families and farmers when those witnesses are no longer present,” Fawadleh said. “No individual should have to risk physical assault simply to harvest olives from their own land.”

On Friday, Israeli militants attacked and severely injured Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine as she reported on the harvest in the town of Abu Falah. She required surgery on Saturday morning and is now in “moderate” condition, according to a spokesperson for Israel’s Beilinson hospital where she is being treated.

US secretary ⁠of ​state Marco Rubio said on Saturday that the United States wants Israel ⁠to do more to deter attacks committed by settlers. “We’re very disturbed by those images and ⁠what we’re seeing,” Rubio said. “We’ve asked the Israelis and continue to ask them to crack ⁠down on that stuff.”

Israel had already severely restricted the harvest this year by imposing new rules barring Palestinians from trees located in Area C, an area under the Israeli military’s control, which comprises most of the West Bank’s agricultural land.

Israel’s foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, condemned the attacks and said police had opened an investigation. He said foreign diplomats risked attacks from Israeli civilians if they travelled in the occupied West Bank without military co-ordination.

Demanding diplomats give advance notification of travel violates both diplomatic conventions and international law, said one western diplomatic source who asked not to be named.

“Israel is in charge of security in Area B and C [the majority of the West Bank], so is obliged to assure safety there for all,” the source said.

A culture of near total impunity for Israeli violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank has prompted former prime minister Ehud Olmert to call for the International Criminal Court to intervene.

[ Opinion: Israel’s settlement policy is designed to bury the idea of a two-state solutionOpens in new window ]

Gadi Eisenkot, an opposition politician and former general hoping to unseat prime minister Binyamin Netanyahu in elections to be held later this month, described the attack as “Jewish terror under the auspices of the Israeli government”.

Eisenkot backs Jewish Israeli expansion in occupied Palestine but wants militant violence brought under control because the attackers are “harming the settlement enterprise in [the West Bank] and national security”. – Guardian
news.summary: French mayor and archbishop also attacked as settler violence surges during the olive harvest
news.author: Emma Graham-Harrison in Taybeh

If Dublin wants to be a city for everyone, it must tackle homelessness 

Seven in 10 people experiencing homelessness are in Dublin. The city now needs its own dedicated strategy to deal with this issue once and for all. 

7.31am, 18 Oct 2026

Share options

Catherine Kenny

DUBLIN IS AT the epicentre of homelessness in Ireland. Homelessness is deeply isolating and stigmatising for those experiencing it, but in a large city it is also a collective experience. When we fail to provide enough homes for our whole community, the consequences are felt not only by those forced into emergency accommodation or onto the streets, but by the city we all share.

This is why homelessness must be part of any serious conversation about Dublin’s future. Improving our capital city means directly confronting a failure that continues to impact thousands of its residents. Every policy, every service provided, every state and semi-state body should be operating in the context of the reality that Dublin has an enduring and systemic homelessness crisis.

Seven in every 10 people experiencing homelessness are in the capital. More than 12,000 people in the city now are in emergency accommodation, an 8% increase compared to last year, while the numbers of those sleeping rough are increasing too. The latest monthly homeless figures show that the people residing in emergency accommodation increased by 358 last month to 17,885, a new record. Of the 7,304 single adults in emergency accommodation nationally, 4,881 are in Dublin.

Figures released to RTÉ One’s Prime Time found that one in 10 people who are homeless are living in a very small, confined area of the north inner city.

We at Dublin Simon Community would like nothing more than to become less necessary. We want to be shrinking, not expanding. We want homelessness to be prevented, rather than managed after it has occurred. Yet the reality is that our services are needed now more than ever.

Why are we ignoring homelessness?

To address the challenge head-on, we need an integrated and dedicated strategy to tackle homelessness in Dublin, one that allows the state, local authorities, service providers and our health system to work together to come up with a solution and to move from reactive responses to proactive prevention.

Introduced by the government, the Dublin City Taskforce headed by Robert Watt continues to pursue several welcome recommendations about the future of our nation’s capital. Among the proposals are the creation of a 10-year Integrated Area Strategy, development of key sites such as the GPO, and working with An Garda Síochána on policing strategies.

The Dublin City Taskforce is wise to focus on what is positive because there is plenty to build on. Dublin can and should be an incredible place to live in. There is already a lot to celebrate. But if we want to realise a true, inclusive and lasting vision for Dublin, we also need to focus on what is not working. And that includes our failure to execute an effective response to the homelessness crisis.

Advertisement

On Dublin’s streets, homelessness is not hidden in doorways after dark. It is in plain sight as we go about our daily business – a figure under a sleeping bag in a doorway as people hurry past; a woman carrying everything she owns in a few plastic bags; people queuing quietly for food; young men trying to sleep in tents exposed to cold, fear and violence.

Behind every figure is a life. Somebody’s son or daughter, brother or sister, reduced to the exhausting daily search for somewhere safe to eat or sleep.

Encouragingly, the foundations for a ‘joined-up’ approach already exist. The creation of the Dublin Region Homeless Executive (DRHE) in 2011 was an acknowledgement that Dublin faced specific and growing challenges around housing and homelessness. The DRHE is led by Dublin City Council and operates as a shared service across Dublin’s four local authorities: Dublin City, Fingal, South Dublin and Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown.

The reorganisation of the HSE has similarly created a more regional approach to managing people’s needs, moving from one centralised structure to nine and ultimately six operational regions.

Why Dublin is key

Dublin is already subject to a vast range of reports, plans and strategies. The problem is not a lack of ideas. The pieces of the puzzle are there. What is missing is the alignment needed to address the root causes of housing insecurity and homelessness, and a mechanism for sharing knowledge and coordinating funding specifically across the greater Dublin region. That means opportunities to learn from what works to prevent homelessness earlier, to improve emergency accommodation and, ultimately, to deliver more homes.

This dedicated Dublin Homelessness strategy and budget, led and funded by national government, can operate with a clear focus on delivery towards 2030. It can work hand in glove with initiatives such as the Dublin Taskforce to secure the provision of social, affordable and cost-rental housing, supported by direct and sustained capital investment.

The government has already committed, through its national housing plan, to delivering 300,000 homes by the end of 2030, alongside ambitions to end homelessness, deliver homes for older people and increase social inclusion. The opportunity now is to make Dublin a focused delivery area within that national ambition.

The Dublin strategy should provide an overarching framework to review, integrate and coordinate existing policies and funding priorities, from the Delivering Homes, Building Communities 2025–2030 document to the National Drugs Strategy.

To ensure urgent delivery of such a strategy, government should establish a Dublin Homelessness Crisis Team reporting directly across the relevant departments and agencies.

Its task should be to oversee implementation and to align housing, health, social protection, justice and local authority responses within a single delivery framework. This approach can facilitate multiannual funding for homelessness services.

Related Reads

Taoiseach takes pot shot at ESRI report which revealed rising child poverty

'This is a human crisis': New record of 16,614 people now in emergency accommodation

Emergency accommodation figures reach record high of over 16,300, including 5,145 children

This is not about creating another layer of bureaucracy. It is about making the structures we already have work together.

The Dublin City Taskforce has set out an ambitious mission: “More people living in the city centre, streets that look cleaner and feel safer, and a healthy, vibrant, always-on city that respects its heritage.”

But if we want more people to live in Dublin, we must first make sure that people can afford to live here.

If we want safer, cleaner and more vibrant streets, we must address the housing insecurity that is visible on those streets every day. And if we want a city that works for everyone, we must put housing at the centre of our definition of our quality of life.

Dublin does not need another collection of disconnected initiatives. It needs a strategy that brings them together, a budget that backs it up and a delivery structure with the authority to make it happen.

If Dublin is to become the city we know it can be, tackling homelessness must be at the heart of the plan.

Catherine Kenny is CEO of Dublin Simon Community.

news.title: Cost of living key to any pay talks, say INMO members
news.text:
As unions prepare to sit down with the Government to hammer out a new pay deal at the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC), there is a determination among those who were on the picket lines earlier this week that any new deal must cover increases in the cost of living.

Nurses, who are members of the Irish Nurses and Midwives Organisation (INMO) at Cork University Hospital (CUH), say cost of living increases are the number one issue for them.

Róisín Duffy, a 23-year old midwife from Minane Bridge, Co Cork, remembers exactly when she decided she wanted to work as a nurse.

She was four years old when she got a doctor's set and went around calling herself "Doctor Róisín".

"I've always wanted to do nursing and then, when I found out what midwifery was, I thought that was the coolest thing ever. I love it. It's exactly what I wanted to do," she says.

Almost two decades on from the child with the doctor's set, Ms Duffy will graduate with her degree in midwifery from University College Cork (UCC) at the end of the month.

A fortnight ago, she started her first full-time job as a midwife in a post-natal ward at Cork University Maternity Hospital.

But, very quickly, she is learning that the job is not exactly what she had been hoping it would be.

On Wednesday, Ms Duffy was one of hundreds of nurses and midwives who picketed CUH, and one thousands around the country on strike to progress the dispute with the Government over a new national pay agreement.

Pay is not the only issue she has encountered in her short career.

For a start, the permanent job she had hoped for as a midwife in Cork has not materialilsed.

Instead, she was offered a "blank" contract, which gives her 37.5 hours work every week, but no guarantee of permanency in the maternity hospital's post-natal ward, where she looks after half a dozen mothers and new-born babies every shift.

"They said they can move us whenever they want, and it's not exactly the permanent position that we were expecting. It's disheartening," she said.

"I have signed no contract, and nothing has been guaranteed."

The lack of certainty has led Ms Murphy and her classmates to consider emigration, possibly to Australia.

"I suppose me and many other people have talked about moving elsewhere," she said.

"There are many other countries in the world that pay almost double what we get here and have an extremely better work environment. We're just run off our feet."

Read more: Talks on a new public sector pay deal will begin on Monday at WRC
Unions suspend next week's planned strike action

Ms Murphy lives at home with her parents, her brother and sister.

She says she would like to think about buying her own home at some stage, but cannot see that happening on her current salary.

She said that is why she was on the picket line, she wants any pay increase agreed between the unions and the Government to match the increase in the cost of living.

"I just think the Government needs to recognise the important role we have in nurses and midwives and match our pay accordingly.

"We're not asking for a lot. We just want to be able to survive with the cost of living.

"I'm in a better position than most, because I live at home. But I'm still commuting, and I still have the cost of living that everyone else. Groceries are extremely expensive, petrol is extremely expensive, and I'm getting by, but I'm finding it extremely hard to save."

Jibin Soman, 39, works in the neurosurgery ward of CHU.

He is one of thousands of foreign nurses working in the health service, as he and his wife Aiswarya came to Ireland from India.

Aiswarya is also a nurse and works in a nursing home in the private sector.

Jibin began working at CUH nine years ago, searching for a better life and a better standard of living.

He says the cost of living is making it extremely difficult to get by, notwithstanding the fact that there are two salaries coming into his household.

The couple have a six-year old daughter and are living in Watergrasshill in north Co Cork.

"It's hard, it's a struggle and it's a pressure.

"So, I would say, if you ask me at this stage, it is not meeting the expectations that I had when I initially moved here. What we get is only to cover the cost of living at the moment; it's not even meeting the cost of living at the moment."

He recalls his motivation for training as a nurse: the passion he felt to care for his patients.

He points to the range of responsibilities he has to fulfil in the neurosurgery ward, before he can have time to actually spend time with and care for his patients.

He questions if there is still space to do that.

"I don't know: we don't have enough time," he said.

"We do try our best."

He is clear about why he went on strike this week.

"It's purely that we don't have enough money. We have been saying that to everyone, that we are not getting enough money to meet the cost of living.

"There's huge inflation and it's visible to everyone. If you go to the petrol station to fill your car, it's visible there. That's huge inflation. If you go to the grocery shop - the inflation is too high. The prices have gone up too much.

"If you compare the point where I came here in 2017 with now, there is a huge difference that you can see in the price of groceries, diesel, everything: energy, oil, gas, electricity."

Mr Soman said that he regularly has to deal with situations where his monthly salary only stretches for a fortnight, and he has to supplement from his wife's salary.

Notwithstanding that struggle, Mr Soman sees his future in Ireland.

"This is a nice country to live in. I expect the Government will listen to us. They will see the struggle that we have, the pressure that we have in our lives, and our desire to stay in this country," he said.

"And I hope they see what we are doing for this country: all the nurses working hard for this country. I hope they listen to us; they hear us and they do what we are asking."

Working conditions 'demoralising'

Jennifer Searle works as a senior staff nurse in the endoscopy department at CUH.

She has been nursing for 28 years, having trained and qualified at St James' Hospital in Dublin.

She lives in Midleton, Co Cork, with her husband and their two children.

Ms Searle was 16 when she first cared for someone: her grandfather, Bernard Jordan.

He had a fall in Ballyhaunis in Co Mayo and his graddaughter was dispatched there from her home in Ballina to help him recuperate after he was discharged from hospital.

"I went into nursing because I absolutely love it," she said.

"I love helping people and being there for people. It's the best job in the world. It's just amazing."

Ms Searle retains her passion for her job, but the frustrations of increased pressure in the workplace are clear.

"It's an amazing job but every day- I've been in nursing such a long time now - it's just more and more pressure. It's a case of not having those minutes to spend with your patients.

"It's having to do things very quickly. You're doing the job of maybe one or two other nurses. The pressure is unbelievable."

"It's not what it used to be at all."

She describes the increased pressure on her and her colleagues as demoralising.

"You leave work and you feel like you just haven't done enough," she said.

Ms Searle spent Wednesday on the picket line with her colleagues at CUH.

"You know, we're not out here for the fun of it. We want fair pay: fair pay for the work we do today. It's as simple as that.

"Like everyone else in this country, everything - even in the last couple of months - everything from groceries to energy to fuel, everything is skyrocketing.

"It's just to keep up with the cost of living."

She is adamant that public sector workers will get a fair pay increase, but she says none of them actually wanted to be on strike.

"I want to be doing my job. I want to be looking after my patients. I want to be doing what I wanted to do all these years," she said.

news.title: Italy postpones Euro 5 diesel traffic bans until October 2027
news.text:
Italy has postponed planned restrictions on Euro 5 diesel vehicles in four northern regions for another year, providing welcome breathing space for transport operators, including Irish hauliers travelling to northern Italy.

The Italian Government has confirmed that the proposed restrictions, originally scheduled to take effect on 1 October 2026, will now be deferred until 1 October 2027.

The decision follows concerns about the economic consequences of restricting older diesel vehicles, particularly for businesses, transport operators and commercial vehicle fleets.

The postponement was formally introduced under Decree-Law No. 167 of 28 September 2026, which came into force the following day.

Four northern regions affected

The restrictions concern four of Italy’s most economically important regions:

Lombardy, including Milan, Bergamo, Brescia and Monza.
Piedmont, including Turin.
Veneto, including Venice and Verona.
Emilia-Romagna, including Bologna, Parma and Modena.

These regions form part of the Po Valley, one of Europe’s most heavily industrialised areas, where air pollution has been a longstanding concern.

The proposed restrictions cover Euro 5 diesel passenger cars and commercial vehicles, including light commercial vehicles, medium-duty trucks and heavy goods vehicles in categories N1, N2 and N3.

The legislation primarily targets urban areas in municipalities with populations exceeding 100,000, rather than imposing a blanket ban across northern Italy.

Government acknowledges impact on transport industry

The Italian Government justified the postponement by highlighting the potential disruption to mobility, transport services and economic activity.

The authorities have recognised that introducing restrictions at this stage could have significant consequences for businesses already facing substantial operating costs.

Italian Infrastructure and Transport Minister Matteo Salvini welcomed the decision, which gives regional administrations additional time to introduce alternative measures to improve air quality without necessarily removing Euro 5 vehicles from the road.

Several regions have already proposed alternative environmental programmes, including incentives for cleaner fuels, improvements to public transport and measures to reduce emissions from other sources.
news.summary:
Italy has postponed planned restrictions on Euro 5 diesel vehicles in four northern regions for another year, providing welcome breathing space for transport operators, including Irish hauliers travelling to northern Italy. The Italian Government has confirmed that the proposed restrictions, originally scheduled to take effect on 1 October 2026, will now be deferred until 1 […]

September’s only council CPO bid to An Coimisiún Pleanála was for 24 houses in a ghost estate

Tipperary County Council was the only local authority to apply to the commission for a CPO last month.

6.01am, 18 Oct 2026

Share options

BOARDED-UP HOUSES AND crumbling buildings are a common feature of towns and cities across Ireland.

Derelict buildings contribute significantly to Ireland’s housing crisis, and bringing them back into use is one of the government’s strategies for addressing social housing shortfalls and getting more homes on the market.

Last month, the compulsory purchase order (CPO) process was used via An Coimisiún Pleanála for 24 properties, though all of these were in one estate.

In September, Tipperary County Council applied to An Coimisiún Pleanála to compulsorily acquire a site at Glen Court in Emly, where local reporting has identified 24 vacant houses.

Under laws introduced in 1990, every local council keeps a Derelict Sites Register to encourage owners to bring vacant houses and land into use through the imposition of an annual levy of 7% of the property’s market value, which applies until the site is no longer derelict.

When someone objects to a local authority’s attempt to obtain a property via the CPO process, the council can apply to An Coimisiún Pleanála to do so.

The Housing Act also allows local authorities to acquire vacant homes via CPO, which they must also apply to do via the commission.

The process is similar to making a standard planning application, and the board weighs up submissions from the council and the owner of the land before deciding whether a site can be subject to a CPO.

The number of properties that councils try to CPO via the commission every month is usually relatively small.

It is worth noting, however, that Ireland’s councils successfully CPO other properties without having to go to the commission, which helps bring derelict properties back into use.

The Journal reported in March that Ireland’s local authorities acquired 99 properties through CPOs in 2025, including houses and land intended for housing.

We have tracked the properties and sites involved in applications to the commission since April last year.

We have also been keeping track of the vacant and derelict properties that councils have applied to the commission to acquire via CPO since April last year.

This list shows the total number of applications made to An Coimisiún Pleanála by councils to CPO derelict properties since our series began in 2025:

April 2025: Six

May 2025: Three

June 2025: Two

August 2025: Two

September 2025: Five

October 2025: Two

November 2025: Three

December 2025: One

January 2026: One

February 2026: Seven

March 2026: Two

April 2026: 13

May 2026: Five

June 2026: 20

July 2026: Four

August 2026: Three

Advertisement

Glen Court, Emly (Tipperary)

Glen Court in TipperaryGoogle Street View

Google Street View

On 15 September, Tipperary County Council submitted an application to acquire a derelict site at Glen Court in Emly.

The bid concerned 24 houses in an estate left unfinished after the economic crash, according to reporting by local radio station Tipp FM, when the council’s compulsory purchase plans were first announced.

The station reported at the time that residents have faced years of infrastructure problems, including difficulties with wastewater treatment, alongside antisocial behaviour and fires which damaged some of the properties.

Another local station, Tipp Mid West Radio, reported in March 2024 that approximately 24 houses in the estate had never been occupied.

It can be considered a ghost estate, a housing development that is left unfinished or largely empty where some homes may still be occupied.

There has been some progress on the estate’s infrastructure more recently.

Council minutes show that councillors approved taking responsibility for Glen Court on 27 January 2025, bringing its roads under the council’s responsibility.

However, the September application to An Coimisiún Pleanála to CPO the site bid quickly stalled.

The commission marked the application invalid on 17 September, and its online case entry does not explain the reason.

Tipp FM reported on 29 September that Sinn Féin councillor Annemarie Ryan Shiner had been assured the council would submit another application to CPO the site.

The attempted CPO is part of a wider programme to tackle dereliction in Tipperary.

In its July management report, the council recorded 141 sites on its derelict sites register, up from 115 in January.

It set a target of issuing derelict-site notices concerning an additional 100 properties during 2026.

The report also said two CPO processes had been completed that year, with acquisitions in Clonmel and Cashel, while 24 had commenced and another 28 were being prepared.

The council said it had issued €1.1 million in derelict-site levies for 2026 and planned to pursue collection.

news.title: How does pen space influence cattle performance?
news.text:
Overcrowding sheds can cost you carcass weight, even when feeding and animal health are right. 

Teagasc beef specialist, Martina Harrington is advising farmers to measure pens before housing and match cattle numbers to the space available.

She provided the following tips on ensuring cattle have enough space when housed:

Lying space: Teagasc research found that finishing cattle given 3m² each produced carcasses 20kg heavier than cattle given only 2m² over 105 days. No further performance benefit was found above 3m² in this trial.

Know your pen capacity: A pen with a usable lying area of 5.6m x 4.8m provides 26.88m². This gives nine cattle approximately 3m² each. Putting 13 cattle into the same pen reduces this to just over 2m² each. 

Check feeding space too: Floor area alone does not decide how many cattle a pen can hold. Plan for their size at the end of winter, not just at housing.

Put a value on space: Using an example beef price of €7.20/kg, an extra 20kg of carcass is worth €144/head, or €1,296 across nine cattle. This is extra carcass value before costs, not a guaranteed increase in pen profit. The overall return also depends on how many cattle are finished.

In a separate Teagasc trial, finishing steers on Durapak rubber mats over concrete slats produced carcasses 11kg heavier after 120 days than those on bare concrete slats. 

They also spent longer lying down and converted feed into weight gain more efficiently. 

Using the same example price of €7.20/kg, that extra carcass weight is worth €79.20/head, before allowing for the cost of the mats. 

The same performance benefit was not found in weanlings.

Agriland spoke to Teagasc about this study earlier this year at the BEEF2026 open day in Grange on July 1.

Teagasc business and technology adviser David Hallissey told Agriland: "Straw bedding didn't show any performance gain over your concrete slats."

The trial found that cattle finished on mats over 120 days had a higher average daily gain (ADG) of 0.18kg/DM compared to concrete.

Cattle on rubber mats spent nearly one extra hour lying down, and had an 11kg heavier carcass-weight on average with no increase in feed intake.

Cleanliness was also measured and interestingly, concrete slats showed the highest cleanliness.

Straw bedding had the lowest cleanliness despite regular removal and replenishing of straw and a 5m² lying space allocation, compared to 3m² for concrete and rubber mats.

news.title: Health service spent €250m more on ‘higher-cost’ agency staff than budgeted for
news.text:
The health service spent more than €250 million on higher-cost temporary staff provided through agencies than the amount set out in its official budget in the first eight months of the year, a new internal Health Service Executive report shows.

The HSE’s cost and productivity oversight group report, dated September 25th, says €522 million had been spent on agency staff by the end of August. The budget for agency personnel for the period had been set at €272 million. 

The report shows spending on staff overtime was about €52 million higher than the official budgetary figure. However, the bill for staff who were directly employed was about €220 million less than the €7.29 billion provided for in the health service budget to the end of August.

The HSE told the Dáil Public Accounts Committee in September that an employee provided through an agency can cost about 40 per cent more than a conventionally-recruited staff member.

The oversight group’s report says that by the end of August the HSE had a financial deficit of just under €660 million.

This was made up of an overspend on pay of €172.5 million, a deficit on non-pay expenditure of €423.6 million and a shortfall in income of €63.2 million.

Within Government there are concerns the overall HSE deficit could hit €1 billion by the end of the year.

The report indicates the health service is experiencing a significant reduction in income as a result of the abolition of private medical practice in public hospitals. Under changes introduced as part of the Sláintecare health reforms, consultants who had signed up to the public-only contract – which offered higher salaries – could not see fee-paying patients from the beginning of this year.

Previously hospitals as well as doctors received payments in respect of private patients treated in public facilities.

[ How can runaway spending in the health service be reined in?Opens in new window ]

“Income remains a challenge, driven by reduced income from private consultant work as a result of public-only consultant contract implementation. Expected income from private consultant activity is behind August year-to-date budget (€99.0 million/44.2 per cent variance) and total such income for August year-to-date is approximately €91 million lower than the same period in 2025,” the report says.

The report maintains that demand for care in hospitals is also significantly higher than set out in the HSE’s national service plan (NSP) for the year.

“Continued demand growth [above NSP levels] is evident across urgent and emergency care. Over 1.1 million people attended emergency departments by August, representing a 7.2 per cent increase on last year and 4.7 per cent more than the NSP plan allowed for.” 

“Admission including over [age] 75-plus remain high year on year.”

The report also says the HSE spent €27 million more than anticipated in its budget to provide what is known as surge capacity to prevent patients having to be treated on trolleys.

“Total surge capacity of 124,288 has been utilised August year-to-date. This is 44.1 per cent more than last year and is necessary to keep patients off trolleys. The incremental costs associated with this are estimated to be €27 million higher than last year.

“Demand has also outpaced targets in other areas such as cancer care and home support (August year-to-date). Demand has risen this year across symptomatic breast and rapid lung clinics with activity running 19.5 per cent and 23.4 per cent above NSP targets respectively. The number of patients having completed radical radiotherapy treatment is 17.5 per cent above the NSP target.”
news.summary: Employees hired via agencies can cost about 40 per cent more than directly employed staff, HSE tells PAC

news.title: Public pay deal must give most to those who are really squeezed
news.text:
“What do they expect us to live on?” one striker on the picket lines asked The Irish Times this week. “Nobody can survive on the wages we’re getting.”

“I think it’s important to say this is for everyone,” said another. “The Government are just squeezing us so hard with the cost of living and yeah, we need more money just to survive.”

It was a refrain heard through the extensive and largely positive media coverage of the strike (RTÉ seems especially keen) on Wednesday: it is impossible to survive on public sector wages. Workers have been hammered by increases in the cost of living. They can’t afford to live.

This is a perhaps understandable exaggeration to make a point, though it is also another example of how moderation is disappearing from our political debate. Public servants are not unable to survive, obviously; they may be short of money, but they are getting by. However, one thing that has been absent from much of the debate is what exactly are public servants – teachers, nurses, gardaí, civil servants and so on – actually paid? Are they all as badly off as the coverage might suggest?

It is certainly true that there are many low-paid workers in the public service who are struggling to get by. They have seen their living standards squeezed and – for younger workers – have little prospect of owning their own home and building the life that they might aspire to. But is low pay endemic across the public sector, in the way that the strikers seem to believe it is?

[ ‘My pay hasn’t gone up – and everything else has’: Public sector workers have their sayOpens in new window ]

This year’s budget estimates show that the State directly employs 403,000 people funded by the exchequer this year, for which the wage bill is €31.2 billion – giving an average of €77,400 per head. Of course that is a clumsy way of looking at it, and it fails to take account of lots of things. But it tells us something, all the same.

Let’s look at some individual sectors. According to data from the Department of Education, there are 43,451 primary teachers at the end of June, with a total wage bill of €3.96 billion, giving an average of more than €91,000 annually.

Letter writers, hold your pens – this does not mean that a typical primary teacher is earning this much. There are principals who earn more, and young teachers who earn a lot less. Teachers may receive allowances and top-ups for good reasons, though they tend not to shout about this (understandably) during pay negotiations. The primary schoolteachers’ union, the Irish National Teachers’ Organisation, cites a figure from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) for average pay as €70,629 in 2025.

For secondary teachers, the total number is 35,707 and the total pay bill is €3.08 billion, so the average figure is €86,000 – again subject to the caveats entered above for primary teachers. The OECD figure for average secondary teacher pay is €69,747.

What about doctors and nurses? The total figure for nurses and midwives employed is just under 50,000, with a total pay bill of €4.4 billion; an average of €88,000 a year. For doctors, the total bill for 15,631 medical and dental staff is €3.1 billion, giving an average of €198,000. 

[ Stephen Collins: Unsustainable pay increases for public sector workers will put Ireland’s stability at riskOpens in new window ]

No, this does not tell us that a typical nurse on the ward earns nearly €90,000. Lots of nurses earn less, and some on higher grades earn more. The averages don’t tell us everything. But they don’t tell us nothing, either.

For gardaí, there is less rooting around in Government budget figures required, as the Central Statistics Office compiles quarterly figures that clearly identify the earnings of gardaí as a distinct category. They show consistently that gardaí are the best paid part of the public service, with average weekly earnings and average weekly paid hours in the second quarter of this year of €1,833.73 and 43.2 hours respectively. It should be said that one of the reasons for these comparatively high garda earnings is that gardaí tend to do a lot of overtime.

Let us leave aside for now three other very important aspects of public sector pay: the value of guaranteed pensions, which are so expensive as to be nowadays unbuyable in the private sector; the value of job security; and the pay premium that many public sector workers enjoy over their private sector counterparts.

Instead, consider another aspect of employment largely confined to the public sector: the system of automatic increments (ie increases in salary), which means that workers are rewarded for getting older, rather than better, at their jobs. These are not, I regret to say, the same thing. Teachers, for instance, have a 25-point scale; nurses have a 13-point scale.

[ The Irish Times view on the public sector strike: mutually agreed obstructionOpens in new window ]

The people in the public sector who are squeezed the most are younger workers who are low on the increments scale, and who have to contend with high rents and housing costs, worst in Dublin. A city where teachers, nurses and gardaí can’t afford to live is a disaster. But the system operated by the unions and the State works to the disadvantage of younger public servants and the advantage of their older colleagues. A flat percentage increase in pay benefits the older public servants more while their younger co-workers struggle.

It follows that the people who should benefit most – or maybe exclusively – from a new pay deal are younger public servants in cities. Older public servants high up the increments scale do not need the help as much as they do. Whatever the total amount of the pay deal, the pay increases funded by it should be targeted towards those who need them most. The increments system should be reformed. The unions should seek and the Government should agree a Dublin or city weighting. That would be a real demonstration of one of the unions’ favourite ideas – solidarity.
news.summary: Those under the greatest pressure are younger workers who have to contend with high rents and housing costs

news.text: Public lotteries have been a popular going concern for centuries. The prospect of winning big with a low stake is undeniably attractive – it could be you, as the famous slogan goes. In a fast-paced, lifestyle-focused social media age, the lottery takes on an ever more enviable quality when you can scroll through video after video of happy jackpot winners enjoying their prizes. Such a strategy is key to the success of competition giveaway platforms like Ooosch, which has been operating in Ireland and the UK since the turn of the decade. But do outlets such as Ooosch represent a form of gambling? If so, is regulation required? And if not, why not? On this episode of The Indo Daily, host Fionnán Sheahan is joined by Irish Independent journalists John Meagher and Sean Pollock to examine the ever-changing face of public giveaways.
