news.title: Crimes committed by Kinahan cartel when alleged gang boss Daniel controlled it
news.text: These are the crimes committed by the Kinahan cartel when Daniel allegedly controlled it. An Irish Sunday Mirror analysis has found a litany of murders and attempted hits carried out by the cartel in the 536 days that Kinahan, 49, is charged with controlling its activities. Most of the offences - between October 18, 2015 and April 6, 2017, happened in Ireland, but two took place in Spain. One was the murder of an innocent man, while the other was an attempt to kill Gerry “The Monk” Hutch . A comprehensive breakdown of this period shows that in early November 2015, there was a botched assassination attempt on Daniel Kinahan at an event in the Red Cow Hotel in West Dublin. Kinahan’s bodyguards noticed the occupants of a car acting suspiciously and threw a bin at them, scaring them off. Gardai believed the Hutch gang were behind the attempted killing, but the Kinahans wrongly blamed David “Daithi” Douglas, who had IRA links, and Darren Kearns, who was a convicted drug dealer. Kinahan is charged with a single offence, but it is understood the Garda file contains several crimes they allege Kinahan directed. The incidents which took place between October 2015 and April, 2017 include: November 9, 2015 : The cartel decides convicted armed robber Daithi Douglas is responsible and shoots him as he walks his dog in Cabra, north Dublin. He survives. December 11, 2015 : The Kinahans order another attack on Derek Hutch in prison. Again, he survives. December 30, 2015 : The Kinahans move against Daithi Douglas’ friend Darren Kearns (35) and shoot him dead in front of his wife as they leave a pub complex in north Dublin. December 31, 2015 : Gerry “The Monk” Hutch escapes a Kinahan assassination attempt while he enjoys New Year’s Eve in a pub in Puerto Del Carmen in Lanzarote. Two men wearing balaclavas and sporting firearms enter Mulligan’s Irish pub in the Old Town – but the Monk had moved away from his seat moments earlier. February 8, 2016 : The Garda’s Emergency Response Unit is brought on to the streets to try to prevent more attacks following the Regency Hotel shooting. But just hours later, a Kinahan gang targets the Monk’s brother, Eddie “Neddy” Hutch (58) and shoots him repeatedly. He dies at the scene. February 29, 2016 : Vinnie Ryan, 25, is blasted to death at McKee Road, Finglas. He was a brother of murdered Real IRA boss Alan Ryan. Gardai blame the Kinahan cartel for his murder. March 23, 2016 : Noel “Kingsize” Duggan, 55, a lifelong pal of The Monk, is shot dead at his home in Ratoath, Co Meath. Gardai believe the Kinahans killed him because of his friendship with Mr Hutch. April 14, 2016 : Innocent Martin O'Rourke , 24 , shot dead on Sheriff St, Dublin by mistake. The Kinahans were looking for another man, who is a friend of the Hutches. April 25, 2016 : Michael Barr, 34, is shot dead at the Sunset House bar, central Dublin by a Kinahan hit team. May 24, 2016 : Gareth Hutch, 35, a nephew of the Monk, is shot dead at Avondale House flats in central Dublin. June 18, 2016 : Gardai arrest a man after seizing a pistol in south Dublin. Officers believe the target was a Hutch gang member. July 1, 2016 : Daithi Douglas is targeted again by the Kinahan cartel in central Dublin. This time they manage to kill him. August 17, 2016 : Innocent Trevor O'Neill, 40. is shot dead in front of his family in Mallorca. The intended target was Jonathan Hutch, a nephew of the Monk. September 2, 2016 : The Monk’s brother Johnny (63) – Jonathan’s father – survives a murder attempt at his home in north central Dublin. Several shots are fired at him, but the hitman misses. December 2, 2016 : Kinahan hitman Glen Clarke is found shot in a car in Leixlip, Co Kildare . He was the suspect for the killings of Martin O’Rourke and Trevor O’Neill – both of whom were shot by mistake. December 22, 2016 : Noel Kirwan, 62, is shot dead in Clondalkin, west Dublin. Gardai believe the Kinahan cartel targeted him because he was seen with the Monk at Eddie Hutch’s funeral. Sean McGovern is currently charged with his murder. January 24, 2017 : Gardai score a massive hit against the Kinahan cartel. Officers from DOCB raid a warehouse near Rathcoole in south Dublin. They find the cartel’s main arsenal of 13 pistols, a submachine gun and an assault rifle. Three men are arrested, including Dubliner Declan Brady, now 59, a key Kinahan ally. April 4, 2017 : Armed gardai arrest Estonian hitman Imre Arakas , 58, in Dublin as he prepares to launch a Kinahan hit against James ”Maggo” Gately, a key Hutch ally. Last week, it emerged that alleged mob boss Daniel Kinahan is set to make a bid for freedom . Darragh Mackin, a solicitor for the 49-year-old, told the three judges of the Special Criminal Court on Monday morning that the accused will be making a bail application in the coming weeks. That will have to be made in front of a High Court judge. And the court also heard that Mr Kinahan had been investigated for two offences - one in Dubai and one in Spain - and had been acquitted of both. Mr Kinahan, who is facing a single charge, appeared in front of the non jury court in central Dublin in person in a hearing that lasted two minutes. It was his third appearance since he was extradited from the United Arab Emirates on August 9 after a long-running Garda inquiry. He was remanded in custody on that occasion and has been in Portlaoise Prison in Co Laois ever since. The businessman is charged with directing the activities of a crime gang between October 18, 2015 and April 6, 2017. His second appearance was last Monday, via video link from Portlaoise, when the court heard Mr Mackin, of Belfast’s Phoenix Law, would be coming on record to represent him. Mr Kinahan, who wore glasses, a grey suit and a black shirt, did not speak during the two-minute hearing, but conferred briefly with Mr Mackin afterwards. Prosecution counsel Dominic McGinn told the court Kinahan had been extradited from the UAE and that it was a complex case. He said there was a “complex factual matrix” in the case and that work has been continuing on the book of evidence against Mr Kinahan since he was charged. To illustrate the complexity, Mr McGinn said Irish authorities had sent a 189 page statement of facts sent to the UAE over the extradition. He asked for a remand to December 21, when the book of evidence will be served on Mr Kinahan. Mr Mackin then told the court that Mr Kinahan would be making a bail application “in the coming weeks”. He said he was also seeking disclosure on two international investigations into Mr Kinahan, and that he had been acquitted on both. Those relate to an organised crime investigation in Spain and a probe into money laundering in Dubai. Mr Macken also said the trial timetable needed to factor in an expert examination of the digital evidence in the case, as the defence is seeking to have this evidence examined by expert witnesses. The case was adjourned to December 21 for service of a book of evidence. Subscribe to our newsletter for the latest news from the Irish Mirror direct to your inbox: Sign up here .

news.title: Cost of living: Minister confirms exact date thousands of workers will get over €1,600 wage increase
news.text: The Minister for Finance has revealed that from January 1, 2027, the national minimum wage will rise by €0.79 per hour to €14.94 per hour, as part of Budget 2027. Workers clocking up 40 hours per week stand to be approximately €31 better off weekly, or roughly €1,600 more per year. This rise will take effect from 1 January 2027. With more than 165,000 people estimated to be earning the minimum wage, the boost will be warmly welcomed by many. While the majority of employees are entitled to the minimum wage, certain exceptions do apply, reports RSVP Live . You are not entitled to get the national minimum wage if you are: Employed by a close relative (for example, a spouse, civil partner or parent) In a statutory apprenticeship Aged under 20 Different minimum wage rates apply for those under the age of 20. The increase arrives as a national living wage is set to replace the national minimum wage in the coming years. The living wage will be calculated at 60% of the median wage in any given year. The national minimum wage will remain in place until the 60% living wage is fully phased in, continuing to rise incrementally in the meantime. This also comes as people can still apply for the Fuel Allowance, following the season's launch at the end of September. The Fuel Allowance is a financial support package designed to help cover heating costs throughout the colder months, with only one person per household eligible to claim it. The Fuel Allowance season generally runs from late September through to April, offering €38 per week across 28 weeks, or as two lump sum payments totalling €1,064. Budget 2027 will see the Fuel Allowance rise by €5, moving from €38 to €43 per week. Additionally, the income threshold for a single person aged 66 or over will jump from €534 to €640.80. The Fuel Allowance remains available this winter, however, should you submit your application after the Fuel Allowance season has commenced, payments will not be backdated. Ireland's Lara Gillespie triumphs at Cycling World Championships in China

It’s the Wicklow native’s second gold at the event, having previously won in 2025.

10.30am, 18 Oct 2026

Share options

IRELAND’S LARA GILLESPIE has won a gold medal after topping the points race at the UCI Track World Championships in Shanghai, China.

The 25km race was 100 laps, with the field contesting 10 sprints.

The 25-year-old Irish star was one of three frontrunners early on.

But Denmark’s Amalie Dideriksen (37 points) and Belgium’s Shari Bossuyt (35 points) finished second and third, as maximum points in sprints two and five were key to Gillespie’s (42 points) triumph.

Advertisement

It made up for the agony of just missing out on gold in the scratch race earlier this week, when Gillespie finished millimetres behind Dutch rider Lorena Wiebes.

“It’s all sinking in now,” she said. “I’m just so happy I could pull this off. I came really close the other day, and I think that really just pushed me on there today because I was really annoyed with that second place.

 ”Overall, a really good week and I really just can’t thank Cycling Ireland and Sport Ireland enough for all the support over the last few years and all the people back home who are getting those key sessions in with me, helping me get fast for the track, so I really just want to say thank you to everyone.”

It is Gillespie’s second World Championship title in two years, having previously claimed gold in the Elimination in Chile in 2025. 

The Wicklow native is set to receive a warm welcome when she arrives back at Dublin Airport at 8am on Monday.

news.title: Lara Gillespie wins gold at track cycling world championships
news.text:
Lara Gillespie produced a sensational ride to win the gold medal in the points race on the final day of the UCI Track World Championships in Shanghai, earning herself another coveted rainbow jersey in utterly commanding style.

A year on from becoming the first Irish woman to win a UCI world track title in any event, Gillespie was prominent throughout the 100 laps of the 25km race, which came down to a three-way battle for gold in the final sprint for the line, where double points were on offer.

By nailing second in that sprint, Gillespie took her total to 42 points, five points ahead of Amalie Dideriksen from Denmark, with Belgium’s Shari Bossuyt, the early leader, winning bronze on 35 points.

Gillespie was unquestionably the strongest and most astute by the end, the 25-year-old Wicklow rider adding to her silver medal won in the scratch race on Wednesday’s opening day of competition.

Points are won in 10 different sprints, after every 10 laps, during the race, with Gillespie, Dideriksen and Bossuyt also the only riders to secure the 20 bonus points for lapping the rest of the bunch. Gillespie won the second and fifth sprint, finished second in the seventh and ninth, before her second place in the final sprint earned her the outright victory.

Just one point up going into that final sprint, critically she finished ahead of Dideriksen, the former road race world champion, with Gillespie timing her last effort to near perfection.

Defending world champion Yareli Acevedo from Mexico won those final sprint points, but finished up a long way back in fourth, with just 13 points.

Gillespie had finished just inches short of gold in the scratch race, won by Dutch star Lorena Wiebes. She then finished fifth in the omnium on Friday, moving up two places in the final race, but just short of the podium.

Her breakthrough win on the track came in the elimination race at last year’s UCI Track World Championships in Santiago, Chile – and she also won bronze in the points race in 2024.

Since winning in Santiago, Gillespie became the first Irish rider to complete all three major stage races for women – finishing fourth in the points classification in the Giro d’Italia, having taken on both the Tour de France Femmes and the Vuelta de España last summer. She then won two Irish national titles in June (the time trial and road race), before finishing third in the women’s Tour of Poland.

[ Meet Lorenzo Finn, Italy’s teenage cycling super talent with an Irish grandmotherOpens in new window ]

Last weekend, Gillespie finished second in the three-day Tour of Chongming Island in Shanghai, with two successive runner-up positions in the last two stages, her best result in a World Tour stage race. She now finishes the season with another rainbow jersey to add to her collection, looking eminently capable of winning many more.

Katie-George Dunlevy has also previously won multiple UCI Para-Cycling track titles.
news.summary: The Wicklow rider adds to her silver medal won on Wednesday’s opening day of competition in Shanghai
news.author: Ian O'riordan

A PROPOSAL TO establish a national office for women in the Catholic Church in Ireland has been rejected by a majority of delegates at a major assembly examining the future of the church.

More than 300 delegates gathered in Gormanston, Co Meath, on Saturday for the Irish National Synodal Assembly, where they considered 35 proposals aimed at shaping the Church’s future.

The gathering brought together lay people, clergy and members of religious communities from across Ireland, as part of a consultation process launched by the country’s Catholic bishops in 2021.

The process sought to examine issues including the role of women, the legacy of abuse, declining religious participation and how the Church should respond to changing Irish society.

Among the proposals put before delegates was the establishment of a national office for women, described in the assembly’s voting document as an initiative aimed at “mainstreaming women’s inclusion”.

The proposal was one of several concerning women’s roles in the Church, an issue which has featured prominently in discussions about reform.

According to voting results released following the assembly, 56% of delegates said they did not recommend establishing the office.

Fewer than one in five delegates supported the establishment of the national office: just 12% said they highly recommended the proposal, while a further 6% recommended it.

Another 27% said the proposal required further discernment.

The recommendations from the assembly will now be passed to the Irish Catholic Bishops’ Conference, which is due to meet next week.

The voting results yesterday are recommendations from the assembly rather than binding decisions, with the bishops responsible for considering what measures will be taken forward.

The national office proposal attracted the highest proportion of “do not recommend” responses of the 35 proposals considered by delegates.

Other proposals concerning women’s participation received varying levels of support.

A proposal for women to be more visible and valued in liturgy, public prayer and public discourse was highly recommended by 38% of delegates and recommended by a further 23%.

Meanwhile, 42% highly recommended an ongoing exploration of women’s ministry, including the diaconate, with another 12% recommending it.

Advertisement

However, 27% said they did not recommend that proposal, while 19% believed it required further discernment.

A separate proposal concerning women and the domestic church received support from 40% of delegates, while another 40% said it required further consideration.

Other reforms

The assembly also considered proposals concerning healing within the Church, including the need to address the harm experienced by survivors of abuse and others who have been excluded or hurt.

Some 89% of delegates recommended or highly recommended making healing a priority in the future work of the synodal process.

A separate proposal to establish a commission for healing received support from 64% of delegates.

Una Allen, from the Archdiocese of Tuam and convenor of the Synodal Pathway’s working group on healing, said the Church now needed to move beyond listening to people’s experiences.

“Healing needs to be front and centre on our ongoing Synodal Journey,” Allen said.

“Listening to each other’s concerns may be all very well and good, but now the Church needs to act to benefit all those who have been excluded, abused, wounded and hurt.”

There was also strong support for measures aimed at engaging young people.

Some 84% of delegates backed youth coordinators and youth advisory committees, while the same proportion supported a national formation and training pathway for youth and young adult ministry.

‘Manage a diminishing ecclesial landscape’

The assembly also heard an address from Cardinal Mario Grech, Secretary General of the Synod of Bishops, who warned that the Catholic Church in Ireland needed to make concrete changes rather than simply manage its decline.

Grech, who addressed delegates by video link, pointed to declining religious practice, an ageing priesthood and the legacy of abuse as challenges facing the Church.

He said the Church needed to review its existing structures, including parish pastoral councils and bishops’ conferences, and consider whether they remained fit for purpose.

“The danger in all of this is that management of decline becomes the operative pastoral paradigm,” Grech said.

“Do not measure the future of the Church simply by what is disappearing. Discern what the Holy Spirit is bringing to birth. Do not simply manage a diminishing ecclesial landscape. Re-position the Church for mission within it.”

Grech also described Ireland as “missionary territory”, despite its long history of sending Catholic missionaries abroad.

He urged the Church to move from discussing reforms towards implementing them.

Andrew Walsh

news.title: Is it cheaper to leave heating on low all day? Martin Lewis finally settles the debate
news.text: As the heating season begins, the perennial question resurfaces - is it cheaper to keep your heating running throughout the day, or switch it off when you're out? Advocates of the "low and slow" approach argue that keeping radiators at a steady low temperature all day offers superior energy efficiency. Energy bills shot up this month a number of major suppliers recently announced price hikes which are set to take effect in October. Bord Gáis Energy increased its prices for both gas and electricity customers from October 9, with an analysis from Bonkers.ie concluding that this will add €177 a year to a household's annual electricity bill and €140 to their yearly gas bill. Meanwhile Gas and electricity prices for SSE Airtricity customers increased by almost 10 per cent this month. The major energy supplier is increasing the unit rate of its electricity by 9.4 per cent and its daily standing charge by 6.1 per cent. This means the typical electricity bill will go up by 8.9 per cent or €172 a year if based on average usage, according to the supplier. With daytime temperatures plummeting as we hurtle towards winter, many households are once again questioning the most cost effective way to keep warm. And with energy bills still high amid the ongoing cost of living crisis, heating homes has become a major source of stress for many households. For years, one question has sparked endless debate - is it cheaper to leave the heating on low all day, or only turn it on when you need it? Some swear by keeping a constant low heat. However, not everyone agrees. Martin Lewis ' Money Saving Expert has stepped in to resolve the debate definitively. Drawing on expertise from the Energy Saving Trust, British Gas, an independent plumber and MoneySavers social media, this represents the most thoroughly researched answer available. The conclusion appears to be that "leaving the heating on all day leads to greater heat loss and means higher cost", according to MSE. That being said, there are legitimate arguments on both sides - and the right answer may depend on your particular situation. The Energy Saving Trust maintains that keeping the heating on all day is the less efficient option. Its guidance is simple: only warm your home when it's genuinely necessary, ensuring you're paying exclusively for what you actually use, reports the Mirror Fitting a programmable thermostat is commonly considered the most efficient method to maintain your home at the ideal temperature during times that suit your routine. That being said, if you have a contemporary boiler or heat pump, work remotely, or spend the majority of your evenings and weekends indoors, Heat Geek argues that the gradual, consistent heating strategy proves more cost-effective. Heat pumps are a low-carbon type of electric heating that extract warmth from outdoor air, while a modern condensing boiler, installed after 2005, recaptures some waste heat before it escapes. In these circumstances, maintaining a constant indoor temperature of 18 or 19°C could work out more affordable. Sustaining lower temperatures with gentle heating - meaning you avoid cranking up the thermostat whenever you sense cold - enables the boiler to reclaim more waste heat during operation. However, this technique might not suit those who are frequently away from home or have plasterboard walls, which typically warm up considerably faster. Conversely, if your property has cavity wall and loft insulation or underfloor heating, the gradual, steady approach is the one to choose. Some also advocate for maintaining heating on a low, constant setting, contending that it stops moisture accumulating within the walls each time the system is turned off - which can drain heat from your property while also promoting the development of damp and mould. Since there isn't a straightforward solution, MSE suggests a trial and error method - measuring your energy consumption with each approach. Record meter readings at the beginning and conclusion of each testing period and evaluate the outcomes, ensuring the temperatures during the comparison weeks are as alike as possible. news.summary: Money Saving Expert Martin Lewis has weighed in on the age-old debate about whether it's cheaper to leave your heating on all day or turn it off when you're not at home, sharing key energy saving tips to help you save money on energy bills

This Halloween, think of the Ulsterwomen labelled as witches by Irish-speaking southerners

Bean Ultach speaks to a universal truth, the bad people are from somewhere else. 

10.01am, 18 Oct 2026

Share options

Darach Ó Séaghdha

Author and linguist

In Calling 353, bestselling Motherfoclóir author and podcaster Darach Ó Séaghdha casts a linguistic eye on how we talk about what it means to be Irish, the signs we post to each other about Irishness – and what really lies beneath it all. 

SPOOKY SEASON IS in full swing at the moment, despite certain shops and taverns already putting Christmas decorations up.

Around the estate where I live, all sorts of plastic ghouls decorate the doors of houses who intend to participate in the scary festivities of late October.

The neighbourhood WhatsApp group has already flipped from passive-aggressive seething to aggressive-aggressive mayhem as representatives of different parenting styles accuse each other of being The Worst. Maybe they should dress up as each other on the 31st?

One enduringly popular costume for adults, especially the Mams doling out sweets at the door, is that of the witch.

Like a Christmas tree, it can be as simple or as elaborate as you like. If Halloween is as Irish as they say, and if the witch is such a timeless cultural motif, then we can expect a similarly enduring word in Irish for witches, can’t we? Well…

There are actually a few words and terms for witch in Irish, which hint at how the concept wasn’t as rigid here as elsewhere.

Witch hunts in Ireland did not happen at the scale noted in other European countries or the American places those European countries colonised.

If you ever want to fall down an internet wormhole, you could do worse than click on The Survey of Scottish Witchcraft which is a database of over 4,000 people in Scotland accused of witchery, searchable by name, location, witch-hunter, nature of demonic pact (kissing the devil’s bottom appears to have been popular), ritual objects used, and year.

The critical mass for such a database in Ireland just isn’t there, which leads me to the first Irish term for witch we will discuss today: Bean Ultach, literally meaning an Ulsterwoman.

In Dinneen’s dictionary, the meanings listed for Ultach are “Ulster, Ultonian, uncouth, cruel, “wise” (his air quotes, not mine), magical”… and the Jesuit lexicographer adds that this magical meaning is shared by tuaisceartach (northern).

And in case you thought that if a Bean Ultach was a witch then a teenage witch must be the cailín version, you’d be wrong: a Cailín Ultáin is the name for “a girl frequenting St Ultan’s Pattern”, which was a pilgrimage in Cavan where participants would leave an item of clothing behind after visiting a dried out holy well surrounded by whitethorn bushes (which are, of course, not to be trifled with).

If you think there’s something spooky and significant about the holy well in question being empty and surrounded by fairy bushes, well you wouldn’t be alone.

Speakers of Ulster Irish don’t call witches that, and it speaks to a universal truth – the bad people are from somewhere else, and if they’re actually not from somewhere else then we will call the part of here they are from “somewhere else”.

Advertisement

The Derry Girls, having the craic at Halloween.Channel 4 Comedy

Channel 4 Comedy

Consider how Americans resile against using the metric system unless they’re talking about imported drugs – the foreignness of cocaine and heroin are underlined by their existence in grams and kilos.

We translate the titles of The Three Musketeers and The Little Prince but not Das Kapital or Mein Kampf. If it’s foreign it’s bad, and if it’s bad it’s foreign.

So in the southern parts of Ireland the witches are from Ulster and in the work of the most celebrated English writer, the witches are Scottish. Or are they from Ulster too?

Aye of Newt

The English language doesn’t need much protection, but those who take it upon themselves to do so will often call it “the language of Shakespeare”.

Their implication is that when a language is lost, a treasury of poetry and wisdom is lost with it. And I agree wholeheartedly, which is why English should be able to exist without erasing other languages!

Recently, Shakespeare in film has been intimately linked to the Irish cultural moment – Jessie Buckley and Paul Mescal in Hamnet, Michael Fassbender in Macbeth and Andrew Scott’s forthcoming film Elsinore.

I suppose Kenneth Branagh has done a bit of Shakespeare too. And the line “I have done the State some service” has such a prominent place in recent Irish history that you’d almost forget the Bard said it first.

Of Shakespeare’s 37 plays, only 13 are set in England (the only one of his works to mention America is, prophetically, The Comedy of Errors).

Most of them were set in places that he and his audiences would never see, and have contributed more to the Anglophone perception of these places than any local achievement – if someone says “a forest near Athens”, you will think of A Midsummer Night’s Dream before you think of Mount Parnitha, home to Europe’s only rainforest (even the people who claim it isn’t a “true” rainforest consider it to be an ecological wonder in need of protection).

Shakespeare’s plays are a foundational body of work in the Anglosphere and while they speak to the human condition in a powerful and resonant way, they are exotic by design. So what happens when a character who is themselves foreign to audiences meets someone who is foreign to them – such as three witches?

Macbeth has been translated into Irish, Lowland Scots and Scots Gaelic – the name Mac Beatha, the son of life, uncovers a new meaning in an old and very familiar text.

And having the witches speak Irish rather than Scots Gaelic in the Scots Gaelic version (and Scots Gaelic in the Lowland Scots version) has been an effective way to establish that spooky difference.

Halloween isn’t far away now and if you do meet a Bean Ultach, do say “cad é mar atá tú (k’jay mar a tahtoo) by way of a friendly greeting.

They’re not as scary as the old dictionaries would have you believe – sure I married one of them.

Darach Ó Séaghdha

news.title: Limerick farm offers unique support for people with dementia
news.text:
Social farming for the brain' is a new dementia support group that meets weekly on Doon Social Farm in Co. Limerick.

A collaboration between the Alzheimer Society of Ireland (ASI) and Doon Social Farm in Doon, the initiative is aimed at people living with dementia who still enjoy activities, especially outdoors such as gardening or farming, according to Marian Clarke, farm manager.

Doon social Farm is a certified organic farm, social enterprise and charity.

"Every Tuesday between 11:00am and 1:00pm the group gets together to have a cup of tea before setting out on the farm. 

"Activities include cleaning vegetables for the shops; putting labels on bags or egg boxes; cleaning the goat shed; or even just walking around the wetlands.

"Bianca Barry and Aoife Nolan, the two facilitators, throw in a bit of nature, art, music, and of course, there is plenty of chat and laughs," the farm manager told Agriland.

"Social farming for the brain is a practical, community-based support that helps people with young-onset and early-stage dementia stay active, connected and involved in the things that matter to them," said Sean Donal O'Shea, dementia advisor, Limerick city and county.

The placements continue as long as the individuals are able to participate and benefit from them to improve their quality of life, he said.

"The initiative is about person-centred support and living well after diagnosis; helping people maintain connection, confidence, meaningful activity and involvement in their community," he said.

"A dementia diagnosis can be isolating and one of the questions people often ask is: 'What can I do now?' 'Social farming for the brain' offers a practical response," O'Shea added. 

"It gives people an opportunity to stay active, spend time outdoors, take part in meaningful activities, and connect with people who understand their experience."

As farm manager, Clarke said she enjoys seeing Doon Social Farm come alive with all the diverse groups that participate in the programme.

"The farming for the brain group thrive in the outdoor world of nature.

"Farming gives them meaningful activities that contribute to a healthy food system that cares for nature, and best of all, they get on and have a laugh with everyone," she said.

"We are delighted to be collaborating with the Alzheimer Society of Ireland to make this experience possible for people living with dementia in our community.

"Our mission at Doon is to provide farm-based programmes and activities for communities to foster wellness and connection in the healing embrace of nature," the farm manager said. 

The farm operates independently of the Social Farming Ireland network.

Doon Social Farm was started in 2019 by Ballyhoura Rural Services (BRS) CLG, a charity that set out to reduce rural isolation through a "befriending service". 

"BRS operates in north Cork and east Limerick - the Ballyhoura region - and has grown since it started in 2010. 

"When it decided to start a social farm, the Sisters of Mercy in Doon offered the convent, the school and the farm," said Clarke.

There are 64,000 people living with dementia in Ireland, with 30 people being diagnosed every day, or 11,000 every year. 

More than 4,000 people living with dementia in Ireland are under the age of 65.

About 63% of people with dementia live at home in the community rather than in residential care, and the number of people with dementia is expected to more than double to over 150,000 by 2045 as the population ages, according to the ASI.

Much positive feedback is received from the group's members visiting Doon Social Farm: 

"Being outdoors, getting involved in the activities and spending time with people who understand what you're going through makes a real difference," one of the members told Agriland.

"Having somewhere you feel comfortable and welcome is so important. I always leave the farm in great form."

There are still places available on the programme, which is free of charge. For further details, contact the Alzheimer Society of Ireland, or Doon Social Farm.

news.title: Ireland weather: Expert pinpoints exact day first named storm of season could batter country
news.text: Ireland could see the first named storm of the year later this week, with some weather models predicting that heavy rainfall and powerful gusts will batter the country over the October Bank Holiday weekend. The country looks set to endure an extended spell of stormy weather, with two major weather models—the European ECMWF and the American GFS—signalling a prolonged period of wet and windy conditions kicking off from Thursday and persisting right through to the end of October. A number of Irish forecasters have already warned that a pair of nasty low-pressure systems could hit over the October bank holiday weekend, which runs from Saturday, October 24, to Monday, October 26, unleashing a spell of unsettled conditions. Kenneth Mc Donagh, who runs Donegal Weather Channel on Facebook, has said that a "big storm" looks set to hit Ireland next weekend following a spell of dry and sunny weather over the coming days. Now Cathal Nolan, climate scientist and founder of Ireland's Weather Channel, has revealed that one weather model shows a severe storm developing to the south of Ireland on Thursday night , which would bring " storm-force winds, heavy rain, localised flooding and the risk of some storm damage." "The GFS ( Global Forecast System) for the last couple of runs has picked up on this area of low pressure. It takes it on a track that is favourable for rapid development and for the development of some stormy conditions," Cathal said. "Perhaps gales, severe gales, even storm-force winds in this scenario but it is not the only scenario. "With The GFS as we play on during the evening, we see if developing quite rapidly and we see some storm-force winds associated with that. "If that is to materialise, it will become the first named storm of the year and it will bring with it the potential for some heavy rain, localised flooding and also the risk of some storm damage in places as well." However, Cathal cautioned that the forecast remains uncertain this far out, with another weather model predicting that the stormy conditions won't be as severe, although heavy rain is still expected to lash the country as we head towards the weekend. "If we skip across to the ECMWF ( the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecast) and we look at its outcome as we head towards the same period, it shows the same area of low pressure, the same storm depression, but it's nowhere near as deep first and foremost. "While there is still gale-force winds associated with this, it wouldn't bring significant stormy conditions, at least not for us, because it's on a more southerly track. "It would bring heavy rain and localised flooding, but not quite the same intensity in winds speeds because it's on a slightly more southerly track, it doesn't engage quite as quickly with the jetstream, therefore it doesn't develop quite as significantly. "There are some models that keep it even further to the south which would mean it hardly interacts with the jetstream at all, it doesn't get spun up and severe. "So what we are saying is, there is the potential for stormy conditions on Thursday night in particular and thereafter it looks like remaining pretty mixed and unsettled, but there is still a lot to be determined in terms of its exact track, its depth and its intensity." news.summary: The forecaster warned that the first named storm of the year could bring heavy rain, localised flooding and the risk of storm damage

news.title: ‘Canada didn’t dilute my Irish identity. It gave me the distance to understand its value’
news.text:
Growing up in south Co Dublin and attending school in Mount Anville, Jackie Gilna credits her father for giving her the broadest possible appreciation of Irish culture. Wherever possible, the family were exposed to their farming heritage. 

“My dad was from Longford. I was that Dublin jackeen. My grandmother would say how awful it was that I was being brought up in the city, and I would be made to drink the milk from a cow. But that brought me closer to an Irish experience than I would not have experienced in Dublin. 

“We were also brought all around Ireland, and my dad told me, ‘You will not leave these shores until you know every corner and you are an ambassador for your country’.”

Earlier immersion in Irish culture was a formative influence, she says, in a career that has been shaped around promoting Ireland abroad and bringing the diaspora closer. Gilna, the founder of We Are Global Irish, is on a mission to harness and grow networks of Irish communities throughout the world to support each other, places where businesses and professionals can come together to share information and help each other in practical ways. 

We Are Global Irish was launched in 2024 as a private sector company complementing the work of State agencies. As well as networking and introductions, it provides a range of practical business supports and publishes a monthly online magazine called the Irish Exchange. 

The business is registered in Canada and, while the largest element of the Irish diaspora is in North America, the venture has a global reach, she says.

“One thing that stands out to me was that the world we live in as the Irish abroad is very fragmented but, when you bring people together, everyone knows someone who knows somebody; there’s only a couple of degrees of separation. 

“We have State agencies who do phenomenal work, such as Enterprise Ireland and IDA Ireland, for example – the envy of other countries – and we work closely with them but there needed to be something in the private sector.”

[ ‘There are 30 Irish people in Brandon, Canada. You miss the craic living in a small place’Opens in new window ]

Gilna’s corporate career took shape in the Netherlands and later Canada, where she moved with her Canadian husband and their familyin 2000. For more than three decades she worked mainly with small and medium-sized businesses, helping them establish, structure and reshape for growth. 

“The diaspora didn’t really exist in the Netherlands. It was too close to home. When you come across the pond here, however, the notion of being Irish is very different ... Canada didn’t dilute my Irish identity. It gave me the distance to understand its value, commercially and culturally.”

In a forerunner of what she was to do later, Gilna helped establish the Irish Chamber of Commerce in Ottawa at the invitation of the then ambassador and says that listening to Irish people abroad over the years gave her an understanding of their desire to contribute to Ireland. 

She is very grateful to Canada for giving her the opportunity to build an independent career, build new connections, stay connected to Ireland and to add value between both countries. In this, she is in good company: some 4½ million people in Canada claim some Irish DNA, according to census data. 

Asked about the current strains in relations between Canada and the United States, and prime minister Mark Carney’s desire to form closer relations with the EU, Gilna is characteristically diplomatic. She says that, ultimately, the fundamentally strong historic and good neighbourly relationship between Canada and the United States will endure but that forging closer relations with Europe also makes sense for cultural as well as more obvious economic reasons, given the strong European roots of much of the population. 

[ ‘We’re an Irish-Canadian-French household. I’m finally getting some return on my Leaving Cert French’Opens in new window ]

She and her family have enjoyed life in the Canadian capital, where the climate varies enormously. “It can get into the minus-30s in winter but with blue skies and crisp snow. A calmness comes over us in those months. In the summer we enjoy high temperatures from May to September.

“In Ottawa you can be who you are. You don’t have to blend in and be Canadian, so it’s not a melting pot and that’s a cultural difference between here and other places.” 

Canadians can be risk averse and polite. There is a different style of doing business from the way it is done in Ireland, she says. Anyone doing business with Canada also needs to factor in the wide regional divergence between different parts of this vast country. 

“In Ireland we operate at a fast pace and the craic comes into everything, as professional and all as we are in our engagement. However, Canadians like to take things a bit slower, and they take time to adapt to our humour and our way of doing business.” 

While there are economic opportunities for Irish people wishing to find a home in Canada, she cautions anyone interested in this to do their homework thoroughly in advance, not to underestimate the challenges and, most importantly, “don’t arrive without a job”.
news.summary: Wild Geese: Jackie Gilna, Ottawa
news.author: Frank Dillon

news.title: West Dublin residents appeal for final vote against controversial land rezoning
news.text:
Dublin residents have protested against a final vote on the controversial rezoning of “ecologically unique” land due to take place on Monday. 

A demonstration against the move was held in Lucan, west Dublin, on Saturday, calling on local councillors to vote against the proposal. 

The Save St Edmundsbury Protest Committee held a walk to oppose the rezoning of the St Edmundsbury site in the Liffey valley, owned by businessmen John Magnier and JP McManus. 

The land is currently zoned as “high amenity” due to its environmental and natural amenity value.

Sites at Finnstown Castle, between Lucan and Adamstown, and at Coldcut Road, south of the Liffey Valley shopping centre, have also been proposed for rezoning.

Committee member and Independent councillor on South Dublin County Council Helen Farrell said it was not about “refusing housing in our area”.

“Rezoning has to happen in some places but the lands at St Edmundsbury are ecologically unique,” she said. 

She described the area as a “very ancient landscape and an ancient farmland and the two landscapes kind of work together.

“So there’s a very rich biodiversity and we really want to see these lands saved.”

[ Removal of ‘unconscionable’ housing ban on Magnier and McManus Liffey Valley lands urgedOpens in new window ]

Residential rezoning for the area has been proposed on numerous occasions over recent decades but refused.

Farrell believes efforts should be focused on “getting high density housing into the city centre on some of the vacant properties that have laid vacant for decades”.

Dereliction needed to be tackled, she argued, rather than building on “highly fertile agricultural lands in the middle of a food crisis and a climate crisis”. 

Councillors previously voted against rezoning the land. Now, protesters are calling on them “to vote against residential rezoning, as they did the last time”, Farrell said. 

A final vote is scheduled for Monday.

“We really want the Government to notice that this should be part of the Liffey Valley Park going forward and this is what we should leave for future generations.”

Saturday’s protest walk began outside the main entrance gates at St Edmundsbury and finished at the village green in Lucan.

[ John Magnier and JP McManus could see rich returns if €4m Liffey Valley lands are rezonedOpens in new window ]

The Irish Times previously reported that the council’s chief executive, Colm Ward, had proposed rezoning the three sites, which combined could accommodate more than 1,700 homes.

It followed an edict last summer from Minister for Housing James Browne that all local authorities must provide significant additional land for housing.

More than 1,600 submissions opposed the rezoning of the St Edmundsbury site.
news.summary: Councillors previously rejected changing the zoning of sites at St Edmundsbury, Finnstown Castle and Coldcut Road

Sitdown Sunday: Why the Cornell story is resonating worldwide

Settle down in a comfy chair with some of the week’s best longreads.

9.01am, 18 Oct 2026

Share options

IT’S A DAY of rest, and you may be in the mood for a quiet corner and a comfy chair.

We’ve hand-picked some of the week’s best reads for you to savour.

1. Why the Cornell story resonates

Alamy Stock Photo

Alamy Stock Photo

German journalist Katrin Bennhold says that the toxic ingredients which caused the alleged Cornell gang rape are not unique to American fraternities. 

(The New York Times, approx. six mins reading time)

“No matter the verdict, the defendants aren’t the only ones facing judgment. So is a culture that to this day has failed to keep women safe, in America and everywhere else.”

2. Forgiving your abductor

Michael was kidnapped in Galkayo, Somalia.Alamy Stock Photo

Alamy Stock Photo

Journalist Michael Scott Moore details his 977 days in captivity and his journey to forgiveness.

(The Guardian, approx. 30 mins reading time)

“I spent most of my time on a thin, sweat-soaked foam mattress on the floor of a dusty room. The dim concrete prison houses changed, but the filth and the circumstances didn’t. Sometimes my captors moved me into the Somali savannah – where we camped in the open and slept on the ground – and for a six-month stretch, I was held on a hijacked tuna vessel, where I joined 28 fishers from east Asia who had been captured about three weeks before I was placed on board.”

3. Only his sled dogs returned

Alamy Stock Photo

Alamy Stock Photo

Norwegian man Steffen Skjottelvik set off on a multi-year adventure through the Canadian wilderness with a pack of sled dogs – but only the dogs returned.

(The New York Times, approx. 25 mins reading time)

Advertisement

“Togo would wait for Steffen right here, among the horsetails and ferns. They had been inseparable for almost a decade, since Togo was a tiny pup — sharing their fish and caribou meat, sleeping together on a caribou hide at night. Togo knew Steffen would climb from the river and sit beside him, and they would rest their heads on each other, the way they liked to do. Steffen always came.”

4. Lazy or smart?

Alamy Stock Photo

Alamy Stock Photo

This exploratory essay looks into how elite Victorians were so successful when, in the modern era, success is seen as something you must get up early and work hard for. 

(Work in Progress, approx. 24 mins reading time)

“Maybe the Victorian elite succeeded in spite of being feckless and incompetent: the Industrial Revolution created great wealth, which they enjoyed passively and parasitically. We cannot run controlled experiments on Victorian Britain, so this thesis is hard to test. But I want to explore the possibility that a relentless focus on soft skills, team building, and intra-elite networking actually worked rather well. Huel, STEM, and cold baths have their merits. But the example of the Victorians should make us hesitate before concluding that there is only one way to rule the world.” 

5. life in lowercase

Have you noticed more people writing in lowercase? Apparently, it’s cool now.

(Wired, approx. 10 mins reading time)

“They’ll tell you it’s an aesthetic choice, a testament to informality. they’re likely a twentysomething brooklyn resident like myself, bullish on being not the voice of their generation but a voice of a generation, and definitely guilty of posting performative notes-app screenshots and pseudointellectual, stream-of-consciousness “musings” that compare charli xcx to the pope.”

6. How El Niño is impacting global fish stocks

Peruvian anchoveta.Alamy Stock Photo

Alamy Stock Photo

Warming seas and overfishing are threatening Peru’s fishing industry, and it could have widespread global consequences. 

(The Guardian, approx. 17 mins reading time)

“The vast majority of the anchoveta industry is concentrated off the coast of north-central Peru, and it is hard to overstate how economically significant this fish is. By weight, Peruvian anchoveta have made up about a 10th of the entire global commercial fishing catch since 1970, more than any other fish. Some years, the anchoveta catch is worth close to $3 billion and directly employs almost 50,000 people, close to a quarter of a million if you include indirect jobs. The Peruvian central bank is forecasting a 30.7% contraction for the fishing sector and about 78,000 job losses in 2026, and another 44,000 in 2027.”

…AND A CLASSIC FROM THE ARCHIVES…

7. Life after a doomsday cult

This BBC World Service article from 2019 looks into the life of Ben Shenton, one of seven children raised in the 1960s Australian doomsday cult The Family.

(BBC, approx. six mins reading time)

“Tucked away in their home on the shores of Australia’s Lake Eildon, behind heavy foliage and barbed wire, seven children in matching outfits and bleached blonde haircuts were finishing their morning hatha yoga practice when they heard a commotion on the stairs.”

news.title: Autumn grass management tips for a successful spring on sheep farms
news.text:
Autumn is the starting point of the grassland year, Teagasc has said.

Management and decisions made in this period have a direct effect on the quality and availability of grass the following spring.

Dr. Philip Creighton of Teagasc's Animal and Grassland Research and Innovation Centre in Athenry, Co. Galway, has shared some key advice.

Dr. Creighton said: "To ensure adequate grass availability for ewes at lambing in March, you should begin to close paddocks from mid to late October onwards.

He stressed that very little grass will be grown during December and January.

"When grass growth starts to increase again in February and March, it is the earlier closed fields that will respond quickest to the increasing temperatures and an early application of fertiliser," he said.

Extended grazing system

Dr. Creighton explained that where winter housing is not available or practical, ewes can be managed in an extended grazing system on grass built up earlier in the autumn with grass allocated daily or every second day. 

He said: "Ewes could also be wintered on forage crops, away to winter grazing or with hay/silage and concentrate supplementation outdoors.

He said the temptation to re-graze closed fields in December/January will always be there.

This is especially in years where autumn grass supply is good or where winter feed reserves are low or poor quality, but this grass is "worth much more in the spring to the freshly-lambed ewe than in mid-pregnancy". 

"A ewe’s feed requirement in mid-pregnancy is approximately half that of a ewe in early lactation producing milk for two lambs," Dr. Creighton added.

He said that the first paddocks closed should be sheltered and close to the lambing area. 

"Where autumn grass covers are high, an electric fence can be used to reduce the area available for grazing at any one time to make ewes graze down to the desired post-grazing height of around 4cm," he said. 

"It is important to clean swards out as tight as possible when closing, as carrying higher residuals over winter will lead to a lot of dead material accumulating at the base of the sward which will depress grass growth in the spring and reduce quality."

International students

news.title: RTSS extension leaves excluded operators facing two different outcomes
news.text:
The extension of the Road Transporters Support Scheme (RTSS) will provide additional support for existing applicants, but operators excluded from the scheme face two different outcomes: an appeals process for those refused support, and no reopening for businesses that did not apply.

The Department of Transport has confirmed that operators who submitted an application but were refused support for some or all of their vehicles will have an opportunity to appeal.

However, businesses that did not submit an application will have no opportunity to enter the scheme under the extension. That distinction is central to what the Government’s decision means for operators who have yet to receive support.

Appeals route for refused applicants

A Department of Transport spokesperson said: “Government approved an extension to the Road Transporters Support Scheme on Tuesday 13 October. The extension will allow applicants to receive an additional payment for the months of September and October. Applicants do not need to submit another application; the Department will issue payments directly to applicants based on the information provided previously. The Scheme will not reopen for new applications. A separate appeals process will be launched for operators that submitted an application but were refused support for some or all of their vehicles. The Department will write to those applicants in the coming days with details of how to submit an appeal. The Department is also working with trade representative bodies to facilitate online information sessions to assist their members with the appeals process.”

For businesses refused support, the appeals process offers an opportunity to have those decisions reviewed. It will also cover operators whose applications were only partially successful because some vehicles were excluded.

The Department will contact affected applicants directly, with online information sessions being organised through trade representative bodies to help members prepare their appeals.

Important questions remain

The statement does not specify the grounds on which appeals can be made, what evidence operators will need to provide, or the deadline for submissions.

It also leaves an important question unanswered: if an appeal succeeds, will the operator receive all support due under the original scheme alongside the additional September and October payment?

Operators will also need clarity on how disputed vehicle eligibility will be assessed and how quickly appeals will be decided.

For a business awaiting a review, the practical value of the process will depend on clear guidance, an opportunity to address the reasons for refusal and a timely decision.

No route for new applicants

The position is different for operators who did not previously submit an application.

The Department’s confirmation that the scheme will not reopen means the extension does not create an application window for those businesses.

The announced appeals process is specifically for operators who submitted an application and were refused support for some or all of their vehicles. It does not establish a route for businesses that never applied.

Whether any provision will be made for disputed late submissions or operators who believe they were unable to complete an application is not addressed in the statement.

The next departmental correspondence will therefore be particularly important for excluded operators. It needs to explain who can appeal, what can be challenged and whether a successful review will unlock both the original support and the extension payments.
news.summary:
The extension of the Road Transporters Support Scheme (RTSS) will provide additional support for existing applicants, but operators excluded from the scheme face two different outcomes: an appeals process for those refused support, and no reopening for businesses that did not apply. The Department of Transport has confirmed that operators who submitted an application but […]

news.title: Christy O'Connor on Glen Rovers and Barrs' modern rivalry: Northsiders have the edge
news.text:
When Glen Rovers and St Finbarr’s met in the 2017 senior hurling championship, the headline of John Horgan’s report in these pages referenced how the Glen had broken the Barrs’ hearts in ‘an old-school club hurling classic’.

Horgan detailed how one of the best games of that era was a throwback to the glory days of old. The Glen, chasing three in-a-row, were on the brink of elimination after a defeat to Sarsfields in the previous round but a goal from David 'Paddy' Cunningham with virtually the last play knocked the Barrs out. 

“The Barrs were crushed, their heroic effort had all been in vain,” wrote Horgan. “It was no consolation to them afterwards that they had fully restored the pride in the old jersey. 

 It was a night to bring back memories of a time long past when these two were kings of Cork hurling.” 

The quality on show that evening carried loud echoes of the past. In the long and storied history of the Glen and the Barrs, that 2017 game was the joint-highest scoring championship match between the pair. It equalled the points total from their previous championship meeting in 2013, which the Glen also won, on a scoreline of 1-22 to 2-11.

There always has been something mythical and highly attractive about the Barrs and the Glen. When the club championships returned in July 2020, and people finally had some form of normality back in their lives again during the pandemic, RTÉ’s first live broadcast was an opening day championship meeting between the two clubs.

It was a local affair, like club games everywhere, but the television audience peaked that night at 140,000. RTÉ knew that going big would bring in the numbers. And the Barrs and the Glen was one of the biggest out there.

Increasingly rare

Incredibly, that 2020 meeting was the last championship match between the two great clubs, who meet in a county final on Sunday for the first time in 38 years. In the intervening years, the clubs have only met eight times, with the Glen having reasserted their traditional dominance over the Barrs with five wins to one, along with two draws.

It's exactly 100 years now since Glen Rovers first joined the senior ranks in Cork in 1926 after back-to-back promotions from the county Junior and Intermediate championships. St Finbarr’s went on to win their eighth Cork senior title that season.

The first recorded meeting of the two senior teams was in the Bride Valley Gold Medal Tournament in March 1927, but it was another seven years before they first met in the championship. Appearing in their first senior final in 1934, the Glen beat the Barrs by five points to secure a maiden title.

In their 38 championship meetings across the last 92 years, the Glen are ahead 21-13, with four of those matches having ended in a draw.

The two clubs were such powerhouses that they always expected to meet on big days. Prior to that their last final meeting, the Barrs and the Glen had met in 12 finals and 10 semi-finals. In the last 38 years though, they never met beyond a quarter-final, which only happened once, in 1996, when the Glen won a replay by three points.

 Incredibly, it would be 14 years before the clubs would meet again in the championship, in 2010, when the Glen won a round four clash again after a replay.

In the first six decades of the rivalry, the longest hiatus between championship meetings was six years – which happened twice – but a 14-year gap between 1996 and 2010 mirrored the struggles of both clubs.

Big day clashes were no longer guaranteed because the Barrs and the Glen were no longer consistently featuring on the big days.

In the 10 years between that clash in 2010 and their opening group clash in 2020 (which was the first season of the championship restructure), the Barrs and the Glen only met in the first round (twice) and in round 2B once, which was that 2017 classic.

Glamour tie

Apart from the rich history and tradition associated with the fixture, what had always made St Finbarr’s-Glen Rovers matches so attractive was the huge volume and cast of Hollywood A-list players involved. That was particularly evident during the peak of the rivalry in the 1970s and 1980s.

When the rivalry became so dormant across the following decades, the lack of star quality on both sides diluted the attraction of the fixture. The Barrs and the Glen was still a huge draw – but it was nothing like it was.

Now that they are finally meeting in a final again, the magic is back, not just because it is such a loud echo to a glorious past, but because of how the star quality on show has added to the mystique.

Cork are no longer hoovering up All-Irelands like they were when the Barrs and the Glen were in their heyday but at least both clubs have strong representation on Cork senior teams again; nine of the players which will feature on Sunday have played senior championship for Cork, while Ben Cunningham has the potential to play at that level.

The prize now on Sunday is colossal for both clubs but it’s also an opportunity for everyone else to bask in the atmosphere and nostalgia of what it used to be like when the Barrs and the Glen were kings of Cork hurling.
news.summary: Clubs have only met eight times since the last county final clash in 1988, with the Glen having reasserted their traditional dominance over the Barrs with five wins to one, along with two draws...

news.title: St Finbarr’s need extra time to beat Brian Dillon’s and claim the Seandún Junior B Hurling title
news.text:
St Finbarr’s 1-20

 Brian Dillon’s 2-17 AET (3-2 pens)

St Finbarr’s needed extra time, followed by penalties to see off last year’s beaten finalists Brian Dillon’s and claim the AOS Security Seandún Junior B Hurling title from the decider, at Ballinlough on Saturday.

Brain Dillon’s made the better start as their two first half goals gave them a four-point interval lead. 

Persistent fouling was to prove costly for Brian Dillon’s in the second half, as St. Finbarr’s scored 1-4 from placed balls. 

In extra time, St. Finbarr’s were leading 1-20 to 2-16, when an equalising point by Brian Dillon’s Kevin Coughlan sent the game to penalties.

Within a minute of the throw-in, Brian Dillon’s Danny McCormack set up Cillian Brosnan for the game’s opening goal. 

St. Finbarr’s replied with points by Faolán Linnane and David Scannell. Ross Murphy pointed the game’s first free for Brian Dillon’s.

St. Finbarr’s Adam Phillips and Cian Buckley each scored points. Glenn O’Connor converted a free, to put St. Finbarr’s ahead for the first time.

Brian Dillon’s regained the lead as Brosnan scored their second goal from the rebound of Ross Murphy’s penalty miss.

Dave Cremin got a point for Brian Dillon’s. Brosnan also got on the scoresheet with three points, including a free. 

Cian Buckley and Matthew Nason replied with points for St. Finbarr’s. This left Brian Dillon’s leading 2-5 to 0-7 at half-time.

Ross Murphy scored a point for Brian Dillon’s, before the tide turned in St. Finbarr’s favour.

Five unanswered points brought St. Finbarr’s level. Brian Dillon’s scored six points in the final quarter, including three by Ross Murphy. O’Connor converted three frees for St. Finbarr’s.

A minute into stoppage time, St. Finbarr’s were awarded a penalty. O’Connor drilled the ball to the back of the net. 

Brian Dillon’s responded with a point by Brosnan, to force extra time.

In the first period of extra time, Gould exchanged points with Brian Dillon’s Oisín Vallely. St. Finbarr’s added two without reply. 

This left St Finbarr’s leading 1-19 to 2-14 at the break.

Phillips pointed a free for St. Finbarr’s, before Brian Dillon’s replied with three unanswered points, to send the game to penalties.

 Scorers for St Finbarr’s: G O’Connor 1-8 (0-5f); J Gould 0-3; A Phillips 0-2 (0-1f); Cian Buckley 0-2, L Twomey, D McGuirk, M Nason, D Scannell, F Linnane 0-1 each.

 Subs: J Gould for O’Shea, J Martin for Corey Buckely, J Goggin for Healy (all h/t), R O’Mahony for Linnane (45), C Kelleher for Scannell (55), C Herlihy for Nason (66), R Fitzpatrick for McCarthy (72).

news.title: Laoise is appointed associate with O’Flynn Exhams in Cork
news.text:
Laoise joins OFX’s corporate, commercial and regulatory team, where she will advise clients from a range of industries and sectors.

Laoise said: "Joining O’Flynn Exhams is an exciting opportunity to build my career in Cork and to work alongside an excellent team of professionals. The team has an excellent reputation and I look forward to supporting clients across the practice.”

“Laoise brings a strong academic background as well as invaluable experience and insights from her past experience. These are important strengths in supporting our clients as they navigate an increasingly complex commercial and regulatory environment.”

news.title: Holders Whitechurch retain Seandún Junior A Hurling title for the third successive year after beating Na Piarsaigh in a great game of hurling
news.text:
Whitechurch 2-17

 Na Piarsaigh 2-16

Holders Whitechurch have won the AOS Security Seandún Junior A Hurling title for the third successive year, as they defeated last year’s beaten finalists Na Piarsaigh, in a nail-biting decider before a good-sized attendance at Ballinlough.

With the sides deadlocked at 2-16 apiece, Jamie Hegarty slotted over his tenth pointed free in stoppage time, to settle the tie.

Na Piarsaigh, who were looking to bridge a 29-year gap, held a four point lead at the break, with two goals to their credit. Whitechurch got their first goal within seconds of the resumption, which brought them back into contention as this game went down to the wire.

Hegarty pointed a free within two minutes of the throw-in. Craig O’Sullivan responded with two unanswered frees for Na Piarsaigh.

Na Piarsaigh began to have Whitechurch pinned back as Jack Scanlon set up Luke Hurley for the game’s opening goal in the seventh minute.

Sean Paul Cooke got Na Piarsaigh’s first point from play, which stretched the margin to 1-3 to 0-1. Ruaraí O’Connell responded with Whitechurch’s first point from play.

Na Piarsaigh’s Alan Keating swapped points with Whitechurch’s Darragh O’Connell. Whitechurch began to turn the screw as Hegarty and Sean Keane each added points, to reduce the deficit to 1-4 to 0-5.

Na Piarsaigh replied with points from Hurley and O’Sullivan, before Na Piarsaigh found themselves pinned back. Persistent fouling was proving to be costly for Na Piarsaigh, as Hegarty converted three unanswered frees.

O’Sullivan tagged on his second point from play for Na Piarsaigh, while Hegarty pointed his fifth free.

Entering stoppage time at the end of the opening half, Gordon Joyce set up Shane Galgey for Na Piarsaigh’s second goal. This left Na Piarsaigh leading 2-7 to 0-9 at the break.

Whitechurch upped the ante after the interval. Within a minute of the restart, Daniel Kelleher set up Ronan Murphy for Whitechurch’s first goal.

Daniel Kelleher tagged on a point for Whitechurch and Hegarty got three, including two frees. Na Piarsaigh responded with points from Dayne Lee, Keating and Galgey. O’Sullivan also pointed two frees. This left Na Piarsaigh leading by two points.

Entering the second quarter, Mark Callanan embarked on a solo run, to set up Cillian Egan for Whitechurch’s second goal, which gave them a single point lead.

Na Piarsaigh scored four points from play to Hegarty’s three frees, which tied the scores and set the scene for a dramatic finish.

news.title: Major fire breaks out in Alberta after deadly incident at military base
news.text:
It was not immediately clear how many people were killed or injured, but a doctor at a hospital in the city of Edmonton, 120 miles north west, told Canada’s national broadcaster that patients were being brought to hospitals across the city as healthcare facilities around the base became “completely overwhelmed” by the number of people needing care.

“This number of patients would overwhelm the city of Edmonton,” Dr Warren Thirsk, an emergency department physician at the Royal Alexandra Hospital, told CBC News.

“It is more patients than any of us want to count right now. It’s a disaster. It’s a one in every 15 to 25-year disaster.”

The town of Wainwright, near the base, has about 7,000 residents.

Defence minister David McGuinty said the Royal Canadian Mounted Police were involved in investigating the incident and described the situation as “very, very active and delicate”.

He said authorities were still working to determine what happened and expected to provide further information.

The Royal Canadian Mounted Police said officers were called shortly after 4pm on Saturday following reports of a fire in a training area at the base.

Firefighters faced a volatile situation. Large areas of the province were hit during the day by a windstorm with gusts up to 60 miles an hour. The wind toppled some trees and sent signs flying and rubbish bins rolling down streets.

By 11pm, the Municipal District of Wainwright said on social media the fire was being held and that property and critical infrastructure were protected. There was no evacuation order for residents.

Saskatchewan premier Scott Moe said his province was sending assistance to Alberta but did not specify what resources were being deployed.

“Our thoughts are with all the brave women and men affected,” Prime Minister Mark Carney said earlier in a social media post.

Alberta premier Danielle Smith described the fire as “significant and tragic” and said it was affecting many military personnel.

CFB Wainwright is one of Canada’s busiest military training bases, where soldiers prepare for combat operations.

It is home to the Canadian Manoeuvre Training Centre, which conducts realistic battlefield exercises, and the 3rd Canadian Division Training Centre, which provides military training.

Canadian Conservative opposition leader Pierre Poilievre said he had spoken with Mr Carney and the defence minister to offer support to those affected by the fire.

“Pray for Wainwright, everyone,” Mr Poilievre said in a social media post. He urged people in the area to follow emergency instructions and keep roads clear for first responders.

The fire also disrupted advance voting ahead of Monday’s referendum on whether Alberta should begin a process that could lead to independence from Canada.

Elections Alberta said two polling locations, in Lloydminster and Vermilion, closed early on Saturday and the ballots were transported securely.

What you need to know about the new series VisionQuest

The sci-fi series is streaming on Disney+.

8.06am, 18 Oct 2026

Share options

IF YOU’RE A Marvel fan, you might be already waiting to watch this new entry to its streaming staple.

But if you’re not, here’s what you need to know about VisionQuest.

What’s the basic background on it?

It’s a miniseries and was created by showrunner Terry Matalas. The series features the Marvel Comics character Vision, and it’s a spin-off from the TV miniseries WandaVision, which came out in 2021.

It’s also the 18th television series in the Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU), which is a franchise centred around Marvel superheroes. Think the likes of Iron Man and The Avengers.

So who’s Vision?

Paul Bettany in VisionQuestMarvel

Vision is what’s called a “synthezoid”. Synthezoids basically have a replica of a human body (blood, guts and all), made of a substance called Horton Cells. They’re powered by solar energy. Vision is played by Paul Bettany.

The character has featured in several Marvel films, but was killed in Avengers: Infinity War (2018) before being resurrected in the series WandaVision. Yet even though his memories were restored, he struggles to connect with them. When the series kicks off, he’s working in a pub and pretending to be human.

In VisionQuest, Vision is able to retreat into a mental world where he communicates with AI personas inside his programming. He also goes on the run with a mysterious teenager in foster care who may be his reincarnated son, played by Ruairidh Mollica. Meanwhile, there’s a bounty hunter called Paladin (Todd Stashwick) on his tail. There’s a lot happening here, to say the least.

Advertisement

What else do we know?

Marvel Entertainment / YouTube

The showrunner Terry Matalas told Tech Radar that VisionQuest “takes place in the Marvel Cinematic Universe’s (MCU) present day”, around the same time as Spider-Man: Brand New Day.

If you don’t know anything about the MCU, be warned that some study might be necessary. Rolling Stone says in its review:

A rewatch of WandaVision, still the best show that the company’s small-screen division has produced to date, is a necessity. Ditto a refresher on Avengers: Age of Ultron (2015) if you haven’t seen that movie in a hot minute. Some online breakdowns of Agatha All Along, a witchy spin-off of WandaVision, would definitely help. Maybe consult a Reddit thread or three.

Meanwhile, TechRadar says in its review:

[Bettany] delivers a striking performance as a morally gray Vision, whose emotional turmoil gives rise to a colder, darker version of the character that strays dangerously into Ultron 2.0 territory more than once. Yet there’s a strange delight in seeing this side of Vision fully unleashed on his foes, delivering some unexpectedly bloody, brutal beatdowns along the way.

Who else is in the cast?

James SpaderCourtesy of Marvel

Courtesy of Marvel

There’s a nifty cast here – James Spader plays Ultron, an android with a god complex.

Orla Brady is the AI assistant F.R.I.D.A.Y.

Diane Morgan also stars as The Handler, and Emily Hampshire (Schitt’s Creek) is another AI, E.D.I.T.H.

Where can we watch it?

Orla Brady, James D'Arcy, Johnathan Sayer, and Henry LewisCourtesy of Marvel

Courtesy of Marvel

VisionQuest is streaming on Disney+ now.
