SeriesInternet Diaries

‘Lizard people’ people are studying Trump’s circle: What do their theories tell us about power?

Our FactCheck editor details the internet trends seen by a thirtysomething-year-old man.

8.00am, 18 Oct 2026

Share options

Stephen McDermott

THEY WALK AMONG us.

To the untrained eye, they can be hard to spot in the flesh, but those who know can tell.

These otherworldly beings have an unmistakable intensity, communicate in frantic bursts and appear to have studied human punctuation without fully understanding it.

I’m talking, of course, about the ‘lizard people’ people.

These people believe a conspiracy theory that the world’s elites are actually shape-shifting, reptilian extraterrestrials who secretly control the world by hiding in human form.

Their natural habitat is in the replies and comments sections of social media posts.

I’ve never knowingly seen one of these people in the wild, but the internet has recently shown me a huge amount of evidence that they exist in the form of bizarre theories about women linked to the Trump administration.

It started when I was shown videos of the businesswoman and philanthropist Susan Dell in the Oval Office with Donald Trump last week.

Before I knew why she was visiting the White House, I was being bombarded with posts that claimed she was part of this reptilian conspiracy.

Advertisement

Dell, whose husband Michael founded the technology company that bears their surname, was in Washington to promote a $6.25 billion pledge they’d made to help fund investment accounts for 25 million American children.

That massive act of charity was entirely submerged beneath the deluge of commentary about what they perceived as her strange movements and other remarks about her appearance.

Takes from the lizard people people included things like “I’m telling you now she’s either reptilian, or she’s a robot”, “It looks like Close Encounters of the Third Kind”, and “aliens are already working inside Trump’s world … tell me you don’t see it”.

Other posts soon targeted Kelly Loeffler, the administrator of the US Small Business Administration, and Barbara Thornhill, the new ambassador-at-large to monitor and combat human trafficking.

Loeffler’s looks in a viral TikTok video and Thornhill’s appearance in an image used to announce her appointment were taken as further evidence that the Trump administration “isn’t even trying to hide the aliens anymore bro”.

It was difficult to tell which of the conspiracy theories was in earnest, and which were just leaning into the meme for mean-spirited lulz.

A post on X about Barbara Thornhill and Kelly LoefflerX.com

The distinction mattered less the more of these posts I saw: both types of commentary simply invited me to pick over the details of these women’s appearances before I knew anything about who they were.

What do we learn about powerful people by debating whether they’re human?

Poll Results:

">The impulse to make the rich and powerful look ridiculous is understandable, even if it's outlandish in this instance. (2)

">Elites tend to carefully cultivate their public images, and ridicule levels the playing field for ordinary people who refuse to take them quite as seriously as their power demands. (1)

">Billionaires and politicians are not entitled to our reverence. (1)

">But this kind of punching up on social media only shows us a target; it doesn’t really tell us what we’re taking aim at. (1)

">The impulse to make the rich and powerful look ridiculous is understandable, even if it's outlandish in this instance.

">Elites tend to carefully cultivate their public images, and ridicule levels the playing field for ordinary people who refuse to take them quite as seriously as their power demands.

">Billionaires and politicians are not entitled to our reverence.

">But this kind of punching up on social media only shows us a target; it doesn’t really tell us what we’re taking aim at.

These women, however well-meaning, have access to Trump and the higher reaches of the US government, and present carefully manicured images of authority and glamour.

After several clips, I could recognise Susan Dell immediately but could explain almost nothing about why she was in the Oval Office.

My feed had made her familiar without making me informed.

It’s easy to get stuck down that rabbit hole if you want to because posts about the three women are alluring: they are a kind of engagement bait where users are invited to intensely inspect the women’s gestures and physiognomy, or to go looking for more ‘evidence’. 

Related Reads

Dublin's Winter Lights has moved to January, and the haters expect 'Ramadan lights' will follow

A strange article about Glen Hansard led me to the promise of €500k before it disappeared

What's not enjoyable about the minor panic over a Cat in the Hat prowling the sunny south-east?

When you’re primed to see something and get drawn into the hunt for clues, it’s little wonder that you end up believing a bizarre theory or goading others into doing the same.

Those who genuinely think there are aliens in the White House possibly feel that this can be explained because people with extraordinary wealth and access are fundamentally different from everyone else.

The theory therefore turns a complicated question – how power operates – into a mystery with an identifiable answer and clues that anyone can supposedly spot if they look hard enough.

You don’t have to believe any of it to keep the game going either; it may just be absurd entertainment, a game being played by bored people on the internet that others keep adding to.

But whether you’re playing along or uncovering an intergalactic conspiracy, the conversation ends up in much the same place.

The question of what Susan Dell was doing in the Oval Office has devolved into speculation about whether she is a lizard, a robot or an alien.

When you’re asking bigger, more difficult questions about power and access, recognising someone as human is a fairly modest concession, and might yield a better critique of the genuinely weird state of US politics right now. 

The truth is out there.

Stephen McDermott

news.title: Dear Dáithí: Can we get over Halloween before Christmas begins?
news.text:
I relish the days of putting on the slow cooker and having slow evenings with a book and a blanket on the couch.

 With the pumpkins in the shops, I’ll be stocking up over the next few weeks and will carve pumpkins ahead of Halloween and make plenty of soups and risottos with the pumpkin flesh.

 What is really bothering me, though, is the fact that instead of heralding in the autumn and embracing the season, some people are intent on trying to bring Christmas forward about two months.

 A recent trip to my local shop was like a festive horror scene. Shiny baubles and velvet bows lined in rows across from skeletons and fake blood.

 Once we reach autumn, it feels like we are being rushed into the middle of winter — and I’ve had enough of it. I know I’m not the only one who feels this way and yet, each year, Christmas seems to arrive earlier and earlier.

 When I’ve said it to friends, they’ve reminded me that I can just ignore the decorations on sale and I don’t need to book Christmas outings if I don’t want to.

 They say some people just like to get organised early. I get that... but I would also like not to see barmbracks alongside Christmas cakes.

 My question is: How do we put a stop to it? Can we collectively try to ensure Christmas preparation doesn’t start until Halloween is over so people can enjoy this time of year without feeling they are being rushed through the months?

I AM TOTALLY with you on this one. It drives me cracked when I see the Christmas sweets and all that in the shops at the end of summer, in a small corner at first and then, a week or two later, out the front of the store.

Now the shops are very clever, and you would see a lot of things going at a good price at this early time, and if you can get over the fact that it is still warm out there and if you need to save a few bob, then stock up. 

In the shops’ defence, they are only trying to make money. It is really up to us, the public, to do something about it but I’m not sure what we can do. They are giving the people what they want — and this is what they want.

I know you, me, and others don’t see it that way but that’s the cycle we are in.

For example, the second New Year’s Day is gone, we are straight on to Valentine’s Day, then St Patrick’s Day, and Easter is then landed upon us and on it goes, running a few months ahead of time in a circle. It seems sometimes that we are wishing time away — or is it being wished away for us? No wonder we say all the time that time is flying by.

This might be my favourite time of year, just before the clocks go back. I know loads of people who hate the clocks going back but I love it. I love it equally when they go forward too in spring. 

 It’s a time of year when we should slow down, and I think our bodies need it, so when shops and ads are propelling us forward, I’m not so sure our bodies want that all the time.

Getting back to your question about what we can do collectively. Nothing, is the simple answer. But we can do it for ourselves on an individual basis. It’s the only power we have in this one. We can’t control the radio ads or the TV ones; they have started already.

All we can do is ignore them as best we can and tune in properly sometime in December. There is a shopping mall close to where my wife is from in New Jersey and there is a Christmas shop in there — and it’s open all year round. The crazy thing is I’ve seen the place packed in July and, yes, there were Christmas songs playing.

One of the great things about Halloween is that it originally started here in Ireland and it’s only in recent years that we started celebrating it. It went off to America a few hundred years ago as one thing and came back as another.

 That said, it’s a great time of year for both kids and adults and, again, it’s up to us adults to slow the rush down and make Halloween a great time for us all. 

There are plenty of things to see and do, and we just need to focus on that, and that itself will put Christmas on the back foot for a while.

When we were young, Christmas started on December 8. We had two great weeks of excitement and fun and, to be honest, even with that length of time, it was time to move on. I think the longer the build-up to Christmas, the more diluted it becomes. 

By the time Christmas comes now, I’m kinda tired of the whole thing and it really shouldn’t be like that. Christmas is there to be enjoyed but it does feel sometimes that, when we’re just beginning to enjoy it, the next thing is landed on us to move on. Going from pillar to post on a constant cycle is wearing people out, and I’m one of them.

The only way we can slow all of this down is by changing our focus to what we want — and that is to enjoy each month and season at a time and in time.

So put Christmas out of your head and, for the next week, check out all the things that are happening for Halloween and go do some of them. Eat your barmbrack and don’t even look at another type of cake for a month or two.

As the clocks go back, enjoy it in front of a nice fire, all in the knowledge that Christmas is another bit away.

Sometimes we forget that we all, as individuals, can change things on our own for our own benefit.

news.title: Cork business leaders insist Patrick Street will 'continue to thrive' despite two high-profile closures
news.text:
Business leaders in Cork say Patrick Street will "continue to thrive" despite two high-profile exits from the city's main thoroughfare in the past week.

On Tuesday, it was reported that high-end fashion store Flannels is to close its outlet on Cork's Patrick Street. Two days later, the Flying Tiger Copenhagen outlet began a closing down sale as it departs from its location at 33/34 Patrick Street. 

That site is being incorporated into the planned expansion of Penneys, which will adding 6,000 sq ft to Penneys store and will also bring two vacant units back into use — the former Jack & Jones store, and a vacant unit at No 1 Cook St.

Busy and vibrant

Cork Business Association president Clara O'Neill said Patrick Street remains a busy and vibrant retail destination, offering a diverse mix of businesses. 

"We understand that Flying Tiger’s departure is linked to the planned expansion of Penneys, which will significantly enhance its city centre offering.

“With this investment, alongside the upcoming reopening of the landmark Roches Stores/Debenhams building, we are confident that Patrick Street will continue to thrive."

Conor Healy, CEO of Cork Chamber commented: “It is disappointing to see Flannels and Tiger close, and understand the significant impact on the staff and service providers. Both closures reflect wider changes and restructuring within their groups and the constantly evolving retail environment.

"We also need to recognise the new investments taking place on Patrick Street and across the city centre, but this certainly highlights the challenges businesses continue to face, and the need for ongoing support of our city and town centres in particular.”

Flying Tiger continues to trade at Mahon Point.

Flannels, part of the UK's Frasers Group, opened on the prominent site in the former Eason store in 2023, having acquired the building for €6.5m. 

Closing down sale

However, signs in the store's windows this week advertised a 20% closing-down sale. During the summer, the chain closed its outlet in Dublin's Blanchardstown Centre, which it opened in 2022.

The Cork premises, at 113-115 Patrick Street, was vacated by Eason midway through 2022, when the bookseller and stationer shifted operations after more than 35 years to a new 5,000 sq ft store at 35-36 Patrick Street, on the renovated ground floor of the former Victoria Hotel.

“Flannels is part of the Frasers Group and, while we are not privy to its plans for the premises, we hope to see this landmark building occupied again soon, potentially by another brand within the group," said Ms O'Neill.

“The continued investment across Cork city centre demonstrates its strength and potential as a prime location for retailers and businesses. Cork Business Association will continue to advocate for retail businesses and lobby on their behalf.”
news.summary: Flannels is to close its outlet on Cork's main thoroughfare while Flying Tiger Copenhagen has begun a closing down sale as it departs ahead of the Penneys redevelopment

Trump paused Russia sanctions to 'sort of analyse' the economic impact, Rubio says

The 60-day suspension has drawn criticism from Republicans and Ukraine.

7.50am, 18 Oct 2026

Share options

US SECRETARY OF State Marco Rubio said that President Donald Trump’s waiver of sweeping sanctions and tariffs on Russia would be a 60-day pause to “analyse” their impact on the global economy.

“The president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyse what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the US economy,” Rubio said on Saturday, noting that the economic restrictions involved a number of countries, not just Russia.

He said various conflicts were impacting global energy prices, including the US war on Iran and attacks on Saudi Arabia by Yemen’s Houthis.

“These conflicts around the world are starting to crash into each other, and they’re having an impact not just on global oil and diesel prices but on economies as well,” Rubio said.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio pictured speaking to reporters on Saturday.Alamy Stock Photo

Alamy Stock Photo

Trump said late Saturday his decision would benefit the US, though it was unclear if he had actually made up his mind on the matter.

“We’ll figure it out, and you’ll figure it out,” he said. “It’s a very good decision, and it’s going to be a decision that’s good for the country, and I think good for the world.”

US lawmakers on both sides of the political aisle have sharply criticised Trump after he signed an executive order Friday that waived sweeping sanctions and tariffs targeting Russia – measures adopted by Congress last month.

The law passed in September, and signed by Trump, included sanctions targeting Russian officials, oligarchs and financial institutions, and provided Trump with the authority to impose sanctions on major buyers of Russian oil and gas.

Advertisement

The idea was to cut off sources of funding to supporters of Russian President Vladimir Putin, as well as his war on Ukraine.

But late Friday, two days before the law was due to take effect, Trump exempted Russia from those economic restrictions.

“Beyond irresponsible,” Republican Senator Thom Tillis, a frequent Trump critic who will leave office in January, said in a post on X.

“If the President wants to actually bring down energy prices, he can do it by solving the Iran problem, not by doing a solid for Vladimir Putin.”

Ted Cruz, a senior Republican senator from Texas, called the move “a mistake” in comments aired on Fox News.

Cruz: Tariffs are a tax on consumers, and I'm not a fan of jacking up taxes on American consumers. https://t.co/4H2A5kdHp7— Acyn (@Acyn) April 3, 2025

Trump’s executive order came after he struck a deal with Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin to allow exports of Russian diesel in exchange for the easing of sanctions.

The impact of steep diesel price hikes due to the Iran war are beginning to filter into the US economy, and cost of living worries are top of mind for voters ahead of key midterm elections next month.

Polls show Trump’s Republicans are likely to receive a drubbing at the polls.

“The diesel that Putin was going to sell, they were (going to) make it available to the global market one way or the other. The only difference is how much of it the United States was going to get,” Rubio said, underscoring the importance of the vital fuel powering US road hauling, agriculture and construction.

Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he feared the United States would lift more sanctions on Russia and that Trump’s action “rewards” Putin.

news.title: Kate Nash: 'It was fine until Ed Sheeran dropped Macklemore'
news.text:
“But that was just me at 16, which is when I wrote most of those songs. Don’t get me wrong, I’m so grateful to that 16-year-old for taking such good care of me. But now,” she says from the corner of the foyer in a Dublin City Centre hotel, “I want to tell the world that I have something to say as a woman. And you need to listen to me.”

Now 39, Nash has been making music for more than half of her life, largely as a way to serve urges both insular and environmental. Foundations, the kitchen-sink realist anthem that gained her comrades of the likes of Lily Allen and Jamie T, boasted a visceral pull that permitted whole demographics to feel seen, while also providing melodies so hummable that most could do so dumbly on the treadmill, in the shower, or on the bus.

Her music, now – Nash has been steadily releasing music since the late aughts; Cailín, her seventh studio album, is scheduled for January – still exists along the same parameters, but the method to get there feels utterly different.

“It costs money to make records,” she says. “We’re in a cost-of-living crisis, and as someone who has a commercially successful record in my catalogue, if I just sat on that and lived off of it, I could earn more than spending like I do on my living.”

What is the point? One might ask, in vain. “Because we have to keep trying.” Nash, in a seaweed-green cardigan and hair in loose plaits, looks softer now compared to her noughties aesthetic. Gone are the belted A-line dresses and primary-hued tights [don’t blame her, blame Topshop] and in is her bare face and whimsical Ríon Hannora designs. Nash’s recent run of intimate Irish shows – members of her team waft in and out of the conversation in merch from Ballintemple’s Coughlan’s to Levis’ in Ballydehob – is speaking to her inner child, the one that spent evenings and weekends in North London playing the tin whistle, Irish-dancing and attending Mass with her Irish mother.

“Being in Ireland makes me cry,” she smiles, wiping a sliding tear. “The venues we’ve been to, they are just amazing. And they’re actually reminding me why I’m doing what I’m doing.”

What Nash is doing is attempting to dismantle the entire arts ecosystem as we know it. An undeniably tall order – most notably in the wake of the Ed Sheeran, Robert Kraft saga – but one that doesn’t begin to scare a redheaded, middle-child who survived late-aughts tabloid media. “The grassroots culture is in crisis, and I am so bored of €700 exclusive merch bundles, and how it’s become normalised to pay a grand to go and see your favourite artist,” she says.

“Shows like these are for the people who attend these venues week in, week out. They are the places where you first receive culture, and we need to look after them and value them in the rise of AI and robots on fashion week catwalks.” She pauses to take a sip of her flat white. “I don’t know if any of these people have ever watched a horror or sci-fi film… but they should know, it doesn’t end well.”

There is a bite to Nash’s voice as she navigates this era, one that demands as much as it offers. In 2024, she announced the launch of a campaign on OnlyFans [an online subscription platform for content creators, that due to its preponderance of adult creators, has become shorthand for adult content] called Butts for Tour Buses. “I’m selling pictures of my arse to pay invoices,” she put it succinctly, on the PoliticsJOE podcast.

“I just got fucking sick of it,” she says now. “Even after saving all of my festival earnings, I was bleeding money touring. And as artists, we’re told not to talk about it. I have friends who are selling their furniture in order to pay their band, and so I just felt like I needed to talk about it. So I did; in the [UK] Parliament twice, in Leinster House and in Stormont.”

The pivot to adult content also didn’t take much from her, really.

 My arse is already out in all of the pictures people take of me non-consensually on stage, so I thought, why not? Now it’s given me a marketing budget for this tour.

She pauses. “It’s also got a lot of great puns, which has definitely helped.”

Breaking barriers is core to Nash’s current epoch, one which sees her lean into her Irishness in a way we’ve never quite seen from her before. In recent interviews, she has made use of the pronoun “we” when discussing Irish history, a move that doesn’t always succeed when displayed with a vocalised North London timbre.

“It was actually fine until Ed Sheeran dropped Macklemore,” she laughs. “That has caused some people to say I’m being disrespectful or whatever, which I actually don’t mind, because I think it’s given me the opportunity to explain myself – and we all need to be able to discuss these things and not feel we have to force our opinions on each other to win.”

This perceived disrespect permeated from Nash’s cover of Sinéad O’Connor’s Famine, and its subsequent video which featured a duvet with the embroidery work of artist and activist Tia O’Donnell stating “The English Don’t Know Their History”. Nash was first recommended to record the track by an American producer and friend, a suggestion she thought was “too audacious” to even consider. But after re-examining the traditional folk nature of sharing tunes, and with the blessing of O’Connor’s estate and family, she decided to lean in.

“At the end of the day, the more people who cover that song, the better,” she says. “Because you’re spreading that message to different audiences. If there is ever going to be healing, there has to be remembering and grieving. I’ll always come back to that, with everything I do.” 

Nash challenges this history personally, too. “Part of this journey has been me acknowledging my Englishness, too,” she says. “There’s a rise in nationalism in the UK [ Famine’s cover art features a Saint George’s Cross hanging from the window of a first floor home] and acknowledging that, I feel, brings me closer to an England that acknowledges its colonial past. Because at the end of the day, it doesn’t. There’s still a monarchy, the curriculum doesn’t change and I learned nothing about the Famine in school.

“There was a young boy at my gig in Derry the other night,” she smiles, welling up again.

“On his own, which is firstly such a fucking cool thing to do. Secondly, when Foundations came on, he knew every single word.”

She pauses. “We’re all being preyed on in some way at the moment. Boys by the manosphere, and girls by beauty brands that are forcing their insecurities back on themselves. Did you hear that social media platforms apparently have a way to track when teenage girls are feeling vulnerable, like when they delete selfies, and that’s when they serve them beauty advertisements? That is evil, and it’s worth fighting against.

“That’s exactly why we need to be in small venues, because we need to feel connected again. We need to turn off our phones, sing along with strangers and fight what’s worth fighting for. Because if we don’t… life is only going to get much, much harder from here.” 

 Kate Nash plays Cyprus Avenue, Dolans, Róisín Dubh, The Button Factory and Mandela Hall between February 8 - 14, 2027. Her sixth studio album, Cailín, is out in January.
news.summary: From Sinéad O’Connor and OnlyFans to the politics of claiming Irishness and the crisis facing the live music industry, Kate Nash has plenty to say. By Kate Demolder

Deaths and injuries confirmed after major fire at Canadian military base

The blaze spread rapidly due to high winds at a military base in Alberta, with hospitals reportedly overwhelmed as emergency services responded to the incident.

7.26am, 18 Oct 2026

Share options

SEVERAL PEOPLE HAVE died following a major fire at a military base in western Canada, the country’s defence minister has confirmed.

Canadian Defence Minister David McGuinty said late Saturday that there had been “both fatalities and injuries” following an incident at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta.

Neither the number of casualties nor the cause of the incident has been confirmed.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said earlier on Saturday that “a serious incident creating a major fire” had occurred at the base, located approximately 210 kilometres southeast of Edmonton.

According to local authorities, the fire spread rapidly due to high winds, with emergency services receiving a call for assistance at around 4pm local time (11pm Irish time).

The municipal district of Wainwright said late Saturday that the fire was being held, although crews would continue monitoring the area.

McGuinty described the incident as an “active and delicate situation” and said an investigation would be launched.

Advertisement

The incident also placed significant pressure on nearby hospitals.

According to Canadian broadcaster CBC, a code orange, an emergency response protocol for a large number of patients, was declared in Edmonton.

Dr Warren Thirsk, an emergency department physician at the Royal Alexandra Hospital, said healthcare facilities in Wainwright had been “completely overwhelmed”, with patients being diverted to hospitals across Edmonton.

Canadian Forces Base Wainwright is one of the country’s busiest army bases and is used for military training exercises.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith described the incident as “significant and tragic”, saying it was affecting members of the Canadian military.

Authorities have asked residents to avoid the area and keep roads clear for emergency vehicles. No evacuation order has been issued.

McGuinty said the Canadian Armed Forces and federal, provincial and local authorities were working together to mobilise support.

“We will have more to say in the coming hours and days,” he said.

Additional reporting from Andrew Walsh

news.title: Households urged to stockpile food - what you need to know
news.text: Irish households are being urged to take simple steps to prepare for emergencies as part of the government's national Be Emergency Ready campaign. Minister for Defence Helen McEntee said: "The Be Emergency Ready campaign is about helping people and families take simple actions now so that we are better prepared should disruption occur." Every household in Ireland should have by now received an emergency preparedness booklet through the post, following similar measures promoted by the UK government encouraging citizens to stock tinned food and bottled water. Residents are advised to store two to three litres of drinking water per person daily, along with non-perishable food, a first aid kit, a torch with spare batteries, and alternative heating sources such as sleeping bags or thermal blankets. Householders should also keep a battery or wind-up radio, power banks for mobile phones, and ensure they know the location of their gas and electricity shutoff points. READ THE FULL STORY: Irish households urged to stock up on food and water

Alex Dunne is third in the F2 rankings with two races to go.Alamy Stock Photo

Drive To Survive

'A surplus of talent and a lack of seats’: How Alex Dunne could win F2 and have nowhere to go

The Offaly driver is two big weekends from a title, but his progression is far from straightforward. 

7.16am, 18 Oct 2026

Share options

“IT’S A VERY, very, very horrible situation that Formula 1 has created,” says John Watson, “where there’s a surplus of talent and a total lack of seat availability. And Alex is really in the middle of all that.”

Watson, from Northern Ireland, won five Grand Prix and drove for McLaren in the 1970s and 80s. He does not think he would get the same opportunities if he was in his prime today.

“If I was starting, as I did in 1970, I wouldn’t make it into Formula 1.”

Ireland has not had a driver on the Formula 1 grid since Ralph Firman raced for Jordan in 2003. Alex Dunne is the closest anyone has come since.

At 20, the Offaly man is in his second season in the FIA Formula 2 Championship with Rodin Motorsport, one step below F1. He spent his first year as a McLaren junior driver. This year, he is spending it in the Alpine Academy.

So what are his chances of making the final step? 

With two rounds to go, in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, Dunne sits third on 189 points, 18 behind Brazil’s Rafael Câmara and 11 behind Nikola Tsolov. Each round offers 39 points. To leave Qatar in the lead, Dunne needs to outscore Câmara by 19 and Tsolov by 12. 

Alex Dunne: has the speed but is there an opening?Alamy Stock Photo

Alamy Stock Photo

Perhaps the greater issue, though? A bottleneck in F1. 

Advertisement

The problem starts at the top. Fernando Alonso is 45. Lewis Hamilton is 41. “They’re not about to retire to make way for a youngster coming in,” says Watson.

Below them, seats are filled early and for years ahead. Dunne is an Alpine junior, and Alpine is full: Pierre Gasly is contracted until at least the end of 2028, and Franco Colapinto signed an extension in August covering 2027.

What is left is decided by the academies. Kimi Antonelli finished sixth in F2 in 2024, and is now closing in on the world title with Mercedes. “He stood out like a sore thumb,” says Watson. “Got picked up by Mercedes, put through Formula 2, didn’t have the best results, but they saw something in him.”

Arvid Lindblad finished one place behind Dunne in F2 last year. Red Bull had backed him since he was 13, and he was on the grid by March.

Dunne has never had that kind of patron. He joined McLaren’s programme in 2024 and got his first F1 practice session in Austria last year, the first Irish driver to take part in an F1 weekend in over two decades.

He finished fourth-fastest in Lando Norris’ car, 0.224 of a second off George Russell’s best lap, 0.069 behind Oscar Piastri in the other McLaren, and 0.333 quicker than Lewis Hamilton’s Ferrari.

“I don’t know whether he was running on low fuel, soft tyres,” says Watson. “Nevertheless, I was really impressed.”

By the autumn he had left McLaren. By March he was at Alpine, a team that has been here before. Oscar Piastri won the F2 title as an Alpine junior in 2021 and spent the next year watching from the garage. He ran out of patience and left for McLaren.

On track, Dunne has done his part. A top-three finish in F2 would secure the Super Licence points he needs to race in F1.

“If he won the title, that would certainly increase his options,” says Watson. “But again, there’s really one seat I can see that’s currently available.”

So why not walk? On track, he has done his part. With two rounds left, in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, he is on 189 points, 18 behind Brazil’s Rafael Câmara and 11 behind Bulgaria’s Nikola Tsolov, with 39 on offer at each round. A top-three finish would also secure the Super Licence points he needs to race in F1.

“If he won the title, that would certainly increase his options,” says Watson. Then he lists them, and stops quickly.

Even the title guarantees little. Of the nine F2 champions since 2017, four went straight into an F1 seat. “Fornaroli won the championship in ’25,” says Watson. “He hasn’t got a Formula One drive. All he is is a McLaren reserve driver.”

Only a handful of 2027 seats remain open, and Dunne’s two title rivals are better placed for them than he is.

Câmara is a Ferrari junior, and Haas runs Ferrari engines. “Ferrari might say, take Câmara, because we’ll make sure you get the same engines as the factory,” says Watson. 

And, indeed, since we spoke to Watson, Haas confirmed the signing of Câmara for the 2027 Formula 1 season.

Tsolov is a Red Bull junior. Watson puts it at “50-50" that he takes a Racing Bull seat.

That could leave Dunne as champion with nowhere to race, since the winner cannot return to F2. IndyCar and Formula E are the obvious exits. Watson would hate to see him take either.

“There’s other youngsters coming along who are going to be there with [their] foot in the door. If you take your foot out of the door and disappear, I think that’s probably the end of your opportunities in Formula 1.”

So the choice is between waiting at a team with no vacancy and leaving a sport that rarely lets anyone back in.

“This is going to be the making or breaking of Alex’s career,” says Watson.

Hannah Kate Costello

AnalysisWhere will the profits go?

Takeover of Ireland’s biggest landlord means rent hikes are likely on the cards

Ireland’s biggest private landlord is set to be bought out by US investment firm Barings.

7.01am, 18 Oct 2026

Share options

Paul O'Donoghue

THERE IS NO getting around it – rent hikes are on the way for thousands of Dublin apartments.

Ires REIT, Ireland’s biggest private landlord, is set to be bought out by US investment firm Barings in a €726 million deal.

The new owner will almost certainly move as quickly as possible to raise the rents charged to tenants in an effort to generate higher profits.

After all, this opportunity is likely the single biggest reason why Barings is interested in Ires and its 3,600 properties in the first place.

What happens once Barings takes over will be a live test case of the impact of Ireland’s new rent rules.

These allow landlords to reset rents to market value between tenants, getting around rent caps.

Essentially, this will allow Barings to slowly raise prices across the Ires portfolio as old tenants leave and new ones move in.

The government has repeatedly said that the aim of the new rules is to stimulate private investment in the rental market. I.e., get private investors to build more rental properties and boost supply.

But the case of the Ires sale will function as a test of what happens when a company already owns thousands of apartments.

Will the new owner use the opportunity to reset rents to invest in its business?

Or will it just siphon off the extra profits to executives and shareholders? Let’s look at some of the key issues.

In 2024, Ires REIT was in the doldrums. Its share price was down, and its own investors were trying to oust the company board. Its stock went as low as about €0.84, giving the business a value of around €445 million – well below what Barings is now paying.

So, why the uptick in its value?

As alluded to, the key reason is the change in Ireland’s rent rules.

This has been well covered previously, but the long and short of it is that previously, a rent cap applied to large areas of the country. Landlords could only raise prices by a maximum of 2% per year. This, of course, included Dublin, which is where almost all of Ires’s portfolio is located.

This cap is well under the rate of general rent price inflation, which has been somewhere between 5% and 8% per year since 2021.

Advertisement

As a result, the prices across the Ires portfolio have increased at a rate lower than what they could have. The company charges an average monthly rent of about €1,850 to its tenants. It reckons this is about 20% to 25% below the market rate. This implies that prices could theoretically rise to somewhere between €2,200 and €2,300 before impacting demand. Ires has zero problem here – 99.5% of its apartments are occupied, which indicates that it has plenty of scope to raise rents.

Minister for Housing James BrowneAlamy Stock Photo

Alamy Stock Photo

This year, the government introduced new rules which allow landlords to ‘reset’ rents between tenancies (if the previous tenant left voluntarily or breached obligations) or at the end of a 6-year tenancy cycle.

‘Reset’ here effectively means ‘raise the price’. For example, a tenant could be paying a rent of €1,900 per month in an Ires apartment. Once they leave, Ires (or now Barings) could ‘reset’ the price to the going market rate. In most cases for the Ires apartments, the market rate will almost certainly be significantly higher – say €2,300.

It will take some time for the company to do this. It essentially has to wait for old tenants to leave before it can charge the higher prices. Ires estimates that somewhere from 10% to 14% of its ‘turns over’ like this per year.

But already, we can see how investors are salivating at the thought of hiking prices.

Ires’s profits tripled in the first half of 2026 versus 2025. This was driven largely by a revaluation of its assets, showing optimism that the company’s portfolio is more valuable now with the new rent rules in place.

Ires has also said the new rules can boost its rental income ‘with additional minimal costs’.

Barings has not said much publicly about what it intends to do with the Ires portfolio. But it will almost certainly proceed down the path which Ires laid out to investors – raise rents by as much as it can, as quickly as it can.

Where will the profits go?

What will be interesting is what will happen to the extra cash generated from these rents.

Ires was already generating earnings of about €30 million per year after costs from its portfolio, before the rent rule change.

If the rent it charges at 10% of its tenancies rises by 20% – 25%, the company stands to get an extra €2 million a year, give or take.

Ires previously said that this extra money will allow for “more apartment building”.

But will Barings follow suit?

The rent cap of 2% applies to existing properties but not to homes where construction started after June 2025.Alamy Stock Photo

Alamy Stock Photo

As a REIT, Ires had to distribute 85% of its property earnings to shareholders. Barings will not face the same restrictions, giving it more flexibility on how to spend the cash the apartment portfolio produces annually.

Related Reads

Deemed disposal investment tax sparks anger in Ireland, but is there similar anywhere else? 

The new rent rules have an important clause. The rent cap of 2% applies to existing properties. But it does not cover homes where construction started after June 2025.

The idea is to “attract investment in apartments and increase rental supply”, the government has said, by essentially allowing investors to charge higher rents in new-build homes.

If Barings gets an extra €2 million per year from the Ires portfolio, on top of the €30 million or so it already generates, will it use that cash to build new homes?

Or just sweat the existing 3,600 Ires properties, while investing as little extra money as it can?

There is also a question around investment in the old Ires portfolio.

The properties have an average age of 18 years. While that is not old, all properties need money for maintenance to prevent them falling into poor condition.

The Society of Chartered Surveyors Ireland previously estimated that apartments should budget €2,000 per year for a sinking fund to cover major repairs. For the 3,600 strong Ires portfolio, this works out at about €7 million annually.

And owners, such as Ires and Barings, could face additional costs.

These could include replacing kitchens and bathrooms, or redecorating.

Ires has spent under €10 million on capital investment over the last two years. The company has not necessarily under-invested – again, 18 years is relatively young. The buildings may not need much work to service.

But it is an area where the extra money from higher rents could be well-spent, boosting standards for tenants while increasing asset values for Barings.

This is the heart of the tension with Ireland’s new rent rules. They essentially guarantee that prices will significantly rise at many apartments, such as those Barings will soon own.

But the real question is where the money will go after that.

The hope will be that it either flows into building new apartments, or improving standards in existing ones.

But the pessimists out there may suspect that the extra money will simply flow back to Barings and its owners.

Either way, the deal will present a major test of what impact Ireland’s new rules have on the rental market. As the country’s biggest private landlord, a host of politicians, analysts and economists will be watching closely.

Paul O'Donoghue

A west Co. Cork care farm has introduced a new therapeutic horse-riding service aimed at young teens who struggle with their education experience.

'Giddy Up and Go' was devised by Sandra Schmid of Hairy Henry Care Farm, for 13-17 year-olds dealing with infrequent attendance, school refusal, anxiety in school, or trying alternatives such as home schooling.

A German native, Schmid is a qualified social worker who left her job with Tusla after training as a therapeutic horse riding coach.

She started her small care farm at Ballylickey, Bantry in 2013.

She said: "At first I only offered therapeutic horse riding, then also therapeutic activities with the other animals. 

"We now have sheep; donkeys; goats; hen; a goose; rabbits; guinea pigs; dogs and of course, horses."

The programme supports teens to learn practical skills in a farming environment and in the equine sector. 

This is combined with personal development to help teens grow in confidence, social skills, emotional resilience and stress management skills, aimed at promoting a sense of achievement and importance.

On completion of the programme, there is an option for the teens to return to the farm to train for the first stage of an equine qualification offered through the British Horse Society. 

"This can be a first stepping stone to a professional career in the equine sector," Schmid said.

She explained that school attendance issues are a big problem nationwide with one-in-five students missing a month or more of school every year, which has a direct impact on their career opportunities, mental and emotional health and social skills. 

Schmid added: "Unfortunately, there is no funding for our programme available.

"The programme is free for attendees as we want to make it easily accessible to them, but that means we have to fundraise to cover the €20,000 cost of running the programme. 

"We ran it as a pilot this spring March to June 2026, and we hope to run it again in 2027, depending on funds becoming available," the Hairy Henry founder said.

Regular fundraising events are run throughout the year and Schmid also undertakes a fundraiser ride every summer. 

"This year my ride took me through Mayo and Connemara, and we raised €2,000, which is a good start to collect funds for the 2027 programme," she said.

Schmid has availed of the Agri-Climate Rural Environment Scheme (ACRES). 

"So I was able to get a couple of grants through the Heritage Council and Cork County Council to help with the restoration of two 200-year-old stone buildings and an old well on the farm," she explained

Community hospitals

Schmid also works with community hospitals in Kinsale, Bandon, Fermoy, Skibbereen, and Clonakilty on a fortnightly or monthly basis, bringing in her animals to interact with patients. 

They include the small farm animals such as sheep, a donkey, goats, chicken, rabbits, guinea pigs, dogs and a small pony and pigs.

The team visit other hospitals and nursing homes in the wider Co. Cork area a few times a year such as St Stephen's Hospital in Cork, Farranlea nursing unit in Cork, and Conna nursing home. 

They also visit schools every summer, day care centres and residential homes for Cope Foundation.

Looking to the future Schmid said: "There are always so many plans, but never enough time to make them all happen. 

"My biggest plan is to try and attract a long-term sponsor or funding source for our 'Giddy Up & Go' programme so that we have financial security in running this programme annually."

In the absence of any big funding sources, the Hairy Henry Care Farm is running another fundraiser event on December 6. 

Schmid "We plan to have a show day where all riders who come here regularly can show off their skills in a no pressure celebratory show.

"This will be followed by a Christmas event where all families are welcome to spend the afternoon meeting our enchanting animals, enjoying pony rides and spending a festive time on our wintery farm. 

"I also set up a GoFundMe to help with our costs."

Schmid is currently trying to set up a group aimed at young families with their toddlers to experience the farm and horses in a meaningful educational way.

She runs workshops for adult learners once or twice a year, offering a day with the horses to learn about traditional farming skills. 

"Our therapy horses are also trained to pull the harrow and the cart and help maintain the farm. I don't have a tractor, so their horsepower is much appreciated," the Hairy Henry founder added.

news.title: Rachel O'Dwyer: A food delivery site that promises to deliver no food? At first, I didn’t see the appeal
news.text:
One of the greatest pleasures in my middle-aged life is a Friday takeaway, endlessly debating pizza toppings and portion sizes before buying way too much, watching the little figure bike over the virtual map to our door, only to inevitably get lost in the lane behind our house and need rescuing. 

When I heard about a site that allows users to experience the pleasure of ordering without the cost or calories or, well, delivery of anything yummy for dinner, I could not see the appeal. These are so-called dopamine sites, named for the brain chemical associated with reward seeking. Even the name “Food Never Comes” caused a neurological flare of whatever the opposite of dopamine is – deprivation? hanger? – in my hypothalamus. 

The trend began in South Korea, where youngsters facing soaring living costs turned to virtual window shopping for the thrill of adding to cart and checking out – minus the bills or buyer’s remorse. Dopamine is released when we expect something – less so when we actually get it. The theory is that clicking a “buy” button – even a fake buy button, even when the wished-for item fails to materialise – yields the same rush as a real transaction. “Craving a getaway too?” a banner ad reads, “Trip never leaves. Book the trip, skip the airport”.

Despite my initial recoil, I have to admit this feels familiar. I’ve come home late and scrolled Deliveroo while eating cereal, just for the giddy notion of summoning my heart’s desire to my door at 1am. Only last night, while my husband read a biography of John McGahern like a good example, I drifted around on Vinted, not even looking for any specific item but looking for an item specific enough to fix my desire to. It’s bleak when you realise that one of your favourite pastimes is the unrequited scroll, maybe even a little perverse, like swiping through streaming apps for 28 minutes instead of watching a 28-minute show; suddenly deferred choice becomes its own empty brand of entertainment. 

I wonder if this shopping that isn’t shopping is all that new? Walter Benjamin wrote about the 19th-century glass shopping arcades, where glamorous Parisians turned out to browse and let their attention drift from stall to stall. To be modern was to enter a capitalist dreamworld, a kind of aimless scrolling with your feet. Shopping has always involved a degree of fantasy, where the object – a new dress or a car – allows us to dream about the person we might become if we only possess it. That’s where much of the pleasure lies. But as I scroll Vinted or the “new in” section of Cos, I wonder if this imaginative hedonism is now less about a specific want than the endless possibility of finding something worth wanting, less a daydream than something that threatens to colonise my attention.

[ Ireland is richer and spending more than 30 years ago but is it making us happy?Opens in new window ]

The internet would say I am deficient in dopamine. Or maybe addicted to dopamine? One of those. One reformed shopaholic I follow on YouTube embraced a minimalist lifestyle several years back. Last week I cleaned my downstairs loo while she spoke about decluttering, before revealing that this too was problematic, as tossing out her old stuff gave her the same high as buying something new. Not shopping, it turns out, can also be addictive. We’re encouraged to frame over-consumption as a dopamine problem, to be remedied by deinfluencers, detoxes, no-spends, Marie Kondo-style clear-outs and even something called “Project Pan” (the revolutionary idea of using up your toiletries before buying more). And now it seems, dopamine shopping is another solution – fantasy retail that cures our urge to shop by allowing us to keep on shopping. 

So what are fake sites like Food Never Comes supposed to teach us about real consumption, I wonder, with my finger hovering over a bibimbap, which sits next to some AI slop tentacles labelled “ribs” you could not pay me to eat. 

Some of the simulation sites are designed as critique. On Fakehaul, a Microsoft developer, Jack Yang, has built a Temu version of Temu in response to a friend who struggled with impulse spending. Still, I happily add an aromatherapy diffuser and a chilled neck pillow to my imaginary cart. If there’s a bigger lesson, it’s drowned out by the call of stuff. On the checkout page I click on the “place order” button. I am not charged $287.22. I get a fake reference number and watch as my fake items cycle rapidly from an imaginary warehouse, to in transit, to my unspecified delivery address. The whole process, from browsing to not delivery, takes 10 minutes. I didn’t waste money or accumulate cheap things that will end up in landfill, but I wasted data and attention.

[ ‘We’re living in a capitalist hellscape’: The people learning about money on social mediaOpens in new window ]

Can fake consumption really critique capitalism? I don’t think so. I’m glad I’m not buying real stuff and that Ivan, the DPD driver I’m on first name terms with, is getting a break. But a site for simulated binge scrolling feels less like an incisive critique and more like shopping taken to its extreme, a bleak prospect where our fantasies, desires and leisure have become about what we might consume. We’re still dreaming about stuff we probably don’t need, or the life we don’t have instead of living right now. I’m reminded of a fintech event I attended 10 years ago. A game developer there told me about a failed video game (“for girls!”) where the player could “pretend” to shop. “But it was a stupid idea”, he said, “because women can do that online whenever they feel like adding stuff to a cart.” I can’t help suspecting that I play this game on a regular basis. And I realise what I really want isn’t to be someone who consumes less, but someone who wants less and spends her time better.
news.summary: It’s bleak when you realise that one of your favourite pastimes is the unrequited scroll, maybe even a little perverse
news.author: Rachel O'dwyer

news.title: Multiple deaths and injuries after 'explosion' and major fire at Canada military base
news.text: Multiple people have died and others suffered injuries following a 'serious incident' at a Canadian military base. Reports emerged of a suspected explosion at CFB Wainwright military base in Alberta which triggered a substantial blaze on Saturday, 17 October at approximately 4pm local time. "I'm saddened to share that there have been both fatalities and injuries as a result of an incident on the base," Defence Minister David McGuinty said. While McGuinty declined to disclose casualty numbers or specifics regarding what sparked the incident, it's understood further details will emerge shortly. He confirmed the Royal Canadian Mounted Police were engaged in the investigation and characterised the circumstances as "very, very active and delicate." The Canadian Armed Forces alongside federal, provincial and local agencies were orchestrating the emergency response, he stated. The neighbouring community of Wainwright was supplying hospital and firefighting assistance. Numerous accounts have surfaced of an 'explosion' which subsequently ignited a massive fire, spreading swiftly owing to powerful winds across the region. The Municipal District of Wainwright confirmed the blaze had breached the military base's boundary fence and was advancing rapidly in strong winds. Fire crews from several jurisdictions were attending, and no evacuation directive had been issued. Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe revealed his province was dispatching aid to Alberta though did not detail which resources were being mobilised. "Our thoughts are with all the brave women and men affected," Prime Minister Mark Carney said earlier in a social media post. Alberta Premier Danielle Smith described the fire as "significant and tragic" and said it was affecting many military personnel. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney wrote on X: "A serious incident creating a major fire has occurred at CFB Wainwright, in Alberta. Our thoughts are with all the brave women and men affected. "We are working closely with the Government of Alberta and local authorities. Premier Smith and I are in close contact as are our relevant ministers and officials." Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, situated approximately 180 kilometres (112 miles) southeast of Edmonton, ranks among Canada's most active military training facilities, where troops undergo preparation for combat deployments. The base houses the Canadian Manoeuvre Training Centre, which delivers authentic battlefield simulations, alongside the 3rd Canadian Division Training Centre, responsible for military instruction. Carney confirmed the federal government was collaborating closely with Alberta officials and local authorities. He noted that he and Smith maintained regular communication, as did their respective ministers and officials. Smith expressed gratitude to emergency responders and those delivering care and assistance to those impacted. Canadian Conservative opposition leader Pierre Poilievre revealed he had contacted Carney and the defence minister to extend support to those affected by the blaze. "Pray for Wainwright, everyone," Poilievre wrote in a social media post, urging residents in the affected area to heed emergency instructions and keep roads clear for first responders.
news.summary: There have been fatalities and injuries after a 'serious incident' at a Canadian military base, with reports of a possible explosion at CFB Wainwright in Alberta
news.author: Peter Hennessy

'She wasn't a member of my family': Here are the winners and losers of the political week

With union strife gripping the country for 24 hours, who can claim victory? 

6.31am, 18 Oct 2026

Share options

EVERY WEEKEND, OUR political team casts an eye over the events inside and outside Leinster House that have people talking.

This week, Irish public sector workers hit the pickets and various ministers tried to explain why there was no need for them to.

In the States, the Trump administration looked extra chaotic with fewer than three weeks left before the midterms. 

Fórsa members picket at Leinster House.Leah Farrell

Leah Farrell

Until there’s a resolution to the public sector pay dispute, one can’t definitively pick a winner and a loser. But for now, the unions are probably pleased with how this week’s 24-hour strike went. 

About 300,000 workers across numerous public sector unions took the action, an impressive mobilisation of people and purpose that also seemed to be largely backed by the wider public. 

On Friday, it was confirmed that the planned follow-up strike on Wednesday was called off and as a path to talks at the Workplace Relations Commission was bashed out. 

The development came after a week in which the leaders of the four largest unions on the displayed impressive discipline on the airwaves.

Their coherent messaging has been particularly noteworthy, and they’ve prevented a bitter back-and-forth with the government that would have made a rapprochement more difficult. 

Speaking at the launch of his campaign to become the next director general of the UN’s Food & Agriculture Organization, Phil Hogan says he was “sloppy” with Covid guidelines in 2020 and that he “disappointed people for sure and I disappointed myself in the way I responded”. https://t.co/dU3dFhXjJy— TheJournal Politics (@TJ_Politics) October 13, 2026

Phil Hogan made a public comeback of sorts this week. It came in the salubrious surroundings of Iveagh House, which houses the Department of Foreign Affairs in Dublin. 

The former EU commissioner, government minister and Fine Gael strategist is being backed by the Irish government in his bid to be director-general of the UN Food & Agriculture Organization (FAO). 

The position hasn’t been held by a European for some 50 years and comes with a salary of $265,910 (€236,000) should he win enough support to land it.

The Irish government nominated Hogan for the position back in March, and he formally launched his campaign this week, batting away questions about his resignation from frontline politics in 2020 for failing to adhere to Covid-19 restrictions.

Hogan also said he wasn’t going to get into “revisionism” about the nature of that resignation but there were some ministers there supporting him anyway. 

Advertisement

None of this is a guarantee that Hogan will get the gig, as there’ll be a vote next year by FAO member states, but the full court press the government put on this week shows he’s back in the good books. 

Jack Chambers

Minister fof Public Expenditure Jack Chambers.Alamy

This is a tentative one, as there is an argument that from a certain point of view Jack Chambers isn’t coming off badly from the strike.

As Minister for Public Expenditure, he has to put up a fight when it comes to public money, and if he does ever want to lead Fianna Fáil, having a fight with the unions burnishes certain hard-nosed credentials. 

On balance though, as the minister who effectively pays the wages of the 300,000 people out striking, losing millions of working hours in a single day can only be seen as a net loss. 

If both sides go to the WRC and ultimately there is a new pay deal, you would think Chambers will chalk it up as a victory. For now though, he still has a little way to go to get in the winners circle. 

Kimberly Guilfoyle

Departing US Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle.Alamy Stock Photo

Alamy Stock Photo

In many ways, Kimberly Guilfoyle is the literal embodiment of MAGA. When the phenomenon of ‘Mar-a-Lago face’ was being discussed last year, Guilfoyle’s face was more often than not used to demonstrate the plastic surgery-enhanced look. 

But Guilfoyle’s devotion to MAGA extended way beyond mere facial features.

As National Chair of Trump Victory Finance Committee, she was a part of Trump’s failed reelection bid in 2020 and was the keynote speaker on the opening night of the Republican National Convention that year. 

At that point, she was also dating a Trump, Donald Trump Jr to be exact, and was therefore at the heart of both the familial and administrative nexuses that make up Trumpworld. 

Fast forward a few years and things started falling apart. Her split with Donald Jr in 2024 made things somewhat awkward, so in many ways it suited everyone when she was shipped off to Athens to become the US Ambassador of Greece. 

This, however, has in turn become somewhat of a disaster amid allegations that she sought money from a Trump supporter to pay a credit card bill and also accepted lavish hospitality from wealthy Greek businessmen.

Guilfoyle calls the allegations false, but the White House was having none of it, abruptly declaring this week that Trump had asked her to resign. 

As if to drive it home, Trump was asked about her previous engagement to his son and the fact that she was therefore almost a member of his family. 

“She wasn’t a member of my family. She, I guess, dated my son a long time ago,” he said. 

Rónán Duffy

Exciting O'Shea and Munster's young guns have their say

22-year-old pair Brian Gleeson and Seán Edogbo did well in the back row.

6.31am, 18 Oct 2026

Share options

Murray Kinsella

Reports from Páirc Uí Chaoimh

IT CERTAINLY HELPED Munster’s cause that they had some experience to call on from the bench at Páirc Uí Chaoimh.

36-year-old Kieran Brookes came on for his latest impressive appearance after 58 minutes of strong work from starting tighthead prop Jack Aungier.

Fineen Wycherley scored a try shortly after coming off the Munster bench, while Gavin Coombes and Jack Donoghue brought know-how as back row replacements, and JJ Hanrahan was sent on for the final quarter to help see out the win.

Senior players like Tadhg Beirne and Alex Nankivell were key in the starting XV too, yet there’s no doubt that some of the most thrilling moments of the night for the home fans in Cork were delivered by the fresher-faced Munster players.

20-year-old Charlie O’Shea made his Champions Cup debut at out-half and added to his growing reputation as a game-breaker.

The sheer acceleration he showed for his first-half break sent a frisson of excitement coursing around the Páirc, and O’Shea followed it up with a delightful long pass to Nankivell while on the move.

O’Shea’s cross-kick at the end of that play didn’t come off, yet the intent he brought with his attacking kicking underlined that he is not a player who fears having a go. 

Witness his clever chip in behind Racing’s defence earlier in the first half, forcing Joey Manu to carry the ball over his own try line. Brian Gleeson scored a cracking try off the resulting five-metre scrum.

Advertisement

Munster position O’Shea in the backfield when defending from lineouts, meaning he’s not exposed to as many frontline tackles, but O’Shea isn’t shy about getting stuck into contact. He was their joint top ball-carrier against Racing with 15. 

O’Shea has plenty to learn, of course, but he appears to be unfazed by the challenges head coach Clayton McMillan is presenting him with early on this season.

Seán Edogbo had some strong involvements.Nick Elliott / INPHO

Nick Elliott / INPHO / INPHO

22-year-old blindside flanker Seán Edogbo was the other Champions Cup debutant in Munster’s starting XV and he grew into the game strongly. The Cobh man provided a pair of punchy carries in the build-up to Beirne’s try, which was an excellent team score.

Edogbo’s intent to get stuck into everything was noticeable and though some moments got away from him, this was a promising first outing in the top competition. 

With his older brother, Edwin, nearing a return from injury, it will be exciting to see the Edogbo lads working in tandem again soon.

23-year-old wing Shay McCarthy made his second Champions Cup start for Munster and scored a cracking try in the first half. The ball found its way to him unexpectedly, but the Limerick man didn’t hesitate for a split second in backing himself.

The initial turn of pace and evasion were important, but the dominant way McCarthy bounced off last defender Antoine Gibert stood out too.

McCarthy is not one to shy away from physical confrontation, yet it was also welcome to see him open up and show his speed for that score.

The aforementioned Gleeson is still 22, but he looks ready to nail down a spot as a first-choice player for Munster, despite Coombes only being 28. 

Gleeson is clearly in good form and one suspects he’d love to keep rolling in the number eight jersey. The Irish coaching staff are interested in Gleeson’s development too, given his sheer power and size.

As well as taking his five-metre scrum try emphatically, showing acceleration and explosive power, there were some nice touches on the ball from Gleeson.

His frustration at missing a tackle on Wilfried Hulleu for one of Racing’s tries was clear. Learning to nail moment after moment after moment is always the challenge for younger players, but Gleeson has the goods to get this stuff right.

Ben O'Connor is upended by Racing's Arthur Roche.Dan Clohessy / INPHO

Dan Clohessy / INPHO / INPHO

22-year-old fullback Ben O’Connor had his own frustrations at times, as Munster struggled to get a grip on the aerial contests, but he had plenty of impressive moments in this game too.

O’Connor has become increasingly imposing in contact, using his explosiveness to win collisions when the only route is a direct one, yet he has the pace and footwork to evade defenders too. Most importantly, the fullback continues to hone his rugby instincts.

There were two other Champions Cup debuts off the bench for Munster, but hooker Max Clein and scrum-half Ben O’Donovan only got a minute to mark that milestone. 

All in all, this was a happy outing for the younger guns in the Munster side.

Murray Kinsella

news.title: Mum in tears as family mocks baby boy's name for sounding like prescription meds
news.text: A mum has been slammed for giving her baby boy a name that "sounds like a nasal spray" - but some people believe she isn't the one in the wrong. Explaining the situation, a woman shared how her cousin, Sarah, wanted to give her son a unique name and proudly announced her choice during a family dinner. However, the conversation quickly turned sour when she decided to speak up and "say what everyone was thinking" about the unusual moniker. While she stands by her comments, others believe she was too harsh and the mum shouldn't be shamed for choosing an unconventional name for her baby. Ensure our latest headlines always appear at the top of your Google Search by making us a Preferred Source. Click here to activate or add us as Preferred Source in your Google search settings She said on Reddit: "My cousin Sarah just had her first baby and honestly the name she picked is so ridiculous I couldn't just sit there and pretend it was normal during the family dinner last night. "She named the poor kid Alegron which sounds exactly like something you'd take to stop sneezing in the spring and I'm apparently the massive jerk for pointing that out to everyone. "She was doing that annoying thing where she makes everyone go around and say what their favourite thing about the baby is and when it got to me I just said he's cute but he sounds like a prescription for hay fever." However, Sarah didn't take too kindly to the comment and let out a gasp before bursting into tears. The cousin added: "She said she and her husband spent months finding a name that was 'unique and strong' but come on if you name your kid something that sounds like it should have a warning about drowsiness on the back you have to expect people to notice. "I tried to explain that I was actually doing her a favour because kids in middle school are going to be way meaner than me but she just kept sobbing about how I ruined her first outing since the hospital." All the while, her brother was kicking her under the table, telling her to shut up - but the cousin claimed she "wasn't even being mean". Wanting to know whether she was in the wrong, she added: "I was just being realistic and honestly if she didn't want opinions she shouldn't have asked for them in a room full of people. "Now my mum is blowing up my phone saying I'm 'socially stunted' and demanding I send a formal apology but I feel like I'm the only one being honest while everyone else is just coddling her and letting this kid grow up with a name that belongs in a pharmacy aisle. "I even looked it up later and there is literally a drug called Allegra so I'm not even reaching here but everyone is acting like I slapped the baby instead of just giving some constructive feedback on a terrible naming choice. Am I the a***hole for not wanting my nephew to sound like a nasal spray?" Commenting on her post, one user said: "The child is already named. Just leave little Allegra alone." Another user added: "Little Ben only realised much later that Benadryl was not a regular name." A third user said: "You could've gone about that in a nicer way or just says nothing at all even if the name does sound dumb. I don't think it's necessarily wrong to have that opinion though."
news.summary: A mum was left in tears after her family told her they thought the unique baby name she chose for her newborn son sounded like a nasal spray allergy medication...

news.title: Dairy trade: Heifers selling to €3,700 this week
news.text:
Despite a slow start, the autumn dairy trade is starting to pick up this week, with numerous sales now taking place across the country.

One such sale included the annual Carnaross dairy sale, in Carnaross Mart, Co. Meath.

The sale saw over 50 freshly calved heifers and cows go up for grabs, as well as a number of springing heifers.

A top price of €3,700 was given at the sale for a March-2024-born pedigree Holstein heifer.

Bred by Philip Jones of the renowned Hallow Holsteins, Hallow Lambda Serenity 1995 was full of class.

She was sired by Farnear Delta-Lambda-ET, an elite bull who also sired Knowlesmere Lvictory, the intermediate Holstein champion and overall honourable mention at the recent FBD National Dairy Show.

The heifer was out of Hallow Applicable Senerty EX90, a cow who is projected to produce 13,934kg of milk at 3.87% fat and 3.08% protein. equating to 968kg milk solids, in her sixth lactation this year.

Some other top prices from the sale included:

€3,650 for Hallow Ariel Twizzle, a May-2024-born heifer bred by Hallow Holsteins. She calved down three weeks prior and is currently giving 29L;

€3,600 for Hallow Lambda Serenity 2004, a March-2024-born heifer bred by Hallow Holsteins. Having calved in September, she is projected to produce 8,414kg of milk solids at 3.77% fat and 3.32% protein in her first lactation this year;

€3,500 for Hallow Lambda Grace 1758, a March-2024-born heifer bred by Hallow Holsteins. Her dam produced 6,851kg of milk at 4.12% fat and 3.46% protein in her first lactation in 2024.

UK dairy trade

Across the water in the UK, pedigree heifers are making up to £3,800 in the mart.

The monthly Borderway dairy sale recently took place in the Borderway Mart in Carlisle, England.

Buyers were recorded from 19 counties across the UK as a total of 344 dairy cattle went up for grabs.

These included Holstein cows in milk, Holstein heifers in milk, Holsteins in-calf heifers, Jersey-cross cows and heifers, Ayrshire cows, and bulling heifers.

The top price of £3,800 was achieved twice, the first of which was for a February-2024-born heifer.

She was sired by the well-known Seagull Bay Applejax, and was only calved down a month ago.

The next time the hammer rang to the tune of £3,800 was for an August-2024-born heifer.

The heifer was sired by Aster Dam Butch, and calved down back in August.

A further five animals were sold above £3,700, while another six sold above £3,600.

In total, 101 Holstein heifers in milk sold to an average of £3,034/head, while 40 Holstein cows in milk averaged £2,610/head, and in-calf Holstein heifers averaged £2,569/head on the day.

Meanwhile, Jersey-cross cows were selling to an average price of £1,862/head, while in-calf Jersey were selling for an average of £2,095/head.

According to the mart manager, prices are on the rise as confidence builds in the dairy sector due to the positive direction of milk prices.

news.title: A haulier’s guide to taking on a new customer
news.text:
Winning a new customer is welcome news for any haulage business. However, before accepting the first load, operators should establish exactly what the work involves, how it will be priced and what is required to secure payment.

A few straightforward checks at the outset can help prevent delivery problems, disputed charges and unnecessary administration.

1. Establish who is booking and paying

Confirm the customer’s full business name, billing address and accounts contact. If the business placing the order differs from the company paying the invoice, clarify the arrangement before work begins.

Agree payment terms, consider an appropriate credit check and establish a credit limit suited to the potential exposure.

Ask whether invoices require a purchase-order number, booking reference or submission through a particular portal. Missing information can delay payment even when the transport job has been completed successfully.

2. Get an accurate description of the load

“Ten pallets” tells the transport office relatively little without further detail.

Confirm the goods, total weight, dimensions, packaging and whether pallets can be stacked. Establish whether the consignment needs temperature control, specialist equipment or particular handling arrangements.

Where dangerous goods or other specialist loads are involved, obtain the relevant information and confirm that the business can meet the requirements before accepting the booking.

The vehicle and equipment allocated should reflect the actual load.

3. Check collection and delivery arrangements

Obtain the full addresses, Eircodes where applicable, booking references and working contact numbers for both ends of the journey.

Check opening hours, appointment times and any restrictions on vehicle size or access. Establish how loading and unloading will take place, who will provide the equipment and whether any driver involvement is expected.

A customer’s postal address may differ from the goods entrance. Clear arrival instructions can save the driver an unnecessary detour or a difficult approach.

Any proposed schedule should allow the work to be completed safely and within the applicable driving and working-time requirements.

4. Put the price and scope in writing

The quotation should describe the service being supplied and the assumptions behind the rate.

Clarify arrangements for additional drops, changes of destination, pallet exchanges, cancellations, failed deliveries and goods that must be returned.

Agree how loading and unloading delays will be handled, including any time allowance and additional charges. Where fuel adjustments or other variable charges apply, explain how they will be calculated.

Confirm the agreed terms before dispatch. An unexpected charge is harder to resolve once the job is finished.

5. Agree the paperwork needed for payment

Ask what constitutes acceptable proof of delivery and how quickly it must be submitted.

Does the customer require a signed delivery docket, an electronic record, a named recipient or supporting photographs? Must original documents follow?

Drivers should know how to record shortages, damage or a refusal to accept goods and when to contact the transport office.

A completed delivery should trigger a clear process for checking documents and issuing the invoice promptly.

6. Give drivers a clear escalation route

Identify who can authorise changes to the job and approve additional costs.

If the goods differ from the booking, access is unsuitable or the delivery cannot proceed, the driver needs a reliable transport-office contact. The office, in turn, needs someone at the customer’s business who can make a decision.

Record revised instructions and approvals in writing wherever practicable. Drivers should not be left to negotiate commercial arrangements at the delivery point.

7. Review the first few jobs

Compare the work performed with the original quotation.

Were the load details accurate? Did the delivery arrangements work? Were documents accepted and invoices paid as agreed?

Use those findings to correct instructions, adjust the service or discuss pricing before problems become routine.

A simple customer setup form gives the transport office, driver and accounts team a shared reference. Completing it before the first load helps establish a working relationship that can deliver reliable service and a worthwhile return.
