Tragedy, commitment, and county stars - the rise of Edendork to their first Tyrone senior final

Sandwiched in one of the hottest GAA areas in the country, Edendork face illustrious opponents in Errigal Ciaran. 

6.01am, 18 Oct 2026

Share options

Declan Bogue

IF THE SECRET sauce that makes Tyrone club rivalry so spicy is close-quarters combat, then Edendork St Malachy’s must have a raging appetite for success.

This Sunday, they appear in their first-ever Tyrone senior final.

Waiting for them in Healy Park, Omagh (throw-in 4.30pm) are scalding-hot favourites Errigal Ciaran.

Should Errigal win, it moves them into second on the Tyrone roll of honour on 12 titles (including two titles in 1926 and 1931 as Ballygawley St Ciaran’s), just three behind Carrickmore on 15.

Meanwhile, Edendork have been choosing from the pauper’s menu. Their honours came in junior titles of 1938 and 1957, intermediate successes coming in 1969, 1985, 2015 and 2020.

The excellence of their players of recent vintage has elevated their profile.

Darren McCurry was the man-of-the-match in the 2021 All-Ireland final with 1-4 on the board when Tyrone won their fourth Sam Maguire, beating Mayo in the final, and was duly rewarded with an All-Star.

Tyrone have a second goal, with a lightning attack from one end to the other finished off by Darren McCurry in another body blow for Mayo #RTEGAA #MAYOvTYRONE 

📺 Watch Live - https://t.co/IdpkJmuz4B

📱 Live updates- https://t.co/8TNdjy2oh7 https://t.co/gISq8I9AXf— The Sunday Game (@TheSundayGame) September 11, 2021

Goalkeeper Niall Morgan has been one of the best exponents of that position and hit 0-3 from dead balls in that aforementioned final, one from over 50 metres. Morgan has All-Stars from 2021 and 2024, and was a mainstay of the Ireland International Rules team when they played Australia.

In midfield in 2021 was Conn Kilpatrick, who looks nailed on to become an All-Star himself after his year with Tyrone.

Niall Morgan playing for Ireland.Alamy Stock Photo

Alamy Stock Photo

Nothing motivates GAA clubs quite like the success of neighbours, but Edendork’s situation, when all is considered, is rather incredible.

From Arthur Mallon Park, no fewer than 12 clubs are within a 10-mile radius, and it’s worth detailing them here: Coalisland Fianna (2.5 miles), Dungannon Thomas Clarkes (2.9), Galbally (6.9), Brackaville Owen Roes (2.3), Donaghmore St Patrick’s (3.9), Clonoe O’Rahilly’s (3.3), Stewartstown (3.8), Killyman St Mary’s (5.5), Derrytresk (7.5), Derrylaughan Kevin Barrys (8.4), Brockagh Emmets (7.9) and Eglish St Patrick’s (6.6).

Add in hurling clubs Eoghan Ruadh (1.9) and Naomh Colum Cille (4.3). 

By way of contrast, Errigal Ciaran come from a much more mountainous, rural region in the west of the county. Their most local club is Beragh Red Knights at 5.1 miles away, but the two have seldom met.

After that, it’s Carrickmore St Colmcilles (7.4), Killeeshil St Mary’s (7.7), Augher St Macartan’s (9), Pomeroy Plunketts (10), Eskra Emmets (10.4) and Galbally Pearses (10.7).

You get the picture.

Edendork have always recruited out of the local primary school, and demand has shot up in recent years with a new school being constructed on the site of the former Edendork Ballroom, a place of dancing, hi-jinks and bingo.

Former player Ronan Murphy played 17 years of adult football for the club and was taking the U14 team this season. They won a Grade 3 league, but when he was asked why Edendork were playing Grade 3, it’s because they didn’t have enough players to field 15-a-side, which is a requirement from Grade 2 up.

“But we punch above our weight in terms of what we have at underage and what we are able to put out at senior,” says Murphy.

Advertisement

Ronan Murphy.Tom Maher / INPHO

Tom Maher / INPHO / INPHO

“The other side of it is people get playing football. Around Edendork, you are not like others that sit on a load of teams. Here, you get to play and you get developed as a player.”

“And that happens when they play at underage and have loads of exposure. Then, when they want to play senior, you can really go to town.

“But you always want to beat or match your neighbours. That brings up the standards and healthy competition is good for an area.

“Boys go to school together and they realise, ‘Sure I am as good as him.’ And schools play a part in that too. If they are playing a high level at school it helps to push them on.”

The McGuckin clan are synonymous with Ballinderry Shamrocks. When Mick married Margeurite, they found themselves a site on the Bush Road, built a house, but he still was drawn to home.

This is a man, after all, who captained Derry in the early ‘70s and once held Mick O’Dwyer scoreless in a game. 

He played on with Ballinderry before becoming manager. By 1982, Edendork convinced him to join their ranks, courtesy of Jim Devlin’s persuasiveness.

McGuckin was never one for half measures, signing up as a trainer and manager and they won the championship and league double in 1985. 

On that team was the likes of Joe Mallon, father of current captain, Conor.

The Mallons are another name that runs through Edendork like a stick of rock. The late John Mallon was a grandfather of Conn Kilpatrick.

Conn Kilpatrick.James Crombie / INPHO

James Crombie / INPHO / INPHO

John’s desire to progress the club made them hugely forward-thinking. He would travel over to Scotland to auctions and bid on galvanised fencing materials, shipping them back to close in the perimeter of the pitch. He was involved in the shuttering of the steps around the pitch that has made it such an important venue, not only for hosting Tyrone championship games, but also schools and college fixtures.

Every year he took his family holidays in Arklow, Wicklow. But they were as much about fact-finding as he scoured all the club pitches on the way up and down to find out what Edendork could implement.

Mick’s son Brian played for Tyrone and is the current Edendork manager. Another son, Joe, is in the backroom. He has another son, John, who managed Edendork to the 2020 intermediate championship and is currently over Sarsfields in Armagh.

Brian McGuckin.Lorcan Doherty / INPHO

Lorcan Doherty / INPHO / INPHO

While Mick was playing football at Queen’s University, he became friendly with Des Fox, who was an administrator for the university’s GAA club.

When he came to build his house, he ended up next-door neighbour of Fox and the two families not so much mingled, as merged.

Edendork have a rich tradition of music and culture, with the Fox and McGuckin families being to the fore.

Fox was a bookmaker that travelled to the race meetings all around the country. In September 1990, he was on his way to The Curragh when his Mercedes was intercepted and fired upon by a gang using two vehicles with false plates.

Fox tried to reverse away, but his car ran off the road. He had been shot through his leg, a main femoral artery, and bled to death at the scene.

The gang made off with a sum of around €20,000 in a black leather briefcase.

“It was a tragic day, a day that shouldn’t have happened,” recalls McGuckin.

“I was in the house here and the rumours were coming through about him being shot and then dying.

“I had to go in next door with the parish priest to say it to his wives and daughters. It was a day I will never forget.”

His loss has been impossible to replace.

“Des was the energy in Edendork club for a long, long number of years. He was devoted to it, he was excited by it. He was committed. And I mean every last bit of it,” says McGuckin.

“He had three girls, very good instrumentalists and my girls used to do a bit of singing. Dessie would have had them all involved in the Scór every year. As well as that, he was the chairman of the club when they were building the pavilion and the new pitch.

“He would have been committed in every way. Financially, he would have been putting in a few pounds, quietly. People wouldn’t have known about it.”

In November 2008, the Edendork clubhouse was burned down. A group calling itself the ‘Orange Volunteers’ called the UTV studios to claim responsibility. 

That morning, the club volunteers cleared all the debris and they went ahead and hosted a relegation play-off against Pomeroy with the main building still smouldering as a backdrop.

Edendork clubrooms after the arson attack.Alamy Stock Photo

Alamy Stock Photo

After a major fundraising drive, they rebuilt magnificent, state-of-the-art facilities. When it came to the grand re-opening, they named it ‘The Des Fox Pavilion’.

“I wonder what his position would have been now. He was a top-notch bookmaker. He was a great punter and wasn’t afraid to put on big bets and take big bets as I understand it,” says McGuckin.

In February 2020, just before Covid closed the world down, the waterlogged Healy Park pitch meant that Tyrone’s league game against Kerry had to be switched. Edendork took the game.

Niall Morgan, Conn Kilpatrick and Darren McCurry all played. McCurry converted a series of difficult frees. Afterwards, he talked about picturing his late mother at the back door of his family home, within sight of the pitch.

In a ragged and tough game, David Clifford was sent off for a second yellow card towards the end. As frustrated as Clifford was, he still donated his jersey to the club.

They have it framed in the Des Fox Pavilion, muck and all still intact.

David Clifford in the jersey that hangs, unwashed, in Edendork.Bryan Keane / INPHO

Bryan Keane / INPHO / INPHO

When it comes to Healy Park on Sunday, all reasoning points to an Errigal Ciaran win.

It is accepted that Edendork do not possess the same depth of panel as Errigal Ciaran. Few do.

But in their path to the final in beating Ardboe, Clonoe and Donaghmore, they have become the Mayo of this local championship. They have taken 37 shots for two-pointers, nailing 18 of them. Errigal have had 17 attempts at two-pointers, converting just three.

God rest Dessie Fox, but if he were alive today, he’d have a nibble at Edendork at 15/8.

Edendork will keep swinging.

Declan Bogue

news.title: Newtown Blues v St Mochtas streaming details and more for Louth SFC final
news.text: Newtown Blues and St Mochtas face off this Sunday in the Louth Senior Football Championship final, with the prestigious Joe Ward Cup up for grabs at the Integral GAA Grounds in Drogheda. The Blues are gunning to end a seven-year drought and claim a 24th county title. Blocking their path is a St Mochtas outfit chasing their first-ever Louth senior football championship crown, having fallen short in their sole previous final appearance back in 2021. Newtown Blues scraped through against Ardee St Mary's by the narrowest of margins in the semi-final, triumphing 1-15 to 2-11. St Mochtas, by contrast, delivered a commanding performance to dismantle St Joseph's 1-21 to 0-8 and secure their spot in the showpiece decider. Here's everything you need to know ahead of Sunday's clash: The final is being held at the Integral GAA Grounds in Drogheda, Co Louth. Throw-in is scheduled for 3.30pm on Sunday, October 18, 2026. The game is being shown live on Clubber. news.title: Truagh Gaels v Scotstown streaming details for Monaghan SFC final
news.text: Truagh Gaels and Scotstown are set to battle it out for the Monaghan Senior Football Championship crown on Sunday, with Truagh gunning to topple the reigning champions in a rematch of the 2021 decider. Truagh sealed their spot in the final after a dramatic six-goal thriller against Clontibret, edging through 4-16 to 2-19. Scotstown booked their place with a win over Inniskeen and will be looking to extend their extraordinary record of county final appearances. news.title: A Belfast designer on making it big in New York: ‘There are still days when I have to pinch myself’
news.text:
As anyone who runs their own business knows, life is busy, often chaotic, and can come at you fast. Throw a schedule that requires transatlantic travel into the mix and things get even busier. But this doesn’t faze Ryan Crown, who runs his own design business, Crown Creative, while dividing his time between his home near Belfast and New York City. 

The business began in the Big Apple in 2018, but the writing was in the stars two years before that. Crown wet his feet working as a marketing manager for The Dead Rabbit, named “the world’s best bar” in 2016 and founded by Belfast natives Sean Muldoon and Jack McGarry. He then moved to a larger hospitality group as creative director, working across everything from Michelin-starred restaurants and cocktail bars to food halls, Italian restaurants and steakhouses. 

The variety of projects saw him fall in love with the job and the city itself, but it wasn’t long before he decided he wanted to branch out on his own. After convincing his employer that “they weren’t losing an employee, they were gaining an entire creative studio”, Crown Creative had its first client. 

Now, eight years on, the company has a team of 25 working in Belfast, New York and London, and has grown from a branding and design agency, into a full-service studio offering brand strategy, graphic design, interiors and digital, all under one roof.

“That model came from my own frustration as a client, having to co-ordinate several different agencies on a single project,” he says. “We wanted to offer something more joined-up: a single team which understands the entire vision and behaves like an extension of the client’s own business. We describe ourselves as a creative partner because, on the best projects, that’s genuinely what we become.

“There are still days when I have to pinch myself at the calibre of the clients and projects coming through our doors. To see work created by our team in Belfast, London and New York come to life globally is genuinely humbling. It feels as though we’re not simply designing places – we’re helping to create brands and experiences with a real legacy. In the last year we’ve seen a luxury safari resort open in Africa, a restaurant we designed in Grand Central Terminal in New York and a boutique wine hotel in Oregon.”

The 35-year-old, who has a 20-month old daughter with his partner, Ema, wasn’t always destined to be a designer as he studied drama and English at college, before doing a master’s in drama at Queen’s University Belfast. But, although he never trained as a designer, he says that his background taught him “a great deal about storytelling and how to understand an audience – both of which are fundamental to the work undertaken at Crown today”.

Travel is another great source of inspiration for the designer, who says that being away for “at least one week a month”, and also looking beyond his own industry, helps to get the creative juices flowing. 

“Inspiration often comes from somewhere unexpected: the pacing of a theatrical production, the typography on an old street sign, or the way a small neighbourhood restaurant makes people feel completely at home,” he says. “Also, my guilty pleasure is magazines. I subscribe to far too many – Monocle, Bon Appétit and Wallpaper among them – and feel guilty every month when I don’t get through the pile. But I love the discovery involved in print, and the physical experience of holding a beautifully made magazine in my hands.”

The projects undertaken by Crown can vary vastly in size – from the St Regis Cap Cana Resort in the Dominican Republic, where the team created nine individual food-and-beverage brands over the course of two years, to the Neighbourhood Cafe in Belfast, which the founder co-owns with his business partner and best friend, Oisín McEvoy.

Another recent project was The Kithmore in St Andrews, and also a refreshing of the global identity of Peacock Alley, the historic institution associated with the Waldorf Astoria.

But, regardless of the scale, each job is meticulously thought out and executed. 

“The budgets and commercial details of many of these projects are confidential, but the developments range from independent hospitality businesses to significant, multimillion-pound international hotel investments,” says Crown. “What matters to us is the same at every scale: finding the story, expressing it consistently, and making every detail feel intentional.

“And there’s something quite surreal about standing in one of New York’s most iconic hotels and seeing a brand developed by our team in Belfast.”

Fashion trends are constantly changing, and the interior design world is no different. But the businessman says while that he and his team are conscious of trends, they “try not to follow them too closely, because if a design is built around a passing visual fashion, it can date very quickly”.

“The strongest movement I see is away from the generic, copy-and-paste international aesthetic and towards spaces that feel rooted in their location,” he says. “There’s a renewed appreciation for character, craft, natural materials and vintage pieces – interiors which can develop a patina over time, rather than looking perfect only on opening day.

“When we began, there was a great deal of emphasis on creating highly ‘Instagrammable’ moments. And while that still has its place, clients are now looking for something deeper. They want comfort, atmosphere, authenticity and a sense that a space could only exist in that particular place.

“Every detail matters, but people rarely leave a hotel remembering a particular wallpaper or bed throw. They remember how the place made them feel. A trend might give you a moment, but a strong narrative gives longevity to a project.”

The design expert says there are many large-scale ideas that can be adapted and work very well in the home, but it is important to be aware of your own style and environment. 

“With so many beautiful interiors online it’s tempting to go Pinterest shopping and turn your home into one large mood board,” he says. “But before buying anything, it’s worth understanding your own taste and how you actually want your home to feel. The most interesting homes say something about the people living in them, rather than replicating a nice image online.

“Lighting is the quickest transformation for me. I’ll always choose several small lamps at different heights over switching on the ‘big light’ as warm, layered lighting can change the atmosphere of a room immediately and make even an inexpensive interior feel considered.

“With more of us working from home, it’s also important to create some separation between working and living – even if that simply means a good chair, a dedicated lamp, and being able to put the laptop out of sight at the end of the day. Your home should support the way you actually live, not just photograph well.”

While Crown and his team are currently working on several beautiful Michelin-starred restaurant projects in New York, as well as beginning the interior design of two restaurant and bar spaces at The Ritz-Carlton in Geneva, they have also just launched a Substack called Hospitality Everywhere, which is a home for the team’s “observations, opinions and discoveries – from travel and current projects to the bigger questions shaping hospitality”.

[ A Wicklow mansion rescued from ruin by seven people: ‘I felt sorry for the house’Opens in new window ]

So the future looks bright as he is looking forward to further success and new developments both in his personal and professional life. 

“We have such a breadth of experience within the studio, so I’m excited to give more of the team a platform [with the Substack] and see where it goes,” he says. “But, personally, my next major project is the arrival of our second child in October. And amid the nappies, sleepless nights and chaos of having two children under two, I’m also hugely excited about continuing to grow Crown. I genuinely feel we’re only at the beginning of what the agency can achieve, and I’m incredibly thankful for the people I get to work alongside every day.

[ Why you should choose your furniture before renovating your homeOpens in new window ]

“Looking further ahead, I think the word ‘luxury’ has become overused. We’re going to see a return to a more meaningful idea of it – less about marble, thread counts or the size of a bedroom, and more about genuine, authentic experience. 

“As our lives become increasingly digital, people will place greater value on experiences that feel human, generous and connected to their location. They won’t necessarily remember every object in a room, but they’ll remember how warmly they were welcomed, who they met and how it all made them feel. To me, that’s the future of hospitality [and design].”
news.summary: Ryan Crown has worked on projects as diverse as a luxury safari resort in Africa, Michelin-starred restaurants in New York and Geneva’s Ritz Carlton hotel
news.author: Arlene Harris

news.title: A generation late: 900,000 children have been denied treatment at the overdue Children’s Hospital
news.text:
Two significant things happened in January 2007. Apple unveiled the iPhone to the world. In Ireland, the government formally decided to build a new national children’s hospital, and promised it would be ready by 2011.

So how has that turned out, almost 20 years on? The iPhone has revolutionised how people live and redefined communication; more than three billion of them have been sold around the globe. The children’s hospital – well, we’re still waiting, and we don’t even know when it will open.

How can that be? How can a project everyone supported and desperately wanted be arriving so late? How is it that the hospital is going to cost a multiple of what we were originally promised? What does this mean for other big projects in the offing – the new National Maternity Hospital and MetroLink, for a start? And, more generally, how we run our country?

Stranger still is the lack of outrage at the waste of money. The media has, by and large, switched off on this story; the Opposition too. The public, fed a circular narrative of ‘Bam [the main contractor] versus hospital development board’, shows little interest. As Paul Weller sang so long ago, “the public wants what the public gets”.

But then Irish public life has become pretty surreal in the third decade of the 21st century. Billions of euros flow into the public coffers from international tax arrangements. We hardly have to worry about funding the present, though we’re fearful about the future. What if the tech tax pipeline gets switched off? Will we wait till then to start bemoaning the waste incurred on public projects? And our failure to even start other much-needed pieces of infrastructure?

Public spending profligacy was a recurring theme in my journalistic career, from interminable tribunals to botched IT projects and repeated overspending in health. Small scandals – such as the Leinster House bike shed or the National Gallery printer – seem to catch the public imagination while larger overspends induce a weary shrug of the shoulders.

Like Paul Weller, however, “I don’t get what this society wants”. Overspending at the children’s hospital bugs me; it’s our money as citizens, my money even. So I started digging deeper into the project, trying to understand what happened, interviewing dozens of people involved at various stages of its development. I talked to patients and their families, politicians, policymakers, builders and architects, on and off the record. I didn’t believe anyone deliberately set out to deliver an over-priced, massively-delayed hospital, but I wanted to see if the errors made could be identified and lessons learned.

The result is Billion Dollar Baby, a detailed but by no means exhaustive look at how the hospital is heading for a €3 billion pricetag and being completed a generation late. The problems on this project, I found, have roots going back many decades but which were made worse at nearly every turn through hubris, over-optimism, inattention to detail and institutional infighting. Many could have been avoided, or at least minimised.

I had lived with this story for many years. In 2014, I was the first journalist to tour the proposed site for the facility, which was then a jumble of old buildings and overgrown patches of weeds at the western end of St James’s Hospital. Even by then, the project had had a controversial history, marked by political machinations, resignations and money issues. The location had been changed once, but planning permission to build it southwest of the city centre had been granted two years earlier. 

Gazing over the area from an elevated vantage point, the project director and I tried to imagine the giant building that was to arise on this spot. Ireland’s biggest construction project; a cutting-edge hospital for the sickest children. It was hard not to be excited at this impending symbol of the country’s modernisation. 

After that visit, the site was cleared and an enormous hole was dug for the foundations of the hospital. But for a long time, and with apologies for the punning, nothing concrete appeared above the hoardings. Something was amiss. 

[ Delay of children’s hospital would ‘impose considerable additional costs’, Minister warnsOpens in new window ]

In 2018, rumours reached me of money problems at the hospital. Just as construction was due to get under way, I started hearing how the bill for the project was increasing by millions of euro every week. How the final cost of a hospital that started with a €650 million pricetag was now heading for well over €1 billion. How, if this continued, the building could become the most expensive hospital in the world. 

While the public remained blithely in the dark, officials in several government departments were aware of the problem, I was told. Some had even given the increasingly grandiose project a nickname – the Edifice Complex. 

At the time, I was living nearby. I would often cycle past the site hoardings, gaily decorated with computer-generated images showing happy patients and doctors inside the clean-edged concrete and glass of a brash building. There was a panel illustrating the timeline of the project, which was regularly updated, yet always seemed to be out of date as deadlines constantly slipped. 

No one would confirm the rumours. No firm information was available, I was informed. Finally, in December 2018, the exact figures for the overrun were set down in a cabinet memo, which was leaked to this newspaper. In just six weeks, the officially cited cost of the project had grown by €400 million. And further increases were forecast.

These were telephone-book numbers, in an era when telephone directories still existed. Their revelation triggered a political firestorm. A plethora of reports and investigations was ordered. The government of the time tottered but ultimately survived. After all, as Leo Varadkar tells me in an interview for the book, “the hospital was always a ‘hundreds of millions problem’ rather than a ‘billions problem’ like Brexit or tax policy”. 

Construction started – and so did further problems. Turmoil in the wider world intruded. Covid-19. The Ukraine War. The aforementioned Brexit. As costs further escalated, the development board and Bam, fell out in the most public manner and ended up suing each other. 

Fast forward almost a decade, and the cost is officially estimated at €2.24 billion, though few would be surprised if the final bill reaches €3 billion. There is still no end date for a project that was promised over 20 years ago. The completion date at St James’s has been delayed almost 20 times. 

In 1919, Kathleen Lynn founded St Ultan’s children’s hospital in Dublin with £70 in the bank and two cots in a room. Over a century later, the national children’s hospital will open at some point with almost 480 beds and an operating budget likely to exceed €1 billion a year. It is not the most expensive hospital in the world, we are officially told.

I toured the as yet incomplete facility earlier this year. On the day of my visit, the vast interior space was eerily silent save for the sound of beeping alarms. The only people traversing the tiled ground-floor concourse were building workers and delivery staff kitted out in hard hats, high-vis jackets and plastic shoe-covers. The planned shops and food outlets along the concourse remained boarded up and empty. 

The architecture is impressive, the materials used top-notch. The design, encompassing generous use of granite, glass and aluminium, shouts ‘no expense spared’. There are generous play areas between each finger of the building, a ‘meadow garden’ sits at the end of the concourse, a state-of-the-art hydrotherapy pool and gyms on upper floors, a rooftop helipad.

Standing above the atrium, the real meaning of the building can be gleaned not from these fancy elements, but from the fresh air in front of me – four storeys of it rising up from the entrance area and three more above me. This is dead space that would never exist in a private facility, the clearest expression that this is a statement building, designed to boost the morale of citizens. As my guide for the day remarked, “this is the sort of thing you see in Dubai”.

The building is a wonder, and I wish it well. But my concerns won’t go away once it opens. It will be expensive to operate, staff and expand. The job of amalgamating staff from different institutions with different work cultures is a mammoth undertaking, as the ongoing scandals at Children’s Health Ireland show. There is little sign that the promised maternity hospital will be built on the St James’s site in the near future, though this tri-location of adult, children’s and maternity hospital is regarded as the gold standard for patient care.

This is the story of a building but with patients at its heart. For many years, children’s care was the Cinderella of Irish health. Extremely sick patients were – and still are – being treated in often crumbling facilities in our existing, dilapidated children’s hospitals. With the hospital being completed almost a generation late, something like 900,000 children have missed out on the chance of being treated in it. Meanwhile, at a rough estimate, about 5,000 social homes could have been built with the over-spend on the project, or more than 1,500 hospital beds. Depending on what eventually happens in the courts between Bam and the development board, the final overrun on this project could be higher than currently projected. 

The story of the children’s hospital, in all its twists and turns, its shocks and reverses, fascinates and appals in equal measure. It is a story about Dublin, and great rivalries in a small place. About promises that were made to a generation of children who, ultimately, were let down by the delays that occurred. It touches on medicine and money, obviously, but also politics, religion, academia and business. 

Current headlines tell us only part of the story; the project’s problems have their roots in decisions and events from years, even decades, ago. Overspending, delays and underestimation of costs occurred well before Bam got involved. One minister summed it up pithily as “the wrong design, on the wrong site, contracted in the wrong way and built by the wrong main contractor”.

Most of all, this story is about people; families who have been let down too often before, and whose children have had to wait far too long for the world-class hospital in which they were promised they would receive treatment. 

Paul Cullen is a former health editor of The Irish Times. Billion Dollar Baby – How Ireland Built Its National Children’s Hospital – At Any Cost, is published by Hachette Ireland
news.summary: My concerns won’t go away once it opens, as it will be expensive to operate, staff and expand.

news.title: The curious backlash against Nick Griggs taking up a US athletics scholarship
news.text:
The announcement by the University of Oregon earlier this week that Nick Griggs was officially “Flying with the Flock”, a reference to Oregon’s sports teams also being known as the Ducks, certainly appears to have ruffled a few feathers.

In continuing the long history of Irish athletes taking up a US scholarship, Griggs has brought some wider attention to the rules of the National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA), the governors of all US college sport since 1906.

Griggs is unquestionably a major catch for Oregon. The Tyrone runner is the reigning European Under-23 Cross-Country champion, and Irish under-23 record holder over 1,500m (3:35.04), the mile (3:52.42), 3,000m (7:32.79) and 5,000m (13:05.75). He’d broken all those records at Under-20 level too. 

His exceptional talent has been known about for many years; in 2022, less than three months after turning 17, Griggs became the youngest Irish runner to break four minutes for the mile, clocking 3:56.40 at the Sport Ireland Arena in Dublin.

Although he had received several offers of a US scholarship before, he’d so far chosen to remain close to home, and for the last two years has attended Ulster University in Belfast, studying sport and exercise sciences, while coached by Mark Kirk. Still, the possibility of a transfer to the US was always in the back of his mind and, prompted this summer by fellow Irish runner Abdel Laadjel, who last year finished up his final season of eligibility at Oregon, moves were swiftly afoot.

At 21, Griggs has already run at the World and European Athletics Championships and the Commonwealth Games, although he narrowly missed out on the Paris Olympics. He also signed a professional contract with Puma, back in 2022, and is looked after by Pace Sports Management, among the biggest professional athlete representatives in the sport. On the good days, he might have picked up a little prize money along the way too. 

Until relatively recently, all this would have gone against the rules of the NCAA. Then in July 2021, in arguably the biggest change in NCAA history, student athletes were allowed to generate their own income from selling their name, image and likeness – otherwise known as the NIL deal.

This has impacted on US athletes to varying degrees, depending on the popularity of their sport, with Miami Hurricanes quarterback Darian Mensah currently boasting the highest NIL deal, reportedly worth around $6.5 million (€5.79 million).

Griggs isn’t in that league, although his signing with Oregon has been met with some curious backlash, and the cause of some debate on both sides on the Atlantic. Partly because of his age (he turns 22 in December), his considerable international experience, and his “pro” contract with Puma, some believe Griggs has no place in the NCAA, or will at least make things a lot harder on young US or other foreign athletes starting out in their college career.

Things are a little different when it comes to football and basketball, as under NCAA rules, any player who has signed with the NFL or NBA is prohibited from returning to college (although some of those cases have gone to court). The NCAA have also revised their age eligibility this season, so that athletes only have a continuous five-year eligibility period from the time they start college. This means, all going to plan, Griggs still has three years of eligibility at Oregon, which will see him through the LA 2028 Olympics. 

[ Nick Griggs takes lessons from finishing ninth as Josh Kerr wins World Indoor 3,000mOpens in new window ]

Some of the backlash on social media has pointed to the fact Oregon is already a powerhouse of US collegiate distance running (and has been going back to Steve Prefontaine in the 1970s), and they shouldn’t be going after an athlete of Griggs’ age or calibre. But again, Griggs isn’t breaking any NCAA rules here, and nor indeed are Oregon, with Griggs himself responding to that with a telling comment: “Don’t hate the player, hate the game ...”

A lot of things have changed since the first Irish athletes went on scholarship to the US, starting back in 1948, with a simple proposition to Jimmy Reardon: “We could sure use you guys at Villanova.”

The story goes that Reardon, a 400m runner and captain of the Irish athletics team at the 1948 London Olympics, was sitting in the dining hall with thrower Cummin Clancy and miler John Joe Barry. They got chatting with US runners George Guida and Browning Ross, both scholarship athletes at Villanova University, just outside of Philadelphia, who reckoned their famous coach Jumbo Elliott would be delighted to snap up these already famous Irish athletes.

In Barry’s autobiography The Ballincurry Hare, a gem long out of print, he recalls how Reardon sparked the idea, before all three sealed the deal: “It was Reardon who put the question to him, ‘George, you’re telling me if you could run or jump well enough, you’d get a scholarship to an American university, which would include full tuition, full board, books, etc?’”

That began what was originally known as the Irish pipeline, with Ronnie Delany soon following in their footsteps, paving the way for the likes Eamonn Coghlan, John Treacy, Marcus O’Sullivan, Frank O’Mara, Sonia O’Sullivan, and more recently, Rhasidat Adeleke. Spreading from the east coast to the west, north and south, and most places in between, the presence of Irish athletes in US colleges, and their success far beyond, has been a constant during those near 80 years since.

Success has never been any barrier to NCAA eligibility in all the years since, and nor was age. Delany, remember, won an Olympic gold medal while in college in the US, his 1,500m triumph in Melbourne in 1956 coming during his last year at Villanova, and in 1978, a 20-year-old Treacy won the World Cross-Country during his final year at Providence College.

Griggs will take any of this backlash in his stride. Currently recovering from a knee injury, he’s used to adversity. After winning silver in the Under-23 race at the 2024 European Cross-Country, he developed a serious knee infection, osteomyelitis. Back in 2021, less than six weeks after losing his older brother Josh in a work accident, he won the European Under-20 3,000m gold in breathtaking style, when still only 16.

And as for Griggs now signing with Oregon, Jumbo Elliott would no doubt have approved.
news.summary: At 21, after four years of running ‘pro’, his signing with Oregon is all within the NCAA rules

news.title: German hauliers squeezed by diesel costs, tolls and slow-paying customers
news.text:
German hauliers are facing a difficult combination of diesel costs, CO₂-related toll charges and lengthy waits for payment, while weak freight demand limits their ability to secure better rates.

For Irish operators carrying goods to and from Germany, the pressures underline the importance of recovering journey costs and keeping a close watch on customer payment terms.

Germany’s road haulage association, BGL, warned in September that higher diesel costs were placing substantial financial strain on small and medium-sized transport businesses. In an appeal to Chancellor Friedrich Merz, it argued that traditionally narrow margins leave many operators unable to absorb sustained cost increases.

BGL is seeking an end to what it describes as a double CO₂ burden through Germany’s national emissions trading system for fuel and the CO₂ component of truck tolls.

The association has also called for a commercial diesel arrangement, with energy taxation reduced to the EU minimum. These are industry demands rather than confirmation of a permanent support package.

For a haulier, the commercial problem is straightforward: diesel and tolls must be funded as journeys take place, but recovering those costs depends on both the agreed transport rate and when the customer pays.

Credit insurer Atradius highlighted this funding gap in its June transport and logistics assessment. It reported that German road freight businesses can face immediate diesel payments while waiting around 60 days for customer invoices to be settled.

With margins below 3%, according to Atradius, financing that gap creates considerable pressure. Its assessment also identifies rising labour costs, driver shortages and strong competition from Central and Eastern Europe as additional challenges.

Lengthy payment terms do not automatically mean an invoice is overdue. However, even customers paying within agreed terms can leave a haulier financing several weeks of operating costs. Any further delay extends that exposure.

At the same time, the German freight market offers limited scope for businesses to grow their way out of trouble.

Deutsche Bahn’s 2026 interim outlook expects German road freight to remain broadly flat this year. It points to a sluggish economy and high cost pressures, with sustained stabilisation in the wider freight market not expected until 2027. The report also highlights continued weakness in key industrial sectors, including automotive and chemicals.

That combination creates a difficult negotiating environment. Operators need rates that reflect their costs, while customers facing their own commercial pressures have an incentive to resist increases.

For Irish hauliers serving the German market, the practical response is to examine the full cost of each movement, including tolls, empty running and waiting time, alongside the payment record of the customer.

Fuel surcharge arrangements also need to respond quickly enough to changing costs. A surcharge recovered weeks after a fuel increase may protect the eventual margin while still leaving an immediate cash-flow gap.

The German experience highlights a familiar vulnerability across European haulage: keeping trucks busy is only commercially sustainable when the rate covers the work and payment arrives in time to fund the next journey.

news.title: 'Fly high, Rob': Tears flow following tragic death of 'exceptional' young Aer Lingus pilot
news.text: Heartbreaking tributes have been paid to a young Aer Lingus pilot from Co Tipperary who tragically passed away earlier this week. Robert 'Rob' Gallagher, who was originally from Roscrea but had been living in Donnybrook, Co Dublin, passed away at home on Wednesday, October 14. A death notice shared on RIP.ie said Robert is "deeply mourned and sadly missed by his heartbroken parents Marian and Gary, brothers Peter and Sam, sisters-in-law Lisa and Sarah, nieces Éabha, Anna and Lily, nephew Ted, aunts Joan Egan, Sally Devlin, June and Mary Gallagher, Rita Delaney, his uncles Liam Delaney, Michael Egan, Jim Feeley and Sean Devlin, extended family and wide circle of friends including colleagues at Aer Lingus." Robert graduated from UCD in 2011 and c ompleted his training to be a pilot at Atlantic Flight Training Academy in December 2016 before he started his first job as First Officer with Norwegian Airways. After a few years working with the Scandinavian airline, the Tipeprary native landed his "dream job" of being a pilot for the flag carrier of Ireland, Aer Lingus. Rob's tragic death has plunged the local community in Roscrea and beyond into mourning, with tributes pouring in for the popular young pilot. A work college of Rob's from Aer Lingus said: " I’m am so sorry to hear of Robs passing. Rob was always a pleasure to fly with. Thinking of all his family friends and work colleagues at this very sad time. May Rob RIP." Another added: " Shocked and saddened about this tragic loss for all of Rob's family, friends and everyone who had the pleasure of knowing Rob. I have the fondest memories of Rob throughout the years as a friend and a colleague. His smile and lovely manner would always make you feel happy, he was full of wit but also kindness. He truly was a lovely person to be around. He will be missed deeply. I’m so sorry for you all. Rest in peace Rob, lots of love." A third person said: " I had the absolute privilege of operating many flights with Rob. He was a truly competent pilot who took great pride in his operation. Most importantly, however, he was a thorough gentleman, and it was always a pleasure to spend time in his company. I am truly saddened to hear of Rob's most untimely passing, he will be missed by all his friends and colleagues at Aer Lingus. Ar dheis Dé go raibh a anam dílis." Another person added: "Sincere condolences to the Gallagher family on the very sad news of Rob’s passing. Had the pleasure of many a flight with Rob, such a likeable and genuinely nice lad with a great interest in the GAA and cars. A wonderful colleague, he will be sadly missed. Rest In Peace, Rob." Another Aer Lingus colleague said: " Rob was an exceptional pilot but more importantly an exceptional person. I had the pleasure of working with Rob on many occasions and he was someone who you always looked forward to spending your working day with. He will be greatly missed by his colleagues in Aer Lingus. Smooth flight home Rob. May you RIP." While a senior Cabin Crew member at Aer Lingus said: " Rob could light up a room & command attention. A lovable rogue with a razor-sharp wit, a brilliant mind & that unmistakably handsome smile. He made even the most ordinary moments memorable. "He always spoke with such love for his family & pride in his Aer Lingus uniform. I'll always remember our laughs about his "big job in the airport pushing buttons". "I feel so fortunate to have known him & to have shared such wonderful memories with him. Some people leave a lasting impression, & Rob was certainly one of those people. "My thoughts & prayers are with you all. Suaimhneas síoraí agus go lonraí solas na bhFlaitheas ort. Go dtuga Dia sólás díbh sna laethanta atá romhaibh. Fly high Rob." Rob will lie in repose in Tierney's Funeral Home, Roscrea (E53 NY70) on Monday evening. Private removal from his residence on Tuesday morning arriving in St. Cronan's Church, Roscrea (E53 PK82) for Funeral Mass at 12 noon. Burial afterwards in Dungar cemetery, Roscrea (E53 Y184). news.title: Full list of 12 food businesses across Ireland ordered to close in September over health concerns
news.text: A total of 12 food businesses in Ireland were served with closure orders last month - including a popular restaurant and takeaway in south Dublin which was ordered to shut down after an "active infestation" was discovered in the kitchen area. Environmental Health Officers in the Health Service Executive (HSE) s erved 12 Closure Orders on food businesses during the month of September for breaches of food safety legislation, pursuant to the FSAI Act, 1998 and the European Union (Official Controls in Relation to Food Legislation) Regulations, 2020. One establishment which was issued with a Closure Order last month was P izza Petito on Orwell Road in Rathgar, Dublin 6. The health inspector's report said: "There is an active infestation of rats in the premises and in particular in the kitchen area. "Rodent droppings were found along the wall on both sides of the kitchen and underneath a food refrigeration unit. "The kitchen was trading at the time of the inspection, with one customer seated eating a freshly cooked pizza. "The droppings were noted to be spread widely across the kitchen." The inspector noted that "rodents are known to carry pathogenic bacteria in their droppings. This poses a risk to public health." The inspector added: "Food stored, produced or sold from this kitchen is likely to be contaminated, unsafe and poses a grave and immediate danger to the public health." The closure order was issued on September 23 and remains in place. It was one of twelve closure orders issued by the Food Safety Authority of Ireland (FSAI) in September. Meanwhile, a smoothie bar and cafe in Dublin was shut after inspectors discovered a cockroach infestation. The Hopsack, located at Swan Leisure Centre, Lower Rathmines Road, Rathmines, Dublin 6, was issued a closure order on September 10 after "all stages of the cockroach infestation from nymph to adulthood was found in the premises during the inspection". Elsewhere, a n Irish school meals provider was hit with a closure order after rodent droppings were found on ovens and in cupboards. The Lunch Bag, which provides hot meals to school children, and was ordered to close by food safety bosses on September 23. The food outlet was shut after inspectors discovered serious violations of food safety legislation, with pest activity and inadequate hygiene among the problems found. The order against The Lunch Bag applied to all areas connected to food business operations at Timahoe GAA in Pairc Mhochua Cremorgan, Timahoe, Portlaoise. In total, ten Closure Orders were served under the FSAI Act, 1998 on: Furlong’s Bar & Lounge & Nellie’s Takeaway, Curracloe, Wexford Fia’s Café, 57 Thomas Street, Prior’s Land, Limerick The Lunch Bag - Timahoe GAA (all areas pertaining to the food business activities) (Service Sector), Timahoe GAA, Pairc Mhochua Cremorgan, Timahoe, Portlaoise Pizza Petito (Takeaway), 9 Orwell Road, Rathgar, Dublin 6 Centra (Retailer), Ardlo Manor, Mullagh, Cavan Summergrove House (All areas pertaining to the food business activities) (B&B used primarily as a private dwelling), Summergrove, Mountmellick, Portlaoise, Laois Everest Kitchen Nepalese (Restaurant/Café), The Friary Bow, Abbey Street, Ennis, Clare The Thatch (Restaurant/Café), Killenard, Portalington, Laois Marka Cadey 2 (Restaurant/Café), 5 Talbot Street, Dublin 1 The Hopsack (Service Sector), Swan Leisure Centre, Lower Rathmines Road, Rathmines, Dublin 6 Meanwhile, two Closure Orders were served under European Union (Official Controls in Relation to Food Legislation) Regulations, 2020 on: Eskimo Pizza and Indian (Takeaway), Main Street, Ballyheigue, Kerry J2 Sushi & Bento (Restaurant/Café), 75 Main Street, Swords, County Dublin Among the reasons for the Closure Orders in September are: evidence of pest activity, including an active cockroach infestation at all stages of the life cycle; dead cockroaches found on traps beneath the ready-to-eat food service area and in the pot-wash and dish-wash areas; a dead rodent found directly in front of a fridge containing beverages; two dead mice at different stages of decomposition behind a shelving unit in a food storage room, with rodent droppings noted on shelving and preparation surfaces where food utensils and beverages were stored; failure to provide adequate hand-washing facilities. Details of the food businesses served with Enforcement Orders are published on the FSAI’s website . Closure Orders and Improvement Orders will remain listed in the enforcement reports on the website for a period of three months from the date of when a premises is adjudged to have corrected its food safety issue, with Prohibition Orders being listed for a period of one month. news.title: Pharmacist explains how to tell if you have Covid or flu as cases rise
news.text: Experiencing a sore throat, headache and muscle aches can leave you questioning whether you've come down with a seasonal bug or something more serious. With Covid-19 infections on the rise once more across Ireland, people might be inclined to self-diagnose based on how they're feeling, but medical professionals warn that symptoms frequently overlap. 'American Covid', the latest strain of the virus, now accounts for more than half of all cases in Ireland. The XFG variant was first detected in January 2025 and earned its nickname after spreading rapidly across the United States last year. The strain is now responsible for 55% of cases here in Ireland. Dr Neel Patel, Associate Medical Director at LloydsPharmacy Online Doctor, suggests that the duration and progression of an illness might provide some indication, though these factors alone cannot definitively identify which infection you're dealing with. He explained: "People with flu normally feel very unwell for two or three days and will continue to experience symptoms for around another five days. "After that, you may feel tired and run down for a further two or three weeks. However, people with coronavirus usually begin to show symptoms five to six days after being exposed, and symptoms commonly last up to two weeks." Dr Patel also warned that the two illnesses can be difficult to distinguish, stating: "It can be difficult to tell coronavirus apart from the flu as they share many of the same symptoms; however, they may feel more intense than having the flu." The NHS lists fever, cough, tiredness, aches, headache and a sore throat amongst potential Covid-19 symptoms, many of which can also present with flu , reports the Mirror . The only dependable method of checking for Covid-19 is to take a test, rather than relying solely on how long symptoms last. Dr Patel noted: "While Covid-19 tests are no longer freely available on the NHS, you can still buy lateral flow, PCR and antibody tests online." Free testing remains accessible through certain pharmacies for those eligible for Covid-19 treatment, while others are able to purchase tests from pharmacies and retailers. Dr Patel advises that urgent medical attention is required for difficulty breathing at rest, confusion, loss of consciousness or unusual drowsiness, persistent chest pain or pressure, cold or blue-tinged skin, or a sudden loss of speech or movement. The NHS recommends calling 999 for severe breathing difficulties, sudden chest pain, collapse or other potentially life-threatening symptoms. news.summary: With Covid-19 cases rising again in Ireland, people may be tempted to judge their illness by how they feel, but experts warn that symptoms can overlap

news.title: TV chef Neven Maguire opens up about losing his parents and how 'faith' helped him navigate his grief
news.text: Celebrity chef Neven Maguire has opened up about losing his parents and said his “faith” helped him navigate through his grief. The 52-year-old lost his dad, Joe, following a car crash in 1999, while his mum, Vera, died from lung cancer in 2012. Neven revealed he’s since fundraised more than €200,000 for Target Lung Cancer - an ongoing fundraising and awareness initiative operated by the St. James's Hospital Foundation in Dublin. Speaking to the Grief Pod with Venetia Quick, he said: “I remember growing up, we'd say the rosary as a family; we'd be having the craic, you know, young kids you didn't probably know the words, having the craic. “But definitely faith was a big part of our family and still is to this day … which I'm proud of. “I just think it keeps your family together - your faith. It's the way I've grown up and what I believe in, to be honest with you. I'm proud of it.” When asked to describe the impact of his father’s death on his mum, Neven explained: “She was heartbroken and you see the way he suffered and how, how sudden it was, the shock, like he was alive on a Friday, he was gone on a Monday. “That was really, really tough. I suppose she would have been numb for a long time. “I mean that in a nice way because they were very happily married, and rearing a big family.” He then went on to reveal that his Vera was nearly killed in a freak accident a couple of years later. Neven added: “She had her own tragedy …this could be now, let me see, about maybe seven or eight years afterwards, walking across the road and a wheel came off a car and hit her in the back of the head. “It was one of the freakiest accidents. I was in Galway , and I got the phone call to say, listen, your mom's in intensive care, and I said, 'oh no, not again, please.' “So we all went up to the Royal in Belfast , and then she was transferred to Enniskillen, but she was really lucky to be alive.” He said she was diagnosed with lung cancer, which eventually became more advanced, but stressed his mum made peace with dying and was happy because she would be with her husband Joe again. Neven added: “(The lung cancer) came back, you know, quite quickly and took her in the end. “I remember her saying, ‘I'm not afraid of dying. I'm going to go and meet my husband, Joe.’ I thought that's very powerful. “I thought that was a very powerful thing and gave us great comfort as a family.” Subscribe to our newsletter for the latest news from the Irish Mirror direct to your inbox: Sign up here .
news.summary: The 52-year-old lost his dad, Joe, following a car crash in 1999, while his mum, Vera, died from lung cancer in 2012
news.author: Danny de Vaal

news.title: Social welfare Ireland: Parents urged to apply for increased Child Support Payment of €336 a month
news.text: Thousands of parents qualify for a soon-to-be enhanced weekly payment, provided for each child. The Child Support Payment, previously known as the Increase for a Qualified Child, will experience a rate rise next January. This change was announced as part of Budget 2027, and if you meet the criteria, this payment can be added to your current social welfare claim. Parents could receive up to €84 per child each week, or €336 monthly. Here's everything you need to know about it and how to apply Your social welfare payment comprises a weekly sum for yourself, known as the personal rate. You may also qualify for an extra amount for your child, termed a Child Support Payment (CSP) , reports RSVP Live . The CSP was formerly called an Increase for a Qualified Child or IQC. To qualify for a Child Support Payment (CSP), your child must: be resident in the State not be in legal custody satisfy the age condition for that payment live with you Your child doesn't have to be financially dependent on you. Your child can work and earn income, without affecting the increase paid to you. CSP can be claimed for foster children. However, you generally won't receive a CSP if your child is receiving their own social welfare payment, except in particular circumstances. You won't get a Child Support Payment (CSP) with the following payments:. You won't receive a CSP if your spouse, civil partner or cohabitant's gross income surpasses €400, and you're receiving one of the following payments: Working Family Payment Guardian's Payment (Contributory) Guardian's Payment (Non-Contributory) Widow's, Widower's or Surviving Civil Partner's (Non-Contributory) Pension Death Benefit by way of Orphan’s Payment If your child is aged 18 or over, you can continue to get Child Support Payment for three months after he or she leaves second level education or finishes the Leaving Certificate, provided that they are not getting a social welfare payment in their own right. Child Support Payment can continue to be paid if your child starts work immediately after finishing school. Since January 2026, the Child Support Payment (CSP) stands at €58 weekly for children under 12, and €78 weekly for children over 12. Half rates are also available. In January 2027, the Child Support Payment will increase: By €6 from €58 to €64 for children under 12 years of age By €6 from €78 to €84 for children aged 12 years and over To get a Child Support Payment, you must give details your dependent child on your claim form when applying for a social welfare payment. If you failed to claim for your dependent child when submitting your initial claim, you should contact the section within the Department of Social Protection that manages your social welfare payment, or your local Intreo or Branch office. news.summary: The Child Support Payment, formerly known as the Increase for a Qualified Child, will see a rate increase next January as part of Budget 2027

news.title: HSE in talks to fund weight-loss drug Mounjaro for over one million patients across Ireland
news.text: Senior HSE officials gathered this week for a meeting to determine whether funding should be provided to enable Irish patients to obtain the weight-loss medication Mounjaro. While the medication is currently available on prescription, it cannot be reimbursed for Medical Card holders or for its application as a weight-loss treatment under the Drugs Payment Scheme. The HSE meeting will assist in establishing whether the medication should secure funding through these schemes, thus making it accessible to eligible Irish patients either without charge or at a subsidised rate. If given the green light, the scheme is projected to cost up to €3 billion, with over one million patients throughout Ireland potentially qualifying for the prescription. However, experts supporting the medication's approval maintain the advantages would significantly exceed the expenditure. The medication's producer, Eli Lilly, has liaised with the HSE in recent months regarding pricing proposals, and Professor Michael Barry from the National Centre for Pharmacoeconomics indicated the discounted price could render the medication a cost-effective investment, reports Cork Beo . Speaking on RTÉ this week, Professor Barry emphasised how weight loss enhances blood pressure, reduces the likelihood of diabetes and decreases people's chances of developing cancer. The professor also pointed out that the medication could prove especially beneficial for those with Down syndrome, as the weight reduction triggered by the medication could lower their dementia risk. More broadly, however, Professor Barry contends that the far-reaching advantages of widespread weight loss would be more nuanced, as a healthier population would conserve money and resources throughout the health service. It has been suggested that the drug be made accessible to those with a BMI exceeding 30, or those with a BMI of 27 alongside additional risk factors, such as cardiovascular disease or pre-diabetes. At this week's gathering, the HSE received testimony from specialists at the National Centre for Pharmacoeconomics as part of their deliberations, with the group set to reach a final verdict after carefully considering the input of several expert panels. However, no recommendation has been yet made to the HSE Senior Leadership Team on whether public patients should get it. news.summary: The HSE has convened a meeting to discuss whether funding should be allocated to help Irish patients access the weight-loss drug Mounjaro

news.title: M&S shoppers snap up 'best quality' €42 Christmas pyjamas that are 'so soft and warm'
news.text: Marks and Spencer is turning heads amongst shoppers following the launch of its latest Christmas pyjamas, praised as "so soft and warm" and of the "best quality". The Brushed Cotton Checked Christmas Family Pyjamas come in sizes to suit the entire household. The timeless pyjamas showcase a traditional red check design with a long-sleeved button-up top and comfortable elasticated waistband trousers. Made from 100% cotton, they offer equal measures of cosiness and breathability, ideal for nightly use throughout the colder months or saving for Christmas Eve. Available for €42 , the adult options span from size 6 to 22, with short, regular and long lengths on offer. The children's range covers 1-2 years through to 15-16 years, priced between €18 and €20 . Receiving nothing but five-star reviews thus far on the M&S website, one customer said of the pyjamas : " Cosy pjs . Lovely cosy winter pyjamas . Available in shorter length and the perfect size. Very comfortable to wear." Another customer said: "Feel so soft and warm. Material is excellent and good value and so nice for winter I would definitely recommend.", While a third customer added: "Best quality! This is not the kind of flannel you get with cheap pjs. This is a nice hefty smooth fabric that is holding up well to washing. The length did shrink significantly, but happily the 'average' length was extra long before washing, so they're perfect. Nicely finished details and so lovely to have roomy pockets for my phone!" Meanwhile, Next features the Ecru Happy Holidays Matching Family Christmas Short Sleeve Pyjamas which combine red, green, and white striped trousers with a comfortable white T-shirt adorned with a festive graphic. The children's sizes range from €13 - €21.50 , while the ladies' sizes are €36, and the gentlemen's are €35. Matalan similarly offers several choices including the Navy Check Matching Family Christmas Pyjamas and the Beige Gingham Gingerbread Matching Family Christmas Pyjamas. In additional M&S updates, customers have been adoring the recently launched Fairisle Funnel Neck Christmas Jumper With Wool , €47 , which boasts a classic fairisle pattern with a contemporary funnel neck. Crafted in a soft grey tone with a wool blend material, it features a relaxed fit, rendering it a warm and comfortable option. Shoppers have been purchasing the jumper to style with jeans throughout the winter months, insisting it's "too nice to save for Christmas." Sizes span from extra small to extra large, with full stock availability at the time of writing, reports the Liverpool Echo . news.summary: Marks and Spencer's new Brushed Cotton Checked Christmas Family Pyjamas are flying off the shelves, with shoppers praising their softness, warmth and best-in-class quality

news.title: €495k Clonakilty home is an A-rated West Cork renovation success story
news.text:
While this four-bed home is eye-catching with its crisp neatness inside and out, if you want to be really impressed then have a look at the older versions of Google Streetview. Seeing what it’s been developed from really helps you appreciate this four-bed Daffodil House at Ahidelake, Middle Ring, just outside Clonakilty.

From a pretty typical 1970s bungalow which had been let fall into disrepair to an A2-rated sleek yet warm home — all the hard work has been done here.

Liam Harnedy of Bantry-based Liam Harnedy Construction took on the task, in late 2024 (for €191k according to the Property Price Register).

Since then, the house, which is a five-minute walk from the coastal village of Ring and a 10-minute spin to Clonakilty town, has been extended and totally renovated to 1250 sq ft. New flooring, underfloor heating, new kitchen, insulation and a switch from oil heating to air-to-water heating are among the upgrades.

There are new windows and doors throughout too and the energy rating is commendable.

Outside too has been totally refreshened with overgrowth cleared — though mature trees and an attractive old drystone wall have been maintained.

“This has been a super job, there was a small driveway but you have more than enough space for parking now and the house itself is lovely altogether with external insulation at the front and a modern extension,” notes Keith O’Sullivan of Hodnett Forde Property Services.

The L-shaped layout means that the patio doors look south and the back of the €495k house gets the morning light, with evening light in the three bedrooms at the front of the house. There’s also one bedroom at the back of the property. Three rooflights bring great light into the large kitchen/dining room.

Interest so far is coming from quite a variety of sectors says Mr O’Sullivan: “We have young couples who are currently selling or thinking of selling their homes in the town as they want to move a bit further out and have more space while still being close to Clonakilty.”

“As well as locals we also have interest from people living in Britain as well as Offaly, Wicklow, Dublin and Cork city, many with connections to the West Cork area — and they’re all drawn to the fact that it’s a turnkey property. All the viewers so far are looking at this as a permanent home.”
news.summary: Daffodil House's transformation to a modern coastal home is impressive — especially when you see the 'before' pictures below
news.author: Caroline Delaney,Irishexaminer.com
